stem: A 35-year-old woman has an enlarging left-sided neck swelling, 9 kg weight loss, lethargy, and a diffuse, rubbery, firm mass in the left anterior triangle with cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy.
explanation: Lymphoma presents with rubbery lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms.
topics: Thyroglossal cyst; Branchial cyst; Lymphadenopathy; Cystic hygroma

stem: A 28-year-old woman, a smoker with five children (all breast-fed), has had bloody nipple discharge from the right breast for 6 months. At times the area swells with a foul-smelling discharge; antibiotics did not help. Tests show mildly dilated multiple lactiferous ducts. What is the management?
explanation: Duct ectasia/periductal mastitis is benign: reassure, stop smoking and follow up; total duct excision only for persistent discharge or recurrent sepsis.

stem: A 28-year-old woman, a smoker with five children (all breast-fed), has had bloody nipple discharge from the right breast for 6 months. At times the area swells with a foul-smelling discharge; antibiotics did not help. Which of the following is NOT useful in investigating her condition?
explanation: Triple assessment (examination, ultrasound/mammography, cytology) suffices; MRI adds nothing in benign duct ectasia.

stem: A 28-year-old woman, a smoker with five children (all breast-fed), has had bloody nipple discharge from the right breast for 6 months. At times the area swells with a foul-smelling discharge; antibiotics did not help. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Smoking, multiparity and multiple dilated ducts with discharge and recurrent periareolar inflammation are typical of duct ectasia/periductal mastitis.

source: Bailey Breast and Neck lumps MCQ
stem: Which of the following statements are true? (Benign Breast Disease)
option_A: Nipple retraction always indicates an underlying malignancy.
option_B: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause for lactational mastitis.
option_C: Fibroadenomas should always be offered excision, as they are associated with a high risk of malignancy.
option_D: The histology of phyllodes tumour may be benign, intermediate or malignant.
option_E: Blood-stained nipple discharge is usually due to a breast carcinoma.
answer_text: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause for lactational mastitis. | The histology of phyllodes tumour may be benign, intermediate or malignant.
explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the usual cause of lactational mastitis and phyllodes tumours may be benign, intermediate or malignant.

stem: You are a house officer in breast surgery and are clerking in a 45-year-old woman for excision of a benign breast lump. She has no known past medical or surgical history. Which investigation is most highly recommended prior to her surgery?
explanation: NICE guidance suggests no routine tests if no comorbidities/low-risk surgery.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a unilateral erythematous, itchy rash around her nipple and inversion of the nipple. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: (Paget disease of nipple) Unilateral eczematous rash of nipple often indicates Paget (DCIS).
topics: Paget disease of the nipple; DCIS

stem: A 35-year-old woman has a lump in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast that becomes tender pre-menses. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Cyclic breast pain/lumpiness, worse pre-menses.

stem: A 31-year-old woman has a nontender, rubbery, mobile lump in her left breast. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: ‘Breast mouse’: rubbery, mobile, painless.

stem: A 67-year-old woman 2 weeks post breast-conserving surgery notices a painless lump beneath the incision, nontender, firm, well-circumscribed. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Benign post-trauma/surgery; can mimic recurrence but typically non-tender.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has a tense, mobile breast lump that yields straw-coloured fluid on fine-needle aspiration. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Discrete tense lump with straw-coloured fluid on aspiration.

stem: A 34-year-old female smoker has a green discharge from both nipples, with nipple retraction and lumpiness. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Greenish discharge + retraction in smokers => duct ectasia.

stem: A middle-aged woman has a serous discharge from one nipple on deep palpation. The breast otherwise appears normal. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Serous or bloodstained discharge from a single duct.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has a discrete tense, mobile breast lump suspicious of a cyst. Which investigation is most appropriate?
explanation: Best to distinguish solid vs cystic, especially <35 yrs (dense breasts).

stem: A 52-year-old woman has a large painless breast lump, fleshy with a tear-drop shape. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Leaf-like tumour, can be large/fleshy, tear-drop shape.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with multiple bilateral breast swellings which cause discomfort, particularly just before her periods. They have been present for several years but appear to be getting worse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Multiple painful nodular changes related to menstrual cycle are characteristic of fibrocystic disease.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with subareolar pain in the left breast and occasional blood-stained nipple discharge. Examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A small tumour in the lactiferous duct often presents with bloody discharge and no palpable lump.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents with a single lump in the left breast that has been present for 6 months. On examination, there is a 3 cm smooth lump in the upper outer quadrant, mobile and not attached to the skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A painless, mobile ‘breast mouse’ that is common in younger women.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with 3 weeks of left nipple discharge, described as thick and greenish. No mass is palpable. Beta-hCG is negative. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Greenish discharge from dilated subareolar ducts is typical of duct ectasia.

stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to see you at the GP practice having noticed a lump in the right breast. She is concerned that it may be cancer. On examination, you find a smooth, mobile, non-tender mass around 2 cm in diameter in the upper outer quadrant of the breast. There are no overlying skin changes. Which would be the most appropriate action to take?
option_A: Advise the patient to return if the lump gets bigger or starts becoming painful
option_C: Reassure the patient that there is no evidence the lump is cancerous and discharge her
option_D: Refer the patient for urgent mammography
option_E: Refer the patient for urgent ultrasound scan
answer_text: Refer the patient for urgent ultrasound scan
explanation: Younger women have denser breasts, so ultrasound is more sensitive than mammography.

stem: A 22-year old woman presents to the GP complaining of a 2-week history of milky discharge from both her breasts. She is otherwise well. Clinical examination of the breasts is unremarkable and a pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following investigations would be indicated in the first instance?
explanation: Bilateral galactorrhoea suggests hyperprolactinaemia; serum prolactin is first-line test.

stem: A 51-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of right breast blood-tinged nipple discharge from a single duct; mammogram is negative, cytology is non-diagnostic, ductogram shows a solitary filling defect. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Intraductal papilloma Solitary papilloma is the most common cause of pathologic nipple discharge in one duct.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management for the intraductal papilloma?
option_A: collection of discharge for repeat cytologic analysis
option_B: observation, with repeat examination and imaging in 3–6 months
option_D: central lumpectomy (including removal of the nipple/areolar complex)
explanation: Terminal duct excision (microdochectomy) Definitive diagnosis and treatment by excision of the involved duct.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with right breast pain localized to the nipple areolar complex with a subareolar fluid collection. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Presentation is consistent with periductal mastitis.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of the breast mass?
option_A: aspiration of the fluid and antibiotics
option_B: central lumpectomy, axillary node dissection, and radiation therapy
option_D: antibiotics alone with re-evaluation in 1 week
answer_text: aspiration of the fluid and antibiotics
explanation: Management of periductal mastitis with abscess involves aspiration and antibiotics.

stem: A 33-year-old woman with a 2-month left breast mass that is firm, mobile, and well-defined is most consistent with?
explanation: The features most closely match a fibroadenoma.

stem: What management is recommended for the above breast mass?
option_B: re-examination after the next menstrual cycle
explanation: Needle biopsy is advised to confirm the diagnosis.

stem: A 36-year-old multiparous woman attends your clinic with a 7-day history of left breast pain after being involved in a car accident. On examining her breast, you notice a 3-cm hard, irregular, immobile, and tender lump. You also notice some skin tethering and overlying bruising at the region of the lump. Ultrasound features suggest a benign pathology. The most likely diagnosis at this point is:
explanation: A hard, tethered, tender lump with bruising after trauma is fat necrosis; it mimics carcinoma clinically, so triple assessment (imaging ± core biopsy) is still required.

stem: A 32-year-old woman came to the breast clinic with five weeks history of redness and swelling around the right nipple. There is no past medical history but she is a heavy smoker. On examination, there is peri-areolar skin inflammation with a small palpable tender mass just behind the nipple. The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation: Presentation and smoking history indicate peri-ductal mastitis.

stem: A 36-year-old woman complains of a 3-month history of bloody discharge from the nipple. On examination, a small nodule is found deep to the areola. Careful palpation of the nipple-areola complex results in blood appearing at one duct. Mammogram findings are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Bloody discharge with a nodule suggests intraductal papilloma.

stem: A 40-year-old woman has had 3 weeks of unilateral breast pain. The pain has been constant with no relation to her menstrual cycle. She has a past medical history of asthma with a recent episode of exacerbation. There is no evidence of any discrete lumps or axillary lymphadenopathy. There is localized tenderness on palpation of the medial half of the left breast and over the 4th and 5th costochondral junctions. Which is the single most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Tietze’s syndrome is the most likely diagnosis.

stem: A 50-year-old woman has had intermittent nipple discharge. She has noticed that the discharge seems to be coming from one point on the left nipple. The discharge is slightly blood-stained. There are no discrete lumps and no axillary lymphadenopathy. On gentle squeezing of the left nipple there is a single point of discharge. A mammogram is normal. Which is the single most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Duct papilloma occurs within large, central mammary lactiferous ducts and presents with nipple discharge and small-volume bleeding.

stem: A 49-year-old woman undergoes biopsy of a 5.0-cm left breast mass; she has no palpable axillary lymph nodes. Biopsy of the mass shows cystosarcoma phyllodes. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
option_E: Simple mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy
explanation: Cystosarcoma phyllodes tumors are treated with wide local excision with at least 1-cm margins.

stem: A 51-year-old (premenopausal) woman undergoes needle localization biopsy for microcalcifications. Pathology reveals sclerosing adenosis. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
option_C: Simple mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy
option_D: Lumpectomy with axillary lymph node dissection and radiation therapy
explanation: Sclerosing adenosis is a benign lesion and does not require further treatment.

stem: A 55-year-old man with known atrial fibrillation presents to his general practitioner with a 3-month history of gynaecomastia. Which of his following medications is not associated with gynaecomastia?
explanation: Furosemide is not typically associated with gynaecomastia, unlike the other medications listed.

stem: A worried 23-year-old woman, who started taking the combined contraceptive pill 3 months ago, presents with a 1-day history of discovering a painless lump in the right breast. The patient states that the lump was not there a month ago. On examination, a slightly mobile, discrete, well‐defined, non‐tender, firm 1 cm diameter lump is found. There is no lymphadenopathy. The most likely diagnosis here is
explanation: Fibroadenomas typically occur in young women presenting as painless, mobile, firm lumps, differentiating them from cysts, lipomas, and carcinomas.

stem: A 36-year-old nulliparous woman attends your clinic with a 7-day history of left breast pain after being involved in a car accident. On examining her breast, you notice a hard, irregular 3 cm, immobile, tender lump. You also notice some skin tethering and overlying bruising in the region of the lump. Ultrasound features suggest a benign pathology. The most likely diagnosis at this point is
explanation: Recent trauma with bruising and tenderness indicates fat necrosis rather than carcinoma or other pathology.

stem: A 33-year-old, non-smoking, breastfeeding woman is 10 days postpartum. She has a 4-day history of a slight crack on the surface of her left nipple. She presents with a 2-day history of severe continuous pain in the left breast, spiking pyrexia up to 38.8 with rigours which has prevented her from sleeping. On examination, you find the outer quadrants of the left breast to be red, warm and tender with a hard 3 cm lump at the edge of the left nipple. The most likely diagnosis is
explanation: In a lactating woman with a nipple crack and severe localized pain, the findings favor a breast abscess over other conditions.

stem: A 43-year-old woman presents to your clinic with a 2-month history of localized dull pain in the right breast. The pain intensifies just before her period. On examination, you find a discrete 2.5 cm mobile, tense, tender, fluctuant lump in the lower inner quadrant of the right breast. The most likely diagnosis here is
explanation: A mobile, fluctuant lump in a woman over 40 suggests a benign breast cyst.

stem: A 47-year-old perimenopausal woman presents with a 3-week history of green discharge from the right nipple. On examination, the right nipple is non-tender, has a ‘slit-like’ appearance and is retracted. The most likely diagnosis is
explanation: The slit-like nipple with green discharge in a perimenopausal woman points to mammary duct ectasia.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to your clinic after discovering, for the first time, two lumps in the inner lower quadrant of her left breast. On examination you find these lumps to be 2 cm in size, solid, discrete, mobile and non-tender. The right breast is normal and there is no lymphadenopathy. The most appropriate course of management is
option_B: Reassure the patient and discharge her
option_C: Request an ultrasound of the left breast
answer_text: Request an ultrasound of the left breast
explanation: In a 25-year-old with new breast lumps, ultrasound is the most appropriate next step in triple assessment.

stem: A 21-year-old nulliparous woman presents to your clinic with a 1-month history of bilateral breast pain. The pain, which is dull and achy in nature, is poorly localized and widespread across both breasts. The pain gradually increases in severity and is worse just before her menses. The pain usually starts to get better once her menses start. On examination, both breasts are tender. There are no lumps, skin changes or obvious swellings. The most likely diagnosis here is
explanation: Bilateral breast pain that worsens premenstrually is characteristic of cyclical mastalgia.

stem: A 25-year-old woman is diagnosed with a 1.5 cm palpable area of fat necrosis of the left breast by core biopsy following a traumatic injury 14 days earlier. She has slight bruising of the lower outer quadrant of the left breast with moderate tenderness. What would be the most appropriate course of management?
option_B: Follow-up appointment for ultrasound in 3 months
option_E: Follow-up appointment for ultrasound in 6 months
explanation: Traumatic fat necrosis usually resolves without intervention, thus reassurance and discharge is appropriate.

stem: A 38-year-old woman, and mother of two healthy children, is diagnosed with a fluid-filled simple cyst after triple assessment. On ultrasound the inner surface of the cyst looks entirely smooth. The woman does not have any significant family history of carcinoma and the cyst is located in the outer-lower quadrant of the right breast. What would be the most appropriate course of action?
explanation: A simple cyst (smooth wall, anechoic) after triple assessment needs no follow-up: aspirate if symptomatic and discharge; complex or recurrent cysts need biopsy.

stem: A 30-year-old woman who is 12 days postpartum and breastfeeding is diagnosed with acute mastitis of the left breast. Four days earlier, she discovered a painful crack in the region of the left nipple and noticed that the surrounding skin was tender, warm and red in colour. The patient is not allergic to penicillin and you decide to prescribe a course of antibiotics. What would be the most appropriate antibiotic for treating this condition?
explanation: In a breastfeeding woman with acute mastitis, flucloxacillin is the treatment of choice.

stem: After a triple assessment, including core biopsy, a 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with a fibroadenoma of the left breast. The patient has a significant family history of breast carcinoma. The non-tender lump is situated in the inner lower quadrant of the left breast. The lump is approximately 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm. What is the most appropriate course of management?
option_C: The patient should be given the choice of excision or not and if not she could be discharged
option_E: Perform triple assessment again in 6 weeks
answer_text: The patient should be given the choice of excision or not and if not she could be discharged
explanation: A core-biopsy-proven fibroadenoma under 3 cm can be left; excision is offered by patient choice or if large, growing or symptomatic. Family history alone is not an indication.

stem: A 45-year-old perimenopausal woman is diagnosed with mammary duct ectasia of the right breast after having had small and infrequent amounts of milky green discharge from multiple ducts of the right nipple for over 2 months. The patient has no significant family history and mammography findings are normal. What is the most appropriate course of management?
option_B: Surgical resection of the duct system of the right breast (Hadfield’s operation)
option_D: Perform mammography of the right breast in 3 months
explanation: Normal findings in mammary duct ectasia warrant reassurance and discharge.

stem: A 48-year-old perimenopausal woman presents with a 2-month history of a painful lump in her right breast. On examination you find a 2.5 cm tense, fluctuant, mobile lump in the outer lower quadrant of the right breast. The most appropriate next course of action is
explanation: In a woman over 35, combined mammography and ultrasound is the appropriate next step.

stem: A 34-year-old premenopausal woman presents to your clinic with a lump in her right breast. On examination you find a 2.5 cm fluctuant, mobile, tender lump in the inner lower quadrant of the right breast. The ultrasound report suggests a benign fluid-filled cyst. The most appropriate course of action is
explanation: For a benign cystic lesion on ultrasound, fine needle aspiration is the next appropriate step.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has a 3-month painless lump in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast and nipple retraction for 2 weeks. Core biopsy of a palpable axillary node shows invasive carcinoma, hormone-receptor negative; PET shows no metastasis. What is the best next step in management?
explanation: Node-positive cancer with nipple involvement needs mastectomy with axillary clearance; neoadjuvant chemotherapy is often given first for ER-negative disease.

stem: 8 months after her surgery she has difficulty raising her arm and her medial scapula is prominent. What is the cause?
option_C: Tear of the long head of biceps
explanation: Winging of the scapula follows injury to the long thoracic nerve (serratus anterior) during axillary dissection; thoracodorsal injury weakens latissimus dorsi.

source: Bailey Breast and Neck lumps MCQ
stem: Which of the following statements are false? (Carcinoma of the breast)
option_A: Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) increases the risk of breast cancer.
option_B: Inflammatory breast cancer is caused by infection in the breast.
option_C: Medullary carcinoma in the breast is associated with a poor prognosis.
option_D: Van Nuy’s scoring system is used to decide further management after local excision in patients with ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS).
option_E: Oestrogen receptor negative tumours are treated with tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors.
answer_text: Inflammatory breast cancer is caused by infection in the breast. | Medullary carcinoma in the breast is associated with a poor prognosis. | Oestrogen receptor negative tumours are treated with tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors.
explanation: Inflammatory breast cancer is not infective, medullary carcinoma has a better prognosis and ER-negative tumours do not respond to hormone therapy.
topics: Inflammatory breast cancer; Breast cancer; Medullary thyroid carcinoma

source: Bailey Breast and Neck lumps MCQ
stem: Which of the following statements are true? (Carcinoma of the breast)
option_A: Paget’s disease of the breast is usually associated with an underlying invasive carcinoma.
option_B: The survival outcome following breast-conserving treatment and mastectomy are equal.
option_C: Positive resected margins are a significant predictor of recurrence after breast-conserving surgery.
option_D: Sentinel lymph node biopsy should not be offered in clinically node-negative axilla.
option_E: The pectoralis minor and major muscles are removed in Patey’s mastectomy.
answer_text: Paget’s disease of the breast is usually associated with an underlying invasive carcinoma. | The survival outcome following breast-conserving treatment and mastectomy are equal. | Positive resected margins are a significant predictor of recurrence after breast-conserving surgery.
explanation: Paget’s disease is usually linked to underlying invasive carcinoma, survival is equivalent between breast‐conserving therapy and mastectomy, and positive margins increase recurrence risk.
topics: Paget disease of the nipple; Mastectomy; Breast cancer

source: Bailey Breast and Neck lumps MCQ
stem: Which of the following statements are false? (Carcinoma of the Breast)
option_A: Adjuvant chemotherapy is not given to post-menopausal women with ER-positive breast cancer.
option_B: Tamoxifen reduces the risk of contralateral breast cancer.
option_C: Cyclophosphamide chemotherapy is as effective as anthracycline- and taxane-based chemotherapy.
option_D: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy improves breast conservation rates in women with slightly larger primary tumour.
answer_text: Adjuvant chemotherapy is not given to post-menopausal women with ER-positive breast cancer. | Cyclophosphamide chemotherapy is as effective as anthracycline- and taxane-based chemotherapy.
explanation: False: post-menopausal ER-positive women may still need chemotherapy, and anthracycline/taxane regimens beat cyclophosphamide alone. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy does increase breast conservation.

source: Bailey Breast and Neck lumps MCQ
stem: Which of the following statements are true? (Carcinoma of the Breast)
option_A: Lymphoedema in the arm after treatment usually indicates a recurrence.
option_B: Radiotherapy after implant reconstruction of the breast gives poor cosmetic results.
option_C: Chemotherapy is safe in second and third trimester in women with pregnancy-associated breast cancer.
option_D: Male breast cancer carries a poor prognosis when compared with female breast cancer.
answer_text: Radiotherapy after implant reconstruction of the breast gives poor cosmetic results. | Chemotherapy is safe in second and third trimester in women with pregnancy-associated breast cancer. | Male breast cancer carries a poor prognosis when compared with female breast cancer.
explanation: Radiotherapy can worsen cosmetic outcomes post-implant, chemotherapy is safe in later pregnancy and male breast cancer often has a poorer prognosis.

stem: A 57-year-old woman with strong family history of breast cancer is told certain chromosomes are linked. Which chromosome is most associated?
explanation: BRCA1 on 17q, BRCA2 on 13q linked with breast cancer.

stem: A 45-year-old woman asks about screening mammograms in the UK. At what ages do women undergo screening as part of the National Programme?
explanation: The NHS Breast Screening Programme invites women aged 50 to 70 (up to their 71st birthday) for mammography every 3 years.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with a 5 cm right breast lump and fixed axillary nodes, no supraclavicular nodes, moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma, no distant mets. What is the TNM stage?
explanation: Large tumour + fixed ipsilateral axillary nodes, no metastasis => Stage 3.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with a 4 cm breast lump, no palpable nodes. Wide excision and clearance show well-differentiated tumour, no lymph involvement. Approx 5-year survival?
explanation: A 4-cm node-negative well-differentiated tumour is T2N0 (stage IIA); about 70% 5-year survival in the source (higher with modern adjuvant therapy).

stem: A 64-year-old woman with a painless breast lump, skin dimpling, nipple retraction. Biopsy: adenocarcinoma with fibrosis. Most common type?
explanation: Most common histological type is invasive ductal carcinoma.

stem: A 39-year-old woman has left-sided breast cancer, ER–, well-differentiated, ~6.5 cm, ipsilateral nodes, no distant mets. Next step?
option_A: Neoadjuvant chemo then surgery + axillary clearance
answer_text: Neoadjuvant chemo then surgery + axillary clearance
explanation: Stage III ER– tumour => neoadjuvant chemo + definitive surgery.

stem: A middle-aged woman has a scaly red rash on her nipple/areola, sore, bleeds occasionally. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Scaly erythematous nipple lesion is classic Paget’s of breast (DCIS).
topics: Paget disease of the nipple; DCIS

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with itchy, dry skin around the left areola. On examination, the skin is dry and cracked, and there appears to be a 1 cm nodule underlying the affected area. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Eczematous changes of the nipple plus a subareolar lump suggest Paget disease of the breast.

stem: A 46-year-old pre-menopausal woman has a 5 cm lump over her right breast which has been confirmed to be an invasive tumour. She is otherwise fit and well. Which is the next most appropriate course of action?
explanation: Large tumours (>4 cm) typically require mastectomy rather than breast-conserving surgery.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has suspicious calcifications on a screening mammogram but denies any breast masses or symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis (based on Figure 6-3)?
option_B: lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) with or without an invasive component
option_C: ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) with or without an invasive component
explanation: Coarse popcorn-like calcifications are characteristic of a degenerating fibroadenoma.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management (same mammogram scenario)?
option_A: observation, with repeat mammogram in 6–12 months
option_D: lumpectomy, radiation therapy, and sentinel lymph node (SLN) biopsy
answer_text: observation, with repeat mammogram in 6–12 months
explanation: Characteristic benign calcifications require only follow-up imaging to confirm stability.

stem: A 56-year-old woman presents to the physician’s office with complaints of a new left breast mass. She denies any pain, nipple discharge, or skin dimpling. She has a prior history of breast cysts 5 years ago, treated by aspiration at that time. Her last mammogram was at age 53. Past history is pertinent for a 30 pack-year smoking history, prior total abdominal hysterectomy-bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH-BSO) at age 54 for leiomyomas, and current use of hormone replacement therapy (HRT). Family history is negative for breast disease. Examination reveals a firm, well-defined, mobile, 1.5-cm nodule in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast without any regional lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
option_B: discontinuation of HRT and reexamination in 4–6 weeks
explanation: Imaging (diagnostic mammography ± sonography) is required before biopsy.

stem: A 56-year-old woman presents to the clinic for routine health screening. She is concerned about the development of breast cancer. Her past history includes fibrocystic changes with atypical ductal hyperplasia and a fibroadenoma, and her family history is positive only for breast cancer in her mother diagnosed at age 85. Mammograms show dense breasts without suspicious findings. Which of the following is the most common risk factor in evaluating women for breast cancer?
option_A: fibrocystic changes with atypical ductal hyperplasia
explanation: Age is the most common risk factor even though many risk factors exist.

stem: A 42-year-old woman returns to the clinic following an uneventful biopsy for a well-defined, mobile mass. The pathology report describes the mass as a fibroadenoma, but lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) is identified in the adjacent breast parenchyma extending to the resection margin. With no other risk factors and negative family history, what is the most appropriate management?
option_A: re-excision of the biopsy cavity to gain negative margins of resection
explanation: LCIS is a marker for bilateral risk; close observation is appropriate.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with a strong family history of breast cancer (including a sister with a deleterious BRCA1 mutation) is found to carry the same mutation. Which range represents the lifetime risk of breast cancer that should be quoted to her?
explanation: BRCA1 carriers have a lifetime breast cancer risk of about 60–70% (quoted as 50–80%), with a high risk of ovarian cancer too.

stem: For the same patient with a BRCA1 mutation, which of the following management strategies is an accepted option for her high-risk status?
explanation: Options for BRCA carriers are annual MRI (± mammography) surveillance, chemoprevention (tamoxifen) and bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy ± salpingo-oophorectomy; unilateral mastectomy is not enough.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with a 2.5-cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast and a palpable axillary node undergoes evaluation. Imaging shows no other lesions. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option for locoregional control yielding results equally effective as mastectomy?
option_B: lumpectomy, irradiation, and axillary node dissection
option_D: irradiation of the breast and axilla
option_E: quadrantectomy, irradiation, and axillary node dissection
answer_text: lumpectomy, irradiation, and axillary node dissection
explanation: Breast‐conserving therapy with lumpectomy plus radiation is equivalent to mastectomy in early-stage disease.

stem: The same patient asks if she is a candidate for SLN biopsy instead of complete axillary dissection to avoid lymphedema. What is the most appropriate answer?
option_A: Yes, and if the SLN is positive, then a complete axillary dissection should be performed.
option_B: Yes, and if the SLN is negative, then an axillary dissection can be avoided.
option_C: No, because the success of SLN biopsy in patients over age 60 is decreased.
option_D: No, because SLN biopsy is contraindicated when a palpable axillary node is suspicious for metastatic disease.
option_E: No, because SLN biopsy is contraindicated for tumors greater than 2 cm.
answer_text: No, because SLN biopsy is contraindicated when a palpable axillary node is suspicious for metastatic disease.
explanation: A palpable suspicious node contraindicates SLN biopsy.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with an abnormal screening mammogram but no symptoms undergoes imaging. The MLO and magnification CC views of the right breast reveal clustered microcalcifications. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
option_B: LCIS with or without an invasive component
option_C: DCIS with or without an invasive component
answer_text: DCIS with or without an invasive component
explanation: The mammographic features (clustered, irregular calcifications) are most consistent with DCIS.

stem: Following the findings in the previous question, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
option_A: observation, with repeat mammogram in 6 months
option_B: observation, with repeat mammogram on an annual basis
option_D: lumpectomy, radiation therapy, and SLN biopsy
explanation: Biopsy is needed to establish a histologic diagnosis.

stem: An 83-year-old woman undergoing screening mammography is found to have a mass in the lateral right breast. She is asymptomatic. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The mammographic features of an irregular, stellate mass in an older woman are most consistent with invasive carcinoma.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step in management for the mass detected in the previous question?
explanation: A needle (FNA or core) biopsy is indicated to obtain a tissue diagnosis.

stem: A 42-year-old female underwent radical mastectomy with axillary clearance. At her first follow-up, the inferior angle of her ipsilateral scapula translocates medially with any attempt at overhead activity. Injury to which of the following structures would most likely cause this abnormality?
explanation: Radical mastectomy can injure the long thoracic nerve, causing scapular winging.

stem: A 57-year-old woman has noticed a lump in the right breast for 4 weeks. She is otherwise fit and well and is not on any regular medications. On triple assessment she is found to have two foci of invasive ductal carcinoma with widespread ductal carcinoma in situ and FNAB of enlarged axillary lymph nodes confirms tumour involvement. Which is the single most appropriate surgical treatment for this patient?
option_D: Wide local excision and axillary node clearance
option_E: Wide local excision and sentinel node biopsy
explanation: Mastectomy with axillary node clearance is indicated due to multifocal widespread disease and lymph node involvement.

stem: A 40-year-old premenopausal woman has recently been diagnosed with breast cancer. She has had a wide local excision and sentinel node biopsy. Histology of the tumour reveals a 1.8cm grade 2 invasive ductal carcinoma which is oestrogen receptor positive. The sentinel node did not contain tumour. Which is the single most appropriate hormonal treatment for this patient?
explanation: Tamoxifen is the most appropriate hormonal treatment for a premenopausal woman with ER-positive breast cancer.
topics: Tamoxifen; Breast cancer; Sentinel lymph node biopsy

stem: A 70-year-old woman has had a lump in her left breast for 12 months. This lump has gradually increased in size and she has recently noticed that the shape of her breast has changed. She denies any other symptoms. She has evidence of skin dimpling in the outer aspect of the left breast and has a hard fixed mass with palpable axillary lymph nodes. Which is the single most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Skin dimpling and fixed mass with lymphadenopathy strongly suggest breast cancer.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has noticed 10 days of diffuse pain, redness, and swelling of the right breast. A course of antibiotics for the last 5 days has had no effect. Her nipple has changed shape with some associated discharge. A mammogram last year was normal but there is skin and subcutaneous oedema seen on ultrasound scan which is uncomfortable. Her breast is swollen, tender, and firm, as shown in Figure 5.3. Which is the single most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Diffuse pain, redness, and lack of response to antibiotics suggest inflammatory breast cancer.

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast. Which of the following findings would still allow her to receive breast-conservation surgery (partial mastectomy)?
option_A: Diffuse suspicious microcalcifications throughout the breast
option_C: Previous treatment of a breast cancer with lumpectomy and radiation
option_D: Large tumor relative to breast size
option_E: Persistently positive margins after multiple reexcisions of the breast cancer
explanation: Multifocal disease can still allow breast-conservation surgery if lesions are small relative to breast size.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of erythema and edema of the right breast with palpable axillary lymphadenopathy. A punch biopsy of the skin reveals neoplastic cells in the dermal lymphatics. She has a full staging workup, including bilateral mammogram, ultrasound of the bilateral breasts and axillae, and CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. She has no other sites of disease. Which of the following is the best sequence of steps in her management?
option_A: A course of nafcillin to treat the overlying cellulitis and then neoadjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer
option_B: Modified radical mastectomy followed by adjuvant chemotherapy
option_C: Modified radical mastectomy followed by hormonal therapy
option_D: Combined modality chemotherapy and radiation therapy to the right breast with surgery reserved for residual disease
option_E: Combined modality therapy with chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation
answer_text: Combined modality therapy with chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation
explanation: Inflammatory breast cancer (dermal lymphatic invasion) is treated with trimodality therapy: neoadjuvant chemotherapy, modified radical mastectomy, then radiotherapy.
topics: Inflammatory breast cancer; Breast cancer; Mastectomy

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with a lump in the left breast. Her family history is negative for breast cancer. On examination the mass is rubbery, mobile, and nontender to palpation. There are no overlying skin changes and the axilla is negative for lymphadenopathy. An ultrasound demonstrates a simple 1-cm cyst in the area of the palpable mass in the left breast. Which of the following represents the most appropriate management of this patient?
option_C: Aspiration of the cyst with cytologic analysis
explanation: Most cysts in the breast are benign; reassurance and reexamination are appropriate when there are no suspicious features.

stem: A45-year-old woman is found to have suspicious appearing calcifications in the right breast on a screening mammogram. Stereotactic biopsy of the calcifications shows lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS). On examination, both breasts are dense without palpable masses. The cervical, supraclavicular, and bilateral axilla are negative for lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?
option_A: Frequent self-breast examinations and yearly screening mammograms
option_D: Right total mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy
answer_text: Frequent self-breast examinations and yearly screening mammograms
explanation: Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) is considered a risk factor for invasive breast carcinoma and is managed with frequent self-exams and yearly mammograms.

stem: A14-year-old African American girl has her right breast removed because of a large mass. The tumor weighs 1400 g and has a bulging, very firm, lobulated surface with a whorl-like pattern, as illustrated here. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Fibroadenomas are well-demarcated and firm and can be large in young African American girls.

stem: A33-year-old pregnant woman notices a persistent, painless lump in the left breast. On examination the left breast has a single mobile mass without evidence of skin changes or lymphadenopathy in the neck or axilla. An ultrasound demonstrates a solid, 1-cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the breast. A core-needle biopsy shows invasive ductal carcinoma. The patient is in her first trimester of pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?
option_A: Termination of the pregnancy followed by total mastectomy
option_B: Immediate administration of chemotherapy followed by modified radical mastectomy after delivery of the baby
option_C: Segmental mastectomy, sentinel lymph node biopsy, and adjuvant radiation therapy shortly after surgery
option_D: Total mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy
answer_text: Total mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy
explanation: Immediate surgery, such as total mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy, is recommended during the first trimester.
topics: Mastectomy; Sentinel lymph node biopsy; Lymphadenopathy

stem: A40-year-old woman presents with a rash involving the nipple-areola complex for the last month with associated itching. On physical examination there is crusting and ulceration of the nipple with surrounding erythema involving the areola and surrounding skin, no palpable breast masses, and no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
option_B: Corticosteroid cream to the affected area
option_D: Mammogram and biopsy of the affected area
answer_text: Mammogram and biopsy of the affected area
explanation: This patient has Paget disease of the breast and needs a mammogram and biopsy to confirm and manage accordingly.
topics: Paget disease of the nipple; Lymphadenopathy

stem: A35-year-old female has a 6-month history of a 2-cm breast mass which was biopsied and consistent with a fibroadenoma. She now comes into the office reporting that the mass has rapidly enlarged and is now 10 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management strategy for this lesion?
option_A: Wide local excision with a rim of normal tissue
option_E: Excision, postoperative radiotherapy, and systemic chemotherapy
answer_text: Wide local excision with a rim of normal tissue
explanation: Large or rapidly enlarging fibroadenomas may represent phyllodes tumors, which require wide excision with a rim of normal tissue to reduce recurrence risk.

stem: A41-year-old woman has noted unilateral nipple discharge from her right breast. No associated mass is identified on ultrasound or mammogram. Which of the following is the next appropriate step in her management?
option_E: Nipple areolar excision with central lumpectomy
explanation: Pathologic nipple discharge should be further investigated with duct excision if no mass is identified.

stem: A36-year-old woman whose mother has just undergone treatment for breast cancer is asking about how this affects her and what can be done to lessen her chances of having the disease. Which of the following is the least significant risk factor for breast cancer?
option_B: Paternal relative with breast cancer BRCA1 mutation
option_C: Excessive estrogen exposure—early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity
explanation: Dietary fat intake has not been strongly linked to breast cancer risk compared to other factors.

stem: Tumor not palpable, clinically positive ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes fixed to one another; no evidence of metastases.
explanation: Fixed or matted nodes are associated with poor prognosis, corresponding to Stage III.

stem: Tumor 4.0 cm; clinically positive, movable axillary ipsilateral lymph nodes; no evidence of metastases.
explanation: Tumor >2cm but ≤5cm with positive lymph nodes corresponds to Stage II.

stem: Tumor 2.1 cm, clinically negative lymph nodes; no evidence of metastases. Final pathology shows only ductal carcinoma in situ.
explanation: Ductal carcinoma in situ is stage 0, as it is in situ.

stem: Tumor not palpable, but breast diffusely enlarged and erythematous, clinically positive supraclavicular nodes; no evidence of metastases.
explanation: Inflammatory breast cancer with fixed supraclavicular nodes is Stage III.

stem: Tumor 0.5 cm, clinically negative lymph nodes, pathological lumbar fracture.
explanation: Pathological lumbar fracture indicates distant metastasis, corresponding to Stage IV.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has a mammogram that demonstrates diffuse suspicious mammographic calcifications suggestive of multicentric disease. Biopsy of one of the lesions reveals ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). What is the most appropriate surgical management?
option_A: Lumpectomy with axillary lymph node dissection and radiation therapy
option_E: Simple mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy
answer_text: Simple mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy
explanation: Multicentric DCIS is best treated with simple mastectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy.
topics: Mastectomy; Sentinel lymph node biopsy; DCIS

stem: A 49-year-old woman has a 6-cm palpable mass that is biopsy-proven ductal adenocarcinoma. She undergoes neoadjuvant chemotherapy which reduces the tumor to 3 cm in size. stem: A neglected 82-year-old woman presents with a locally advanced breast cancer that is invading the pectoralis major muscle over a broad base. She is otherwise in good health. What is the most appropriate treatment?

stem: What is the recommended chemotherapy regimen for breast cancer?

stem: What are indications for post-mastectomy radiation therapy?
option_C: ≥4 positive lymph nodes or tumor >5 cm in size
option_D: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) with no lymphovascular invasion
option_E: Triple negative breast cancer without lymph node involvement
answer_text: ≥4 positive lymph nodes or tumor >5 cm in size
explanation: Post-mastectomy radiation therapy is indicated when the risk of locoregional recurrence is high, such as in patients with 4 or more positive lymph nodes or large primary tumors >5 cm.

stem: A 46-year-old man is diagnosed with an oestrogen receptor positive invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast after having discovered a lump 3 months before. explanation: B and E are correct because minor salivary glands produce about 10% of saliva and malignant tumours require primary surgical resection; the other options are incorrect.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
option_A: The sublingual glands occupy the anterior floor of mouth.
option_B: The sublingual glands drain both directly into the mouth and into the submandibular duct.
option_C: Tumours of the sublingual glands are rarely malignant.
option_D: The term ranula is applied to mucous retention cysts of the sublingual gland.
option_E: A plunging ranula is the term used to describe a ranula that extends beyond the floor of mouth and into the neck.
answer_text: The sublingual glands occupy the anterior floor of mouth. | The sublingual glands drain both directly into the mouth and into the submandibular duct. | A plunging ranula is the term used to describe a ranula that extends beyond the floor of mouth and into the neck.
explanation: A, B and E are correct based on gland location, drainage pattern and the definition of a plunging ranula; options C and D are incorrect.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
option_A: The two lobes of the submandibular gland communicate around the posterior belly of the digastric muscle.
option_B: 80% of salivary calculi occur in the submandibular duct.
option_C: Calculi identified posterior to the point where the duct crosses the lingual nerve should be removed via a transoral approach.
option_D: The marginal mandibular nerve is at risk during removal of the gland.
option_E: The lingual nerve is divided during removal of the gland to facilitate dissection of the deep lobe of the gland.
answer_text: 80% of salivary calculi occur in the submandibular duct. | The marginal mandibular nerve is at risk during removal of the gland.
explanation: B and D are correct; A, C and E are false due to anatomical inaccuracies.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
option_A: 80% of submandibular gland tumours are benign.
option_B: Submandibular gland masses can be differentiated from lymph nodes by bimanual palpation.
option_C: Facial nerve weakness is a sign suggestive of malignancy.
option_D: Open surgical biopsy is indicated to confirm malignant disease prior to surgery.
option_E: Radiation is the primary modality of treatment for most submandibular gland malignancies.
answer_text: Submandibular gland masses can be differentiated from lymph nodes by bimanual palpation. | Facial nerve weakness is a sign suggestive of malignancy.
explanation: B and C are correct; option A is false since only about 50% are benign and D and E are not standard practice.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
option_A: 80% of the parotid gland lies deep to the facial nerve.
option_B: During parotidectomy, the greater auricular nerve should be included in the skin flap to preserve function.
option_C: The facial nerve is identified using landmarks including the tragal pointer and the posterior belly of digastric.
option_D: If a branch of the facial nerve must be sacrificed during dissection, immediate grafting should be performed.
option_E: Frey’s syndrome results from inappropriate innervation of sweat glands with parasympathetic fibres within the parotid bed.
answer_text: The facial nerve is identified using landmarks including the tragal pointer and the posterior belly of digastric. | Frey’s syndrome results from inappropriate innervation of sweat glands with parasympathetic fibres within the parotid bed.
explanation: C and E are correct; options A, B and D are incorrect based on surgical anatomy.

stem: Which of the following statements is true?
option_A: Viral infection of the parotid glands affects both glands symmetrically.
option_B: Dehydrated patients are at risk from bacterial parotitis.
option_C: Recurrent parotitis of childhood tends to result in abscess formation.
option_D: HIV might present with multiple parotid cysts.
option_E: Chronic trauma to the parotid duct may result in obstruction.
answer_text: Dehydrated patients are at risk from bacterial parotitis. | HIV might present with multiple parotid cysts. | Chronic trauma to the parotid duct may result in obstruction.
explanation: B, D and E are correct; A and C are not consistently true.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
option_A: The most common tumour of the parotid gland is a pleomorphic adenoma.
option_B: Tumour excision for benign disease involves enucleation of the lesion.
option_C: Malignant tumours should be excised with a cuff of normal tissue including the facial nerve.
option_D: Symmetrical swelling of the parotid glands may be due to excess alcohol intake.
option_E: Sjogren’s syndrome is associated with B cell lymphoma.
answer_text: The most common tumour of the parotid gland is a pleomorphic adenoma. | Symmetrical swelling of the parotid glands may be due to excess alcohol intake. | Sjogren’s syndrome is associated with B cell lymphoma.
explanation: A, D and E are correct; B and C are incorrect regarding surgical management.

stem: A 56-year-old woman presents with a lump on the left side of her neck which has been slowly enlarging over the last few months. On examination, there is a 2 cm firm, painless, mobile lump near the angle of the left jaw. She is still able to move her facial muscles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Most common benign parotid tumour, usually painless, no facial nerve involvement.

stem: A 71-year-old man presents to the GP with a painful, enlarging lump just in front of his right ear, which has been present for 2 months. He woke this morning to find that the right side of his face was drooping. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: Malignant parotid tumour often presents with rapid growth and facial nerve involvement.

source: Ministerial Evaluation Exam - Head and Neck
stem: A 40-year-old female presents with an acute onset of fever, pain, and swelling at her right cheek. On examination, there is tenderness and swelling at the area of the right parotid gland. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Acute fever and parotid tenderness indicate sialadenitis.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is diagnosed with a submandibular calculus, having presented with a tender lump below the jaw on eating. Which structure is likely to be obstructed?
explanation: Submandibular calculi typically obstruct Warthin’s duct, leading to pain and swelling during meals.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a month-long history of intermittent, left-sided pain and swelling in the anterior neck under the left jaw. His symptoms are associated with meal times and regress shortly after completing each meal. In recent days however, the pain appears to have become more intense and the swelling more firm. On examination a firm lump is palpable in the left submandibular region, bimanual palpation of which causes the patient to complain of a foul taste in his mouth. The most appropriate diagnostic investigation will be
explanation: A sialogram is used to evaluate salivary duct obstruction.

stem: A 54-year-old builder attends your outpatient clinic with his wife, reporting an 8-month history of a lump on the left side of his face, in front of his ear. It is painless and does not trouble him. He has attended on the insistence of his wife, who is worried that it may be growing larger. On examination, the swelling appears to lie anterior to the angle of the jaw on the left side. It is non-tender and approximately 5 cm in diameter with a clear edge. The skin is easily moved on top of it and the lump itself feels rubbery to touch. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy or facial droop evident on examination. An aspirate is taken which shows cells of many different types. A decision is made at a follow-up appointment to excise the lump under anaesthesia. This is likely to be
explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign parotid tumor, presenting as a rubbery and mobile mass.

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with his mother to the general practice at which you are based, with a 3-week history of bilateral cheek swelling. The family is newly registered and medical records have not yet been transferred to the practice. His mother informs you that the young boy has not received any of his childhood vaccinations, as she has been worried about their possible detrimental effects. The clinical suspicion is of mumps parotitis. Which class of infectious agent is responsible for mumps?
explanation: Mumps is caused by an RNA virus from the paramyxovirus family.

stem: A barium swallow is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis on this image?
explanation: A grossly dilated oesophagus tapering smoothly at the cardia (bird beak) is achalasia.

stem: A barium swallow of a patient with progressive dysphagia and weight loss is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis on this image?
explanation: An irregular stricture with shouldering and proximal dilatation is oesophageal carcinoma.

stem: A 55-year-old man has had intermittent dysphagia for solids and liquids with central chest pain for 4 months. ECG and troponin are normal; sublingual nitrates relieve the pain. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Intermittent dysphagia for solids and liquids with chest pain relieved by nitrates is diffuse oesophageal spasm (corkscrew oesophagus on barium).

stem: A 55-year-old man has had intermittent dysphagia for solids and liquids with central chest pain for 4 months. ECG and troponin are normal; sublingual nitrates relieve the pain. Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
explanation: High-resolution manometry shows premature simultaneous contractions; endoscopy is done first to exclude obstruction.

stem: A 55-year-old man has had intermittent dysphagia for solids and liquids with central chest pain for 4 months. ECG and troponin are normal; sublingual nitrates relieve the pain. What is the best management now?
explanation: Oesophageal spasm is treated medically first (calcium channel blockers or nitrates); POEM is reserved for refractory cases.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
option_B: The oesophagus has five natural constrictions.
option_C: The gastro-oesophageal junction is 40 cm from the incisors.
option_D: The oesophagus is lined by stratified squamous epithelium.
option_E: The oesophageal opening in the diaphragm is at the level of T10 vertebra.
answer_text: The gastro-oesophageal junction is 40 cm from the incisors. | The oesophagus is lined by stratified squamous epithelium. | The oesophageal opening in the diaphragm is at the level of T10 vertebra.
explanation: True: the GOJ lies about 40 cm from the incisors, the lining is stratified squamous and the hiatus is at T10. The oesophagus is ~25 cm long with three constrictions.

stem: The following statements are true except:
option_A: The lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) is an area of high pressure.
option_B: The normal length of the LOS is 3 to 4 cm.
option_C: The three phases of swallowing, oral, pharyngeal and oesophageal, are involuntary.
option_D: Pharyngeal diverticulum occurs because of the incoordination of the pharyngeal phase of deglutition.
option_E: The pressure in the LOS is 10–25 mmHg.
answer_text: The three phases of swallowing, oral, pharyngeal and oesophageal, are involuntary.
explanation: Because the oral phase is voluntary while the pharyngeal and oesophageal phases are involuntary; LOS measurements are correct.

stem: Which of the following statements are false?
option_A: Dysphagia is a cardinal symptom of oesophageal carcinoma.
option_B: Dysphagia associated with cough is a symptom of impending tracheo-oesophageal fistula.
option_C: Dysphagia in the oral and pharyngeal phases of swallowing indicates a neurological rather than a mechanical problem.
option_D: Odynophagia is always of cardiac origin.
option_E: Regurgitation and reflux are the same and caused by dysphagia.
answer_text: Odynophagia is always of cardiac origin. | Regurgitation and reflux are the same and caused by dysphagia.
explanation: Odynophagia is typically due to oesophageal causes and regurgitation and reflux are distinct phenomena.

stem: The following statements are true except:
option_A: Anginal pain can be confused with heartburn.
option_B: Heartburn with weight loss is a ‘red flag’ symptom.
option_C: Barium swallow is the ideal investigation in a patient with heartburn.
option_D: Dysphagia to liquids more than solids is typical of achalasia of cardia.
option_E: Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) is the first line investigation in suspected spontaneous rupture of oesophagus.
answer_text: Barium swallow is the ideal investigation in a patient with heartburn. | Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) is the first line investigation in suspected spontaneous rupture of oesophagus.
explanation: OGD is preferred for heartburn evaluation and in suspected spontaneous oesophageal rupture other imaging is indicated.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
option_A: A barium meal should be the first line of investigation in a patient presenting with heartburn.
option_B: 24-hour pH monitoring is the most accurate method to assess gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD).
option_C: Laparoscopy should be undertaken prior to oesophagectomy.
option_D: Manometry is essential in the diagnosis of motility disorders.
option_E: Raman spectroscopy detects early molecular changes in Barrett’s mucosal neoplasia.
answer_text: 24-hour pH monitoring is the most accurate method to assess gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD). | Laparoscopy should be undertaken prior to oesophagectomy. | Manometry is essential in the diagnosis of motility disorders. | Raman spectroscopy detects early molecular changes in Barrett’s mucosal neoplasia.
explanation: 24-h pH monitoring is the most accurate test for GORD; staging laparoscopy, manometry (motility disorders) and Raman spectroscopy all have roles. OGD, not barium, is first-line for heartburn.

stem: Which of the following statements are false?
option_A: Injection of botulinum toxin is a modality of treatment in achalasia.
option_B: The operation for resection of carcinoma of middle one-third of oesophagus is Heller’s procedure.
option_C: Endoscopic mucosal resection is a surgical option in very early mucosal neoplasia in Barrett’s oesophagus.
option_D: All patients with oesophageal perforation should be treated with surgical repair.
option_E: The ideal surgical treatment for a Zenker’s diverticulum is excision through an incision on the left side of the neck followed by cricopharyngeal myotomy.
answer_text: The operation for resection of carcinoma of middle one-third of oesophagus is Heller’s procedure. | All patients with oesophageal perforation should be treated with surgical repair. | The ideal surgical treatment for a Zenker’s diverticulum is excision through an incision on the left side of the neck followed by cricopharyngeal myotomy.
explanation: Heller’s myotomy is used for achalasia—not cancer—and not all perforations mandate surgery while endoscopic stapling is preferred for Zenker’s diverticulum.

stem: A 45-year-old man has difficulty swallowing liquids/solids. Barium swallow shows narrowing in lower oesophagus; endoscopy excludes organic lesion. Which long-term therapy?
explanation: Achalasia definitive relief from surgical myotomy.

stem: A 10-year-old boy ingests household bleach and has severe mouth/stomach pain. He is febrile, tachycardic. Next most appropriate initial investigation?
explanation: Fever, tachycardia and severe pain after caustic ingestion suggest perforation: erect chest X-ray (then CT) first; endoscopy is contraindicated if perforation is suspected.

stem: After undergoing total gastrectomy, the patient presents with chest pain and sore throat. What could be the cause, and how should it be managed?
option_C: GERD; manage with lifestyle modifications and proton pump inhibitors
answer_text: GERD; manage with lifestyle modifications and proton pump inhibitors
explanation: Post-gastrectomy, GERD is common and is managed with lifestyle changes and PPIs.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with increasing difficulty swallowing over the last few months. He has been working in Mexico for the last two years. He is otherwise well and denies any other symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: Trypanosoma cruzi infection can cause megaoesophagus presenting with progressive dysphagia.

stem: A 56-year-old woman complains of episodes of severe retrosternal chest pain postprandial, with a bitter taste in her mouth, but no difficulty swallowing. Examination is unremarkable. Which investigation is most useful?
explanation: GORD is best diagnosed by prolonged oesophageal pH monitoring.

stem: A 33-year-old woman presents to the surgical outpatient clinic with increasing dysphagia for solids and liquids, retrosternal chest pain on eating, regurgitation of undigested food and weight loss. Oesophageal and gastric biopsy at endoscopy was normal. Oesophageal manometry showed impaired relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter and barium swallow revealed a dilated proximal oesophagus with distal narrowing. Which of the following surgical procedures would be indicated?
explanation: Achalasia is treated surgically by incising the LES (Heller myotomy).

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with acute lower chest and upper abdominal pain following an episode of vomiting. On examination, he has marked tenderness in the epigastrium and you note the presence of subcutaneous emphysema. ECG shows a sinus tachycardia with no ST segment changes, and a chest X-ray demonstrates mediastinal air. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Forceful vomiting caused transmural oesophageal rupture leading to mediastinal air.

stem: A patient has a symptomatic pharyngeal pouch (Zenker diverticulum). What is the most important aspect of treatment?
option_D: elevation of the head of the bed
explanation: Cricopharyngeal muscle myotomy Myotomy is key to relieve the underlying neuromotor dysfunction.

stem: A 55-year-old man with 10 years of heartburn, chronic cough, and regurgitation—whose endoscopy shows Barrett’s esophagus with high-grade dysplasia—would most likely have been prevented by which early treatment?
explanation: Early antireflux surgery may prevent progression to Barrett’s esophagus.

stem: For the same patient with Barrett’s esophagus and high-grade dysplasia, what is recommended?
option_A: double dose proton-pump inhibitor and repeat endoscopy in 3 months
option_B: proton-pump inhibitor and H₂ blocker, followed by repeat endoscopy in 3 months
option_C: antibiotic treatment for Helicobacter pylori with proton-pump inhibitor
option_E: Endoscopic resection and ablation (oesophagectomy if endoscopic therapy is not possible)
answer_text: Endoscopic resection and ablation (oesophagectomy if endoscopic therapy is not possible)
explanation: Barrett oesophagus with high-grade dysplasia is now treated by endoscopic eradication (EMR of visible lesions plus radiofrequency ablation); oesophagectomy is reserved for failures or invasive disease.

stem: A 55-year-old man with acute substernal chest and epigastric pain after prolonged vomiting, subcutaneous emphysema, and a chest X-ray showing pneumomediastinum has which diagnosis?
explanation: The findings are indicative of Boerhaave’s syndrome.

stem: Which diagnostic test is most appropriate for suspected spontaneous oesophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndrome)?
explanation: A water-soluble contrast oesophagogram is the classic test to confirm and localise the leak; CT with oral contrast is used if it is equivocal or the patient is unwell.

stem: Which factor most influences outcome in esophageal perforation?
explanation: Prompt treatment is critical for survival.

stem: A 54-year-old man with recurrent problems with acid reflux despite changes to his diet and reduction of his alcohol intake. An endoscopy is performed which reveals Barrett’s oesophagus. Which of the following is the optimum management for this patient in regards to symptom control and disease monitoring?
option_B: Long term PPI and endoscopy every year
option_C: Long term PPI and endoscopy every five years
option_D: Trial of PPI and endoscopy every five years
answer_text: Long term PPI and endoscopy every five years
explanation: Barrett’s oesophagus requires acid suppression and periodic surveillance with endoscopy.

stem: Shortly after an esophagoscopy, a 30-year-old patient develops shortness of breath, chest pain, and fever. A contrast study shows extravasation of contrast into the left chest cavity. The most appropriate course of action is:
option_A: Perform a cervical esophagostomy, gastrostomy, and insert a chest tube.
option_B: Perform Immediate left thoracotomy and repair the esophageal tear.
option_C: Insert a nasogastric tube and begin high dose antibiotic therapy
option_D: Deploy an endoscopic intra-esophageal stent to plug the hole.
option_E: Stop ingestion of food, insert a chest tube and begin high dose antibiotic therapy.
answer_text: Perform Immediate left thoracotomy and repair the esophageal tear.
explanation: Iatrogenic thoracic perforation recognised early, with free leak into the pleura, is repaired primarily via a left thoracotomy with drainage; stenting or conservative care suits contained leaks or unfit patients.

stem: 28-year-old woman has dysphagia with low retrosternal ‘sticking’ and an occasional sensation of choking. A video barium swallow shows this appearance in the oesophagus (see Figure 6.1). Which is the single most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Achalasia (failure of relaxation of the distal oesophageal musculature associated with degeneration of the myenteric plexus) is among the most common causes of dysphagia in the younger population.

stem: 72-year-old man has had a sensation of retrosternal burning that is worse at night and after meals for the last 4 months. It partially responds to ‘over the counter’ antacid treatment. Which is the single most appropriate initial diagnostic investigation?
explanation: New reflux symptoms in a 72-year-old need OGD first, to see the mucosa, take biopsies and exclude malignancy; pH studies come later if the diagnosis is unclear.

stem: A 41-year-old man complains of regurgitation of saliva and of undigested food. An esophagram reveals a dilated esophagus and a bird’s-beak deformity. Manometry shows a hypertensive lower esophageal sphincter with failure to relax with deglutition. Which of the following is the safest and most effective treatment of this condition?
option_A: Medical treatment with sublingual nitroglycerin, nitrates, or calcium-channel blockers
option_C: Injections of botulinum toxin directly into the lower esophageal sphincter
option_D: Dilation with a Gruntzig-type (volume-limited, pressure-control) balloon
explanation: Surgical esophagomyotomy is the most effective treatment for achalasia.

stem: A 45-year-old executive experiences increasingly painful retrosternal heartburn, especially at night. He has been chewing antacid tablets. EKG and chest x-ray are normal. An esophagram shows a hiatal hernia. In determining the proper treatment for a sliding hiatal hernia, which of the following is the most useful modality?
option_A: Barium swallow with cinefluoroscopy during Valsalva maneuver
option_D: Measurement of the size of the hernia on upper GI
option_E: Assessment of the patient’s smoking and drinking history
explanation: Endoscopy is useful in evaluating esophageal changes in hiatal hernia.

stem: A 65-year-old man has been noticing progressive difficulty swallowing, first solid food and now liquids as well. A barium study shows a narrowing just below the carina. Endoscopic biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following provides the most accurate information regarding the T stage of an esophageal carcinoma?
explanation: Endoscopic ultrasound is the most accurate modality for T staging in esophageal carcinoma.

stem: A 56-year-old woman has nonspecific complaints that include an abnormal sensation when swallowing. An esophagram and EGD are performed. Which of the following is most likely to require surgical correction?
explanation: Paraesophageal hernias pose a risk of strangulation and typically require surgical repair.

stem: The blood supply to the oesophagus is derived from which three vessels?
option_A: Inferior thyroid artery, descending aorta, left gastric artery
option_B: Internal carotid, descending aorta, oesophageal artery
option_C: Lateral thoracic artery, phrenic artery, right gastric artery
option_D: Pharyngeal artery, long thoracic artery, phrenic artery
option_E: Ascending aorta, common hepatic artery, left gastric artery
answer_text: Inferior thyroid artery, descending aorta, left gastric artery
explanation: The cervical oesophagus is supplied by the inferior thyroid artery, the thoracic part by aortic branches and the abdominal part by the left gastric artery.

stem: A 58-year-old patient presents with a 6-week history of increasing difficulty swallowing. He first noticed problems when eating meat which became stuck ‘behind his heart’, but this gradually began to include other foods. He is now struggling with thick fluids and has noticed some unintentional weight loss. What is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation: Endoscopy is the gold standard investigation to assess suspected oesophageal cancer.

stem: A 27-year-old patient presents with a 3-month history of increasing difficulty in swallowing – beginning with fluids and later with solids – accompanied by regurgitation and unintentional weight loss; a chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Achalasia, due to failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax, is the most likely cause.

stem: CREST syndrome is an autoimmune condition associated with atrophy and fibrosis of the oesophageal musculature resulting in dysphagia and reflux‐type symptoms. Which of the following is not a feature of CREST syndrome?
explanation: An erythematous malar rash is not a characteristic feature of CREST syndrome.

stem: The gastro-oesophageal sphincter does not rely on a ring of contractile muscle but on several mechanisms to prevent reflux. Which of the following does not contribute to its function?
option_B: Smooth muscle of the lower oesophageal sphincter
explanation: The left crus does not contribute to the maintenance of sphincter tone.

stem: A 58-year-old builder with a long history of retrosternal chest pain and a hiatus hernia is found on endoscopy to have grade 2 oesophagitis. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation: Acid suppression with a PPI is the first-line treatment for oesophagitis associated with reflux.

stem: Which of the following is not a lifestyle change that might reduce reflux-type symptoms?
option_E: Raise the head of the bed at night
explanation: Abdominal exercise may worsen reflux rather than improve it.

stem: A 65-year-old patient with symptoms of oesophagitis and endoscopic findings of Barrett’s oesophagus with low grade dysplasia is best managed by
option_B: Staging CT chest abdomen and pelvis
option_D: High dose PPI and repeat endoscopy
answer_text: High dose PPI and repeat endoscopy
explanation: Low-grade dysplasia in Barrett oesophagus: high-dose PPI and repeat endoscopy at 6 months; confirmed persistent LGD is then offered radiofrequency ablation.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
option_A: It is easy to get views beyond the ligament of Treitz during an oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD).
option_C: It is not necessary to stop clopidogrel before colonoscopic polypectomy.
option_D: Verbal consent is an accepted practice.
option_E: Perforation and haemorrhage are uncommon but significant complications of the procedure.
answer_text: Perforation and haemorrhage are uncommon but significant complications of the procedure.
explanation: Modern endoscopes are video-based; OGD rarely visualizes beyond the ligament of Treitz, clopidogrel is usually stopped, and written consent is standard.

stem: Gross Anatomy – Blood Supply of the Stomach and Duodenum. Which of the following statements are true regarding blood supply?
option_A: The stomach has an arterial supply on both lesser and greater curves.
option_B: The right gastric artery arises from the common hepatic artery.
option_C: The gastroduodenal artery passes behind the second part of duodenum.
option_D: The short gastric arteries are branches of the left gastric artery.
option_E: The right gastroepiploic artery runs along the greater curvature of the stomach.
answer_text: The stomach has an arterial supply on both lesser and greater curves. | The right gastric artery arises from the common hepatic artery. | The right gastroepiploic artery runs along the greater curvature of the stomach.
explanation: The stomach receives blood along both curvatures; note that the gastroduodenal artery passes behind the first part of the duodenum and short gastrics arise from the splenic artery.

stem: Gross Anatomy – Nerve Supply of the Stomach and Duodenum. Which of the following statements are true regarding the nerve supply?
option_A: The intrinsic nerves exist principally in two plexuses, the myenteric plexus of Auerbach and the submucosal plexus of Meissner.
option_B: There are fewer ganglia in the submucosal plexus of the antrum of the stomach.
option_C: The extrinsic supply is mainly derived from the vagus nerves.
option_D: The vagal fibres are only efferent.
option_E: The sympathetic fibres are derived from the thoracic ganglia.
answer_text: The intrinsic nerves exist principally in two plexuses, the myenteric plexus of Auerbach and the submucosal plexus of Meissner. | The extrinsic supply is mainly derived from the vagus nerves.
explanation: The stomach’s innervation includes intrinsic enteric plexuses and a dominant vagal (both afferent and efferent) parasympathetic supply; sympathetic fibres come via the coeliac ganglia.

stem: Microscopic Anatomy of the Stomach and Duodenum. The following statements are true except:
option_A: The parietal cells are in the body of the stomach.
option_C: The endocrine cells are in the antrum and produce gastrin.
option_D: The endocrine cells in the duodenum produce secretin and cholecystokinin.
option_E: Histologically the chief cells are found at the mucosal surface.
answer_text: Histologically the chief cells are found at the mucosal surface.
explanation: Chief cells are actually located deep within the gastric glands rather than at the mucosal surface.

stem: Physiology of the Stomach and Duodenum – Gastric Acid Secretion. Which of the following statements are true regarding gastric acid secretion?
option_A: Hydrogen ions are produced in the parietal cells by the proton pump.
option_B: The most important factor acting on the chief cell is histamine.
option_C: Vagus nerve is responsible for the gastric phase of acid secretion.
answer_text: Hydrogen ions are produced in the parietal cells by the proton pump. | Somatostatin inhibits acid secretion.
explanation: Parietal cells secrete H⁺ via the H⁺/K⁺ ATPase and somatostatin inhibits acid. Histamine acts on parietal cells, the vagus mediates the cephalic phase and secretin inhibits acid.

stem: Physiology of the Stomach – Functions of the Stomach. Which of the following are functions of the stomach?
answer_text: Reservoir for ingested food. | Mechanically breaks down ingested food. | Starts the process of digestion. | Produces mucus.
explanation: The stomach stores food, mechanically and chemically digests it, and secretes mucus for protection; the proximal part mainly relaxes rather than showing strong peristalsis.

stem: Investigations of the Stomach and Duodenum. Which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Flexible endoscopy is the primary investigation of choice.
option_B: Endoscopic ultrasound is useful in determining the ‘T’ status of tumours.
option_C: CT scan is useful in the staging of gastric cancer.
option_D: PET/CT scan can help avoid radical surgery in approximately 10% of patients with gastric cancer.
option_E: Laparoscopy is helpful in evaluating posterior extension of tumours.
answer_text: Flexible endoscopy is the primary investigation of choice. | Endoscopic ultrasound is useful in determining the ‘T’ status of tumours. | CT scan is useful in the staging of gastric cancer. | PET/CT scan can help avoid radical surgery in approximately 10% of patients with gastric cancer.
explanation: Endoscopy is first-line; EUS, CT and PET/CT all have important roles in staging, while laparoscopy is less useful for assessing posterior extension.
