option_E: The infant has a large tongue, the larynx is high, and minimal access surgery (MAS) can be used at all ages.
answer_text: The ribs are more horizontal and flexible. | The liver and bladder are intra-abdominal. | The infant’s head constitutes 20% of the surface area. | The infant has a large tongue, the larynx is high, and minimal access surgery (MAS) can be used at all ages.
explanation: False: A — in infants a transverse incision gives better access (the abdomen is wider than it is long). Horizontal pliable ribs, intra-abdominal liver/bladder, large head and high larynx are true.

stem: Which of the following statements are false?
option_A: A neonate is a baby up to 4 weeks old.
option_B: The urinary bladder is an intra-abdominal organ in infants and children.
option_C: An infant’s head accounts for 20% of the body surface area.
option_D: Gluconeogenesis in infants is as good as in adults.
option_E: The infant’s immune system is immature.
answer_text: Gluconeogenesis in infants is as good as in adults.
explanation: Only D is false: neonates have small glycogen stores and poor gluconeogenesis, so they become hypoglycaemic quickly. The other statements are true.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Children are regarded as small adults, and therefore their surgical management is adjusted according to their size.
option_B: Attention to thermoregulation is very important.
option_C: Postoperative management requires extreme care because of an inadequate stress response.
option_D: Minimal access surgery (MAS) can be used at all ages.
answer_text: Attention to thermoregulation is very important. | Postoperative management requires extreme care because of an inadequate stress response. | Minimal access surgery (MAS) can be used at all ages.
explanation: False: A — children are not small adults; their anatomy and physiology differ. Thermoregulation and postoperative care need special attention, and MAS is feasible at any age.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding paediatric trauma are true?
option_A: Follow usual Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) rules as in an adult.
option_B: The usual rules of resuscitation apply.
option_C: Blunt trauma is more common than penetrating trauma.
option_D: Splenic injury in the majority should be treated by splenectomy.
option_E: Consideration must be given to non-accidental injury (NAI).
answer_text: The usual rules of resuscitation apply. | Blunt trauma is more common than penetrating trauma. | Consideration must be given to non-accidental injury (NAI).
explanation: In paediatric trauma standard resuscitative measures apply, blunt injuries predominate, and non-accidental injury must be vigilantly considered.

stem: Which of the following statements about inguinoscrotal swellings are false?
option_A: A hydrocele is a patent processus vaginalis, as is a hernia.
option_C: Hernia can be direct or indirect.
option_D: In incarcerated hernia, reduction should be attempted by taxis followed by operation 24 hours later.
option_E: A hydrocele always needs an operation.
answer_text: Hernia can be direct or indirect. | A hydrocele always needs an operation.
explanation: False: C — paediatric inguinal hernias are (virtually) always indirect via a patent processus vaginalis; E — most infant hydroceles resolve spontaneously and are observed until about 2 years.

stem: Which of the following statements are true for undescended testis?
option_A: Orchidopexy in a subdartos pouch is the treatment of choice.
option_B: The operation is recommended at 6–18 months of age.
option_C: When a testis is impalpable and therefore intra-abdominal, laparotomy should be done.
option_D: Laparoscopy is the gold standard procedure for an intra-abdominal testis.
option_E: Orchidopexy reduces the chance of malignancy.
answer_text: Orchidopexy in a subdartos pouch is the treatment of choice. | The operation is recommended at 6–18 months of age. | Laparoscopy is the gold standard procedure for an intra-abdominal testis.
explanation: False: C — an impalpable testis may be inguinal, intra-abdominal or absent, so laparoscopy (not laparotomy) is used; E — orchidopexy aids examination but does not remove the malignancy risk.

stem: Which of the following statements are true with regard to acute scrotal pain?
option_A: Acute testicular pain can be from torsion of the testis, torsion of the hydatid of Morgagni, or acute epididymitis.
option_B: Pain of testicular torsion may originate in the groin or suprapubic area.
option_C: Doppler ultrasound should be done in suspected testicular torsion.
option_D: Incarcerated hernia may cause similar symptoms.
option_E: In case of any doubt, exploration of the scrotum must be carried out.
answer_text: Acute testicular pain can be from torsion of the testis, torsion of the hydatid of Morgagni, or acute epididymitis. | Pain of testicular torsion may originate in the groin or suprapubic area. | Incarcerated hernia may cause similar symptoms. | In case of any doubt, exploration of the scrotum must be carried out.
explanation: False: C — Doppler ultrasound must not delay scrotal exploration when torsion is suspected, and a normal scan does not exclude it.

stem: What is the operation for congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis called?
explanation: Ramstedt’s operation is a pyloromyotomy that carefully splits the hypertrophied pyloric muscle while preserving the mucosa, and is the standard treatment for pyloric stenosis.
topics: Pyloric stenosis; Helicobacter pylori; Gastric outlet obstruction

stem: A 5-week-old baby presents with projectile vomiting within 30 minutes of each feed for 3 days. On examination there is a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Typically presents 2–6 weeks old with projectile non-bile-stained vomiting.
topics: Helicobacter pylori; Gastric outlet obstruction; Pyloric stenosis

stem: A 10-month-old baby has been admitted with vomiting. The parents report he’s crying more than usual and drawing his knees up. Nurses note his stools are loose and redder than normal. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Typical ‘redcurrant jelly’ stools; colicky pain in 5–12 months age group.

stem: A 10-month-old baby has been admitted with vomiting. The parents report he’s crying more than usual and drawing his knees up. Nurses note his stools are loose and redder than normal. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Typical ‘redcurrant jelly’ stools; colicky pain in 5–12 months age group.

stem: A 5-week-old baby presents with projectile vomiting within 30 minutes of each feed for 3 days. On examination there is a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Typically presents 2–6 weeks old with projectile non-bile-stained vomiting.

stem: A 9-month-old child appears to have had a history of 48 hours of colicky abdominal pain described by his parents as episodes of crying and drawing his legs up to the abdomen. Additionally, he has passed some mucus-like blood from the rectum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The classic triad of intussusception includes colicky abdominal pain, red currant jelly stool (mucus-like blood), and vomiting.

stem: What is the most reasonable treatment for intussusception in this child?
explanation: Uncomplicated intussusception in a stable child is reduced by image-guided pneumatic or hydrostatic enema (~80% success); surgery is for peritonitis, perforation or failed reduction.

stem: A 9-month-old child appears to have had a history of 48 hours of colicky abdominal pain described by his parents as episodes of crying and drawing his legs up to the abdomen. Additionally, he has passed some mucus-like blood from the rectum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The classic triad of intussusception includes colicky abdominal pain, red currant jelly stool (mucus-like blood), and vomiting.

stem: What is the most reasonable treatment for intussusception in this child?
explanation: Barium enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic in cases of uncomplicated intussusception.

stem: A 6-month-old boy has had paroxysms of intense abdominal pain since this morning, drawing his legs up and passing some mucus-like blood per rectum. Temperature is 36.8°C. Which of the following would be the best treatment option in the first instance?
explanation: A stable infant with intussusception (colic, ‘red-currant jelly’ stool) is treated first by image-guided air/contrast enema reduction.

stem: A 7-day-old preterm boy develops vomiting and bloody diarrhoea. On examination, his abdomen is grossly distended and discoloured. His temperature is 39.5°C. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Severe neonatal bowel infection/inflammation, especially in preterm infants.

stem: A 5-week-old boy has been having episodes of forceful vomiting after feeds for the last 2 weeks. He is always hungry and now appears lethargic. Examination reveals mild dehydration and a smooth, firm, non-tender mass in the right upper quadrant. Blood tests are sent. What biochemical abnormalities would you expect to find?
explanation: Projectile vomiting of gastric acid leads to loss of HCl and compensatory hypokalaemia with metabolic alkalosis.

stem: A 6-month-old boy has had paroxysms of intense abdominal pain since this morning, drawing his legs up and passing some mucus-like blood per rectum. Temperature is 36.8°C. Which of the following would be the best treatment option in the first instance?
explanation: Intussusception can often be reduced by a contrast enema.

stem: A 1-day-old baby girl has repeated bile-stained vomiting. The mother had polyhydramnios. X-ray shows gas in the stomach and first part of duodenum only. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: ‘Double-bubble’ sign with bilious vomiting in a newborn suggests duodenal atresia.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his father, having told him that he had swallowed a five pence coin earlier that day. The child has not experienced any symptoms and on examination is well. Which of the following investigations would you perform in the first instance?
explanation: Plain X-rays can confirm the position of a swallowed radio-opaque foreign body.

stem: A 3-day-old boy is having increasing abdominal distension and vomiting. He is also noted not to have passed meconium since birth. Which of the following investigations would be most helpful in confirming the cause of obstruction?
explanation: Hirschsprung disease is diagnosed by absent ganglion cells on rectal biopsy.

stem: A newborn baby boy is found to have visible intestine emerging from his abdomen with no covering to the contents. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Abdominal wall defect with exposed bowel loops and no sac covering indicates gastroschisis.

stem: A 10-month-old infant presents with a 24-hour history of low-grade fever, anorexia, vomiting, and loose stools. On exam, there is fullness in the right upper quadrant and passage of a stool with blood mixed in. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Intussusception The infant’s intermittent colicky pain and currant jelly stool are typical for intussusception.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step in the diagnostic evaluation and management of the infant described above?
option_C: IV fluid rehydration and a hydrostatic barium enema
option_E: IV fluid rehydration, NG decompression, and a UGI contrast study
answer_text: IV fluid rehydration and a hydrostatic barium enema
explanation: After IV rehydration, intussusception is reduced by an image-guided enema (air/pneumatic now preferred to barium); surgery if it fails or there is peritonitis.

stem: An 18-month-old boy with intermittent vomiting, RLQ fullness, and currant jelly stools most likely has?
explanation: The classic findings indicate intussusception.

stem: A 5-week-old infant presents with a 1-week history of progressive nonbilious vomiting, decreasing urine output, but remains eager to feed. On examination, a visible peristaltic wave is noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Progressive non-bilious (projectile) vomiting in a hungry 3–6-week-old with visible gastric peristalsis is hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
topics: Helicobacter pylori; Gastric outlet obstruction; Pyloric stenosis

stem: The diagnosis of pyloric stenosis is best confirmed by which of the following?
option_B: Careful clinical examination with palpation of an epigastric mass
explanation: Ultrasound is the investigation of choice, showing a thickened (>3–4 mm), elongated (>15 mm) pyloric muscle; a palpable ‘olive’ is diagnostic but often not felt.
topics: Helicobacter pylori; Gastric outlet obstruction; Pyloric stenosis

stem: An infant with pyloric stenosis is evaluated for possible electrolyte derangements. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely?
option_A: Na 145, K 3.0, Cl 110, CO2 17, urine pH 8.0
option_B: Na 130, K 3.0, Cl 80, CO2 36, urine pH 4.0
option_C: Na 135, K 4.0, Cl 104, CO2 23, urine pH 7.0
option_D: Na 140, K 5.2, Cl 100, CO2 16, urine pH 4.0
option_E: Na 132, K 3.2, Cl 96, CO2 25, urine pH 7.0
answer_text: Na 130, K 3.0, Cl 80, CO2 36, urine pH 4.0
explanation: Loss of gastric HCl gives hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; the kidney then excretes H⁺ to conserve Na⁺ and K⁺, causing paradoxical aciduria.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this infant with pyloric stenosis?
option_B: Send the child home with an oral electrolyte rehydration solution
option_C: Change the infant’s formula and feeding regimen
option_D: IV fluid resuscitation, followed by surgical intervention
option_E: Initiate therapy with a prokinetic agent
answer_text: IV fluid resuscitation, followed by surgical intervention
explanation: Pyloric stenosis is not a surgical emergency: correct dehydration and alkalosis with IV fluids (with potassium) before Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.
topics: Fluid therapy; Helicobacter pylori; Gastric outlet obstruction

stem: A 10-month-old infant presents with a 24-hour history of low-grade fever, anorexia, vomiting, and loose stools. On exam, there is fullness in the right upper quadrant and passage of a stool with blood mixed in. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: intussusception The infant’s intermittent colicky pain and currant jelly stool are typical for intussusception.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step in the diagnostic evaluation and management of the infant described above?
option_C: (C) IV fluid rehydration and a hydrostatic barium enema
option_E: (E) IV fluid rehydration, NG decompression, and a UGI contrast study
answer_text: (C) IV fluid rehydration and a hydrostatic barium enema
explanation: IV fluid rehydration and a hydrostatic barium enema Hydrostatic reduction with a contrast enema is the treatment of choice for intussusception.

stem: A neonate with bile-stained vomiting, abdominal distention, and dilated loops of bowel on plain radiographs with a small-caliber colon on contrast enema is evaluated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Bilious vomiting with dilated small-bowel loops and an unused microcolon on contrast enema indicates jejunoileal atresia; Hirschsprung disease shows a transition zone.

stem: A 1-day-old infant has persistent vomiting and no stools. An abdominal film shows a ‘double bubble’ sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
option_D: esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
explanation: Double bubble sign is characteristic of duodenal atresia.

stem: A 3-day-old term infant with progressive vomiting and abdominal distention—who passed meconium only after a glycerin suppository—requires which essential intervention before transfer?
option_A: nasogastric tube decompression and IV fluid resuscitation
option_D: blood and urine cultures, followed by initiation of broad spectrum antibiotics
answer_text: nasogastric tube decompression and IV fluid resuscitation
explanation: NG decompression and IV fluids are essential before transport.

stem: Upon arrival at the pediatric hospital, what is the best approach to establish a diagnosis?
option_B: plain radiographs, followed by a barium enema, and subsequent rectal biopsy
answer_text: plain radiographs, followed by a barium enema, and subsequent rectal biopsy
explanation: This sequence confirms Hirschsprung’s disease.

stem: An 18-month-old boy with intermittent vomiting, RLQ fullness, and currant jelly stools most likely has?
explanation: The classic findings indicate intussusception.

stem: A 3-day-old infant who has not passed stools since birth and shows abdominal distension is most likely suffering from?
explanation: Failure to pass meconium with distension points to Hirschsprung’s disease.

stem: 8-month-old boy is described by his mother as having 3 days of intermittent severe distress and restlessness and the recent passage of bloody motions and mucus-like material. There has been some vomiting and the abdomen is mildly distended and tender to examination. Which is the single most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Intermittent inconsolable distress, vomiting and ‘red-currant jelly’ stools in an infant is ileocolic intussusception; ultrasound shows a target sign.

stem: 6-week-old boy is brought to hospital with projectile and persistent vomiting. Weight gain has been poor. The child appears listless and quiet. A lump is palpable in the upper abdomen. Pulse is 100bpm, serum electrolytes are sodium 132mmol/L and potassium 3.2mmol/L. A provisional diagnosis of pyloric stenosis is made. Which is the single most appropriate initial intervention?
option_A: Administration of IV bicarbonate 8.4% solution (weight adjusted)
option_B: Administration of IV 0.9% sodium chloride (weight adjusted)
answer_text: Administration of IV 0.9% sodium chloride (weight adjusted)
explanation: Correct dehydration and electrolytes first with weight-adjusted IV 0.9% saline (then dextrose-saline with KCl) before pyloromyotomy; bicarbonate would worsen the alkalosis.
topics: Pyloric stenosis; Acid–base disorders; Helicobacter pylori

stem: 8-month-old boy is described by his mother as having 3 days of intermittent severe distress and restlessness and the recent passage of bloody motions and mucus-like material. There has been some vomiting and the abdomen is mildly distended and tender to examination. Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

A 2-month-old boy is examined because he has been straining while passing stool and has a distended abdomen. He is very low on the growth chart for age. A contrast enema is ordered by the primary care physician which shows a contracted segment of colon with dilated proximal colon. Which of the following is the best test for definitive diagnosis?
explanation: The definitive diagnosis is made by rectal biopsy.

stem: A newborn has an abdominal wall bulge with a 1-cm midline defect. There is no bowel present in the bulge. Which of the following is the best treatment option?
option_B: Observation with primary closure after age 4
option_C: Placement of a silo followed by primary closure
option_D: Emergency primary closure of the defect
option_E: Emergency closure of the defect with a prosthetic mesh
explanation: Umbilical hernias less than 1 cm close spontaneously by age 4.

stem: A neonate is examined in the nursery and found to have no anal orifice; only a small perineal fistulous opening is visualized. Which of the following is associated with this abnormality?
explanation: Imperforate anus is part of VACTERL association, which includes congenital heart disease.

stem: A 36-hour-old infant presents with bilious vomiting and an increasingly distended abdomen. At exploration, the segment pictured here is found as the point of obstruction. What is the likely etiology of this anomaly?
option_B: Failure of rotation of the ventral pancreatic bud
explanation: Ileal atresia is caused by an intrauterine mesenteric vascular accident leading to intestinal obstruction.

stem: Approximately 2 weeks after a viral respiratory illness, an 18-month-old child complains of abdominal pain and passes some bloody mucus per rectum. A long, thin mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. No peritoneal signs are present. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the workup?
explanation: Intussusception is diagnosed and treated with air enema.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain, fever, and leukocytosis. With the presumptive diagnosis of appendicitis, a right lower quadrant (McBurney) incision is made and a lesion 60 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve is identified (see photo). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Meckel diverticulum is a remnant of the omphalomesenteric duct, often located 60 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve.

stem: A newborn infant born with polyhydramnios presents with excessive salivation along with coughing and choking with the first oral feeding. An x-ray of the abdomen shows gas in stomach and a nasogastric tube coiled in the esophagus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Esophageal atresia with TEF is characterized by coiled NG tube and choking on feeding.

stem: A 2-week-old infant presents with sudden onset of bilious emesis. Plain films of the abdomen show evidence of an intestinal obstruction. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this infant?
option_D: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis
explanation: Upper GI series is the test of choice for diagnosing malrotation with volvulus.

stem: A 29-week-old previously healthy male infant presents with fevers, abdominal distention, feeding intolerance, and bloody stools at 3 weeks of age. The patient undergoes x-ray and ultrasound examination for possible necrotizing enterocolitis. Which of the following findings on imaging is an indication for surgical management?
explanation: Pneumoperitoneum indicates bowel perforation requiring surgical intervention.

stem: A newborn presents with signs and symptoms of distal intestinal obstruction. Abdominal x-rays reveal dilated loops of small bowel, absence of air-fluid levels, and a mass of meconium within the right side of the abdomen mixed with gas to give a ground-glass appearance. Which of the following should be performed as the initial management of the patient?
option_E: Resection of the dilated terminal ileum
explanation: Contrast enema is the initial management for meconium ileus to relieve obstruction.

stem: A 4-week-old male infant presents with projectile, nonbilious emesis. Ultrasound of the abdomen reveals a pyloric muscle thickness of 8 mm (normal 3 to 4 mm). Which of the following should be administered to the patient prior to operative intervention?
option_A: Nothing so as not to delay intervention
explanation: Fluid resuscitation with normal saline is needed to correct electrolyte imbalances before surgery.

stem: A 1-month-old female infant presents with persistent jaundice. A serum direct bilirubin is 4.0 mg/dL and an ultrasound of the abdomen shows a shrunken gallbladder and inability to visualize the extrahepatic bile ducts. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management of this patient?
explanation: Exploratory laparotomy is indicated for suspected biliary atresia, typically involving the Kasai procedure.

stem: A full-term male newborn experiences respiratory distress immediately after birth. A prenatal sonogram was read as normal. An emergency radiograph is shown here. The patient is intubated and placed on 100% O2. Arterial blood gases reveal pH 7.24, Po2 60, and Pco2 52. The baby has sternal retractions and a scaphoid abdomen. Which of the following should be performed in the management of this patient?
option_D: Immediate laparotomy with repair of the diaphragm
option_E: Mechanical ventilation with low tidal volumes
answer_text: Mechanical ventilation with low tidal volumes
explanation: Management includes mechanical ventilation with low tidal volumes to prevent lung injury in congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

stem: What is the most common type of tracheoesophageal fistula?
option_B: Type B: Esophageal atresia with proximal trachea fistula
option_C: Type C: Esophageal atresia with distal trachea fistula
option_D: Type D: Esophageal atresia with proximal and distal trachea fistulas
option_E: Type E: Tracheoesophageal fistula without esophageal atresia
answer_text: Type C: Esophageal atresia with distal trachea fistula
explanation: Type C is the most common form of tracheoesophageal fistula.

stem: What is the most common origin for neuroblastomas?
explanation: The adrenal gland is the most common origin for neuroblastomas.

stem: What are the electrolyte abnormalities noted with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
explanation: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis leads to hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

stem: What diagnosis is suggested by a double bubble sign on x-ray?
explanation: A double bubble sign on x-ray suggests duodenal atresia.

stem: What is the procedure for malrotation?
explanation: The Ladd procedure is the standard treatment for malrotation.

stem: Management of intussusception A 13-month-old girl is diagnosed with intussusception. She was admitted 2 hours ago with vomiting, passing red mucus-like stools and persistent crying. What is the most likely first line treatment option?
option_B: Radiological (air or contrast) enema reduction after an abdominal film
answer_text: Radiological (air or contrast) enema reduction after an abdominal film
explanation: First-line treatment of uncomplicated intussusception is image-guided air (pneumatic) or contrast enema reduction; surgery if it fails or there is peritonitis.

stem: Management of intussusception A 13-month-old girl is diagnosed with intussusception. She was admitted 2 hours ago with vomiting, passing red mucus-like stools and persistent crying. What is the most likely first line treatment option?
option_B: Barium enema per rectum and abdominal plain film radiography
answer_text: Barium enema per rectum and abdominal plain film radiography
explanation: Barium enema is the first line treatment for intussusception in children.

stem: A 2-day-old infant with Down syndrome has projectile vomiting and a scaphoid abdomen. X-ray shows a double-bubble sign with no distal bowel gas.
explanation: Double bubble without distal gas in a baby with Down syndrome is duodenal atresia (vomiting is usually bilious if post-ampullary).

emq_options: A) Hirschsprung disease | B) Malrotation with midgut volvulus | C) Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis | D) Meconium ileus | E) Duodenal atresia | F) Jejunoileal atresia | G) Necrotising enterocolitis | H) Intussusception
stem: A 2-week-old infant born at 28 weeks, in the NICU, develops sudden abdominal distension and bloody stool. X-ray shows gas in the bowel wall.
explanation: Pneumatosis intestinalis with distension and bloody stool in a preterm neonate is necrotising enterocolitis.

emq_options: A) Hirschsprung disease | B) Malrotation with midgut volvulus | C) Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis | D) Meconium ileus | E) Duodenal atresia | F) Jejunoileal atresia | G) Necrotising enterocolitis | H) Intussusception
stem: A full-term 2-day-old has not passed meconium, vomits bile and is distended. Rectal examination produces an explosive release of gas and liquid stool.
explanation: Delayed meconium with an explosive decompression on rectal examination is Hirschsprung disease; rectal suction biopsy confirms it.

emq_options: A) Hirschsprung disease | B) Malrotation with midgut volvulus | C) Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis | D) Meconium ileus | E) Duodenal atresia | F) Jejunoileal atresia | G) Necrotising enterocolitis | H) Intussusception
stem: A 5-day-old who was feeding well suddenly has bilious vomiting, tenderness and haemodynamic instability. Contrast shows the duodenojejunal flexure right of the spine with a corkscrew duodenum.
explanation: Bilious vomiting with an abnormally placed DJ flexure and corkscrew duodenum is malrotation with midgut volvulus: emergency Ladd procedure.

emq_options: A) Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis | B) Incarcerated inguinal hernia | C) Intussusception
stem: A 2-year-old boy has been sent in as an emergency with vomiting for 24 hours. According to the parents, the vomitus was greenish to start with but over the past few hours has consisted of dirty brownish fluid. There has been no bowel action. On examination the child looks toxic and is dehydrated - sunken eyes, depressed fontanelles, loss of skin turgor. There is a tympanitic abdomen with a red, irreducible swelling in the left groin not noticed by the parents.
explanation: Bilious then faeculent vomiting with a tender, irreducible groin swelling in a toxic, dehydrated toddler is an incarcerated (obstructed) inguinal hernia.
topics: Strangulated hernia; Inguinal hernia; Helicobacter pylori; Gastric outlet obstruction

emq_options: A) Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis | B) Incarcerated inguinal hernia | C) Intussusception
stem: Jonathan, a 5-week-old boy, has been vomiting intermittently for 2 weeks. This has become incessant for the past 24 hours. The vomitus is clear fluid. The infant seems hungry and takes its feed only to bring it up within a short while. The mother noticed some twitching of muscles. The baby is dehydrated. The paediatrician felt a lump in the upper abdomen when Jonathan was being fed by his mother.
explanation: Non-bilious vomiting in a hungry 5-week-old with a pyloric ‘olive’ felt during a feed is pyloric stenosis; the twitching (tetany) reflects metabolic alkalosis.
topics: Strangulated hernia; Inguinal hernia; Helicobacter pylori; Gastric outlet obstruction

emq_options: A) Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis | B) Incarcerated inguinal hernia | C) Intussusception
stem: Mary-Ann, a 10-month-old girl, has been brought in with occasional vomiting for a couple of days. The parents noticed that the vomitus is sometimes green and at other times brownish. They feel that Mary-Ann is in pain intermittently, because she screams, flexing her knees and elbows, denoting spasms. They noticed that the nappy has bloodstained mucus. On examination she looks ill and dehydrated, and the right side of the abdomen feels empty.
explanation: Colicky screaming episodes, vomiting and redcurrant-jelly stool with an empty right iliac fossa (Dance sign) in a 10-month-old is intussusception.
topics: Strangulated hernia; Inguinal hernia; Helicobacter pylori; Gastric outlet obstruction

emq_options: A) Acute appendicitis | B) Nonspecific abdominal pain | C) Urinary tract infection
stem: George, a 10-year-old boy has been brought in with abdominal pain, vomiting, pyrexia and diarrhoea for the past 24 hours or so. He has been off his food for a couple of days. He has pyrexia of 39°C, tachycardia, looks toxic and has marked lower abdominal tenderness, rigidity and rebound tenderness, and the abdominal wall does not move with respiration.
explanation: High fever, toxicity, rebound and rigidity with an abdominal wall that does not move on respiration indicate perforated appendicitis with peritonitis.
topics: Acute abdomen; Appendicitis; Peritonitis; Acute pyelonephritis

emq_options: A) Acute appendicitis | B) Nonspecific abdominal pain | C) Urinary tract infection
stem: Kerry, a 5-year-old girl, has been brought in by her parents with generalised abdominal pain, which has been recurrent over 6 months or so. On this occasion she looks ill, out of sorts and anorexic, and she has been vomiting. She has marked urinary frequency. On examination she has a temperature of 38°C, looks toxic, listless and dehydrated and has generalised abdominal and bilateral loin tenderness.
explanation: Fever, vomiting, urinary frequency and bilateral loin tenderness indicate UTI (pyelonephritis); recurrent episodes warrant imaging for reflux or obstruction.
topics: Acute abdomen; Appendicitis; Peritonitis; Acute pyelonephritis

emq_options: A) Acute appendicitis | B) Nonspecific abdominal pain | C) Urinary tract infection
stem: Millie, a 10-year-old girl, has been admitted with generalised abdominal pain, vomiting and anorexia for 2 days. She has missed school a few times because of similar attacks of abdominal pain in the past, which has subsided on its own within 24 hours. On this occasion it has persisted. Examination revealed a well-looking introspective child with generalised abdominal tenderness without any rigidity or rebound tenderness, with the abdominal wall moving freely with respiration.
explanation: A well child with recurrent self-limiting pain and soft generalised tenderness without peritonism has non-specific abdominal pain, the commonest diagnosis in children.
topics: Acute abdomen; Appendicitis; Peritonitis; Acute pyelonephritis

stem: A 2-month-old Down’s syndrome baby has been brought in with gradual abdominal distension and intermittent bilious vomiting with a history of delayed passage of meconium. The parents feel that the baby is unduly constipated. Examination shows a baby that has not been thriving normally, with a hugely distended abdomen and gross dehydration.
explanation: Delayed meconium, chronic constipation, distension and failure to thrive in a Down syndrome infant suggest Hirschsprung disease; confirm by suction rectal biopsy.
topics: Hirschsprung disease; Congenital diaphragmatic hernia; Oesophageal atresia; Duodenal atresia

stem: A prenatal ultrasound scan alerted the paediatricians to a congenital abnormality affecting the abdomen and chest. The premature neonate has been born with severe respiratory compromise and is on ventilatory support in the neonatal ICU.
explanation: Antenatally detected abdominal contents in the chest with severe respiratory failure at birth is congenital diaphragmatic hernia; stabilise first, repair later.
topics: Hirschsprung disease; Congenital diaphragmatic hernia; Oesophageal atresia; Duodenal atresia

explanation: Frothy saliva, choking on feeds and an orogastric tube coiled in the chest with gas in the abdomen is oesophageal atresia with distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula.
topics: Hirschsprung disease; Congenital diaphragmatic hernia; Oesophageal atresia; Duodenal atresia

explanation: Polyhydramnios, Down syndrome, bilious vomiting and a ‘double-bubble’ X-ray indicate duodenal atresia, treated by duodenoduodenostomy.
topics: Hirschsprung disease; Congenital diaphragmatic hernia; Oesophageal atresia; Duodenal atresia

explanation: Bilious vomiting with bloody stools and a subhepatic caecum on contrast study is malrotation with midgut volvulus: emergency Ladd procedure.
topics: Hirschsprung disease; Congenital diaphragmatic hernia; Oesophageal atresia; Duodenal atresia

stem: A 2-week-old neonate who was born with jaundice has exhibited increasing yellowish discoloration of skin and conjunctiva ever since birth. There are some superficial skin bruises.
explanation: Jaundice persisting beyond 2 weeks with bruising (vitamin K malabsorption) suggests biliary atresia; Kasai portoenterostomy is best before 6–8 weeks.
topics: Hirschsprung disease; Congenital diaphragmatic hernia; Oesophageal atresia; Duodenal atresia

explanation: Distension, bloody stools and bilious vomiting with septic shock in a neonate is necrotising enterocolitis (pneumatosis intestinalis on X-ray).
topics: Hirschsprung disease; Congenital diaphragmatic hernia; Oesophageal atresia; Duodenal atresia

stem: A 7-month-old child is brought to A&E crying inconsolably and drawing his legs up. He has had one episode of vomiting and has been passing bloody stools. On examination a small mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant.
explanation: Inconsolable colicky crying with legs drawn up, vomiting, bloody stools and a right upper quadrant mass in a 7-month-old is intussusception.
topics: Intussusception; Helicobacter pylori; Gastric outlet obstruction; Pyloric stenosis

There is no history of diarrhoea. On examination the child looks dehydrated and malnourished. Gastric peristalsis is visible.
explanation: Projectile non-bilious vomiting in a hungry 6-week-old with visible gastric peristalsis is pyloric stenosis; rehydrate, then pyloromyotomy.
topics: Intussusception; Helicobacter pylori; Gastric outlet obstruction; Pyloric stenosis

explanation: Failure to pass meconium in 48 hours with distension and no rectal gas is Hirschsprung disease; confirm by suction rectal biopsy.
topics: Intussusception; Helicobacter pylori; Gastric outlet obstruction; Pyloric stenosis

explanation: Bilious vomiting from birth, a scaphoid abdomen and a ‘double bubble’ in a trisomy 21 neonate indicate duodenal atresia.
topics: Intussusception; Helicobacter pylori; Gastric outlet obstruction; Pyloric stenosis

explanation: In the 65-year-old man with suspected diverticulitis not responding to conservative management, a CT abdomen scan is essential to assess for complications.

explanation: Recent URTI, cervical lymphadenopathy, low-grade fever and a normal white count suggest mesenteric adenitis; active observation is appropriate.

explanation: A preterm neonate with bloody stools and pneumatosis but no perforation has necrotising enterocolitis: bowel rest, NG decompression and broad-spectrum antibiotics.

explanation: Bilious vomiting with gas only in the stomach and duodenal cap (‘double bubble’) indicates duodenal atresia.

explanation: Delayed meconium and distension suggest Hirschsprung disease.

explanation: Gastroschisis is a para-umbilical (usually right-sided) defect with uncovered bowel; exomphalos is a central defect with a membrane-covered sac that may contain liver.

explanation: RIF pain with systemic features indicates appendicitis.
topics: Stoma; Duodenal atresia; Hirschsprung disease; Gastroschisis

stem: A 6-year-old girl presents with an episode of painless rectal bleeding. She complains of no other symptoms and she otherwise feels well. Rectal examination shows no obvious abnormality.
explanation: Painless rectal bleeding in a well child is typically a Meckel diverticulum (ectopic gastric mucosa); confirm with a technetium-99m pertechnetate scan.
topics: Stoma; Duodenal atresia; Hirschsprung disease; Gastroschisis

stem: A 71-year-old male smoker with hypertension and type 2 diabetes has felt a pulsating abdominal mass with dull pain radiating to the back for 2 months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A pulsatile, expansile abdominal mass with back pain in an elderly hypertensive smoker is an abdominal aortic aneurysm.

stem: A 71-year-old male smoker with hypertension and type 2 diabetes has felt a pulsating abdominal mass with dull pain radiating to the back for 2 months. What is the gold-standard diagnostic test?
explanation: Ultrasound screens and follows AAA, but CT angiography defines size, extent and neck anatomy for repair planning.

stem: A 71-year-old male smoker with hypertension and type 2 diabetes has felt a pulsating abdominal mass with dull pain radiating to the back for 2 months. He suddenly develops pain in the right leg with an absent dorsalis pedis pulse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sudden pain with a lost pulse is acute limb ischaemia, here from embolism of aneurysm thrombus.

stem: A 71-year-old male smoker with hypertension and type 2 diabetes has felt a pulsating abdominal mass with dull pain radiating to the back for 2 months. What is the first-line management of this complication?
explanation: Give IV unfractionated heparin immediately to stop clot propagation, then embolectomy or thrombolysis according to limb viability.

stem: A young woman has right iliac fossa pain, low-grade fever, anorexia and dysuria, and is diagnosed with appendicitis. Which test is 100% reliable for diagnosing appendicitis?
explanation: Imaging and scores support the diagnosis, but only direct inspection at laparoscopy with histology confirms it.

stem: A young woman has right iliac fossa pain, low-grade fever, anorexia and dysuria, and is diagnosed with appendicitis. Given the presentation, where is the appendix?
explanation: A pelvic appendix lies against the bladder and causes dysuria and frequency (and diarrhoea if near the rectum).

stem: A young woman has right iliac fossa pain, low-grade fever, anorexia and dysuria, and is diagnosed with appendicitis. Which investigation will you request?
explanation: The white-cell count (leucocytosis with left shift) is part of the Alvarado score; urinalysis and a pregnancy test are also essential.

stem: Which two Alvarado (MANTRELS) criteria each score 2 points?
option_B: Right iliac fossa tenderness and leucocytosis
answer_text: Right iliac fossa tenderness and leucocytosis
explanation: RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2 each; migration, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, rebound, fever and left shift score 1 (total 10).

stem: Which is NOT an advantage of laparoscopic over open appendicectomy?
option_C: Shorter stay and earlier return to work
option_D: Allows inspection of the pelvis and other diagnoses
explanation: Laparoscopy reduces pain, wound infection and stay and is diagnostic; the intra-abdominal abscess rate is not lower (it may be slightly higher).

stem: An erect chest X-ray is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis on this image?
explanation: Free gas under both hemidiaphragms on an erect film means pneumoperitoneum, usually a perforated viscus.

stem: Regarding imaging in the acute abdomen, all of the following statements are true except:
option_A: US is a good first-line investigation.
option_B: CT is the best investigation for acute diverticulitis.
option_C: Plain x-ray of KUB (kidney, ureter, bladder) is the best imaging for suspected ureteric colic.
option_D: US and CT can diagnose the cause and site of intestinal obstruction.
option_E: Plain x-ray is the first-line investigation for suspected perforation or obstruction.
answer_text: Plain x-ray of KUB (kidney, ureter, bladder) is the best imaging for suspected ureteric colic.
explanation: Plain films have limited utility in ureteric colic; non-contrast CT is preferred.

stem: Regarding examination of the abdomen, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Abdominal examination must always be preceded by general examination.
option_B: Abdominal discoloration at specific sites denotes underlying serious pathology.
option_C: Free movement of the abdominal wall on respiration makes generalised peritonitis unlikely.
option_D: Rebound tenderness is best tested by gentle percussion.
option_E: An intra-abdominal lump becomes prominent when the patient tenses the abdomen or lifts the head from the bed.
answer_text: Abdominal examination must always be preceded by general examination. | Abdominal discoloration at specific sites denotes underlying serious pathology. | Free movement of the abdominal wall on respiration makes generalised peritonitis unlikely. | Rebound tenderness is best tested by gentle percussion.
explanation: False: E — an intra-abdominal lump becomes less prominent when the abdominal muscles are tensed (head-raising test); a lump in the abdominal wall stays palpable.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
option_A: The surface area of the peritoneum is nearly equal to that of the skin.
option_B: The parietal peritoneum is poorly innervated.
option_C: The peritoneum has the capacity to absorb large volumes of fluid.
option_D: The peritoneum has the ability to produce fibrinolytic activity.
option_E: When injured, the peritoneum produces an inflammatory exudate.
answer_text: The surface area of the peritoneum is nearly equal to that of the skin. | The peritoneum has the capacity to absorb large volumes of fluid. | The peritoneum has the ability to produce fibrinolytic activity. | When injured, the peritoneum produces an inflammatory exudate.
explanation: The peritoneum is extensive, absorptive, and fibrinolytic, producing inflammatory exudate when injured; note that the parietal peritoneum is well innervated.

stem: The following organisms are a gastrointestinal (GI) source of peritonitis except:
explanation: Chlamydia is not typically a GI organism, unlike the other common gut flora.

stem: Regarding localised and diffuse peritonitis, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Peritonitis gets localised because of anatomical factors.
option_B: The greater omentum plays an important role in localising infection.
option_C: Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) has a vital role in diagnosis.
option_D: CT scan is useful for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.
option_E: Operation is not necessary in all patients with peritonitis.
answer_text: Peritonitis gets localised because of anatomical factors. | The greater omentum plays an important role in localising infection. | CT scan is useful for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. | Operation is not necessary in all patients with peritonitis.
explanation: Anatomical factors and the omentum help localise infection; CT scanning aids both diagnosis and management, while DPL is now rarely used.

stem: Regarding the management of peritonitis, which of the following statements is not true?
option_A: All patients should be thoroughly resuscitated.
option_B: A paracolic abscess on CT scan must have open surgery.
option_D: Nutritional support must be instituted in certain patients.
option_E: Young children do not have the natural barrier against the spread of peritonitis.
answer_text: A paracolic abscess on CT scan must have open surgery.
explanation: Most paracolic abscesses are managed by percutaneous drainage rather than open surgery.

stem: Regarding special forms of peritonitis, all of the following statements are true except:
option_A: Bile peritonitis is usually a feature following operation.
option_B: A leucocytosis of >30,000 with 90% polymorphs is suggestive of pneumococcal peritonitis.
option_D: Tuberculosis (TB) spreads from the ileocaecal region.
option_E: Diagnostic smear will be positive in the vast majority of cases of tuberculosis.
answer_text: Diagnostic smear will be positive in the vast majority of cases of tuberculosis.
explanation: Acid-fast smears are positive in only a small percentage of TB peritonitis cases; the other statements are correct.

stem: Regarding intraperitoneal abscess, which of the following statements are correct?
option_A: The pelvis is the commonest site of intraperitoneal abscess.
option_B: Pus can also collect in four other intraperitoneal sites.
option_D: Pain may be a feature well away from the site of pathology.
option_E: Open operation and drainage is the treatment of choice.
answer_text: The pelvis is the commonest site of intraperitoneal abscess. | Pus can also collect in four other intraperitoneal sites. | The usual cause is postoperative. | Pain may be a feature well away from the site of pathology.
explanation: Intraperitoneal abscesses most commonly occur in the pelvis, are often postoperative, and pain may be referred; open drainage is now largely replaced by percutaneous methods.

stem: Regarding ascites, which of the following statements are not true?
option_A: Imbalance between plasma and peritoneal colloid osmotic and hydrostatic pressure causes ascites.
option_B: Shifting dullness is a classical sign in all cases of ascites.
option_C: The protein content determines if the ascitic fluid is a transudate or an exudate.
option_D: A peritoneovenous shunt should be considered in all cases of ascites.
option_E: Chylous ascites is most commonly caused by malignancy.
answer_text: Shifting dullness is a classical sign in all cases of ascites. | A peritoneovenous shunt should be considered in all cases of ascites.
explanation: Shifting dullness may be absent in massive ascites and peritoneovenous shunts are reserved for refractory cases only.

stem: Regarding tumours of the peritoneum, which of the following statements are true?
option_B: Carcinomatosis peritonei is usually a terminal event.
option_C: Pseudomyxoma peritonei arises from a primary tumour from the appendix.
option_D: Repeated ‘debulking surgery’ in pseudomyxoma peritonei gives relief.
option_E: Peritoneal loose bodies are malignant in origin.
answer_text: Secondary tumours are more common. | Carcinomatosis peritonei is usually a terminal event. | Pseudomyxoma peritonei arises from a primary tumour from the appendix. | Repeated ‘debulking surgery’ in pseudomyxoma peritonei gives relief.
explanation: Secondary peritoneal tumours are most common, pseudomyxoma peritonei is typically appendiceal, and debulking can offer symptom relief; peritoneal loose bodies are benign.

stem: Regarding adhesions, all of the following statements are true except:
option_A: Ischaemic tissue inhibits fibrinolysis encouraging formation of adhesions.
option_C: Adhesions are responsible for two-thirds of small bowel obstructions.
option_D: Prevention of adhesions can be actively achieved.
option_E: Intestinal obstruction from sclerosing encapsulating peritonitis should be treated by surgery.
answer_text: Prevention of adhesions can be actively achieved. | Intestinal obstruction from sclerosing encapsulating peritonitis should be treated by surgery.
explanation: There is no guaranteed method to prevent adhesions and sclerosing encapsulating peritonitis is generally managed non‐operatively.

stem: Regarding the omentum and mesentery, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Torsion of the omentum always presents as an emergency.
option_B: Mesenteric injury occurs as a seatbelt syndrome.
option_C: Acute nonspecific ileocaecal mesenteric adenitis can be confused with acute appendicitis.
option_D: A mesenteric cyst clinically presents as a fixed periumbilical mass.
option_E: Chylolymphatic cyst is the commonest type of mesenteric cyst.
answer_text: Torsion of the omentum always presents as an emergency. | Mesenteric injury occurs as a seatbelt syndrome. | Acute nonspecific ileocaecal mesenteric adenitis can be confused with acute appendicitis. | Chylolymphatic cyst is the commonest type of mesenteric cyst.
explanation: False: D — a mesenteric cyst is a mobile periumbilical mass that moves at right angles to the line of the mesentery (Tillaux sign).

stem: Regarding the retroperitoneal space, which of the following statements is not true?
option_A: Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis can present as chronic renal failure.
option_B: An AAA can cause retroperitoneal fibrosis.
option_C: Retroperitoneal fibrosis is always a benign condition.
option_D: Retroperitoneal abscess may be a manifestation of vertebral tuberculosis.
option_E: Retroperitoneal lipoma is often a sarcoma.
answer_text: Retroperitoneal fibrosis is always a benign condition.
explanation: Retroperitoneal fibrosis may be secondary to malignancy and is not always benign.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe epigastric pain and vomiting 3 hours ago. He reports a 6-month history of chronic epigastric pain occurring nearly every day and relieved by antacids. On examination, he appears sweaty and avoids movement. Vital signs reveal a temperature of 100°F, BP of 100/60 mmHg, pulse rate of 110/min, and respiratory rate of 12/min. The remainder of his examination reveals diminished bowel sounds and a markedly tender and rigid abdomen. A chest x-ray and abdominal films reveal pneumoperitoneum. For the patient with a perforated duodenal ulcer described above, what is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?
explanation: Peritonitis with pneumoperitoneum on plain films in a patient with ulcer symptoms is enough to proceed to surgery; further imaging only delays treatment.
topics: Peritonitis; Perforated peptic ulcer; Peptic ulcer

stem: What is the most appropriate next step in management for the perforated duodenal ulcer patient?
option_B: Non-operative management with NG decompression and antibiotics
option_E: Placement of a central venous line
explanation: Resuscitate with IV fluids (plus analgesia, antibiotics and a urinary catheter) before urgent laparotomy and omental patch repair; a central line is not the priority.
topics: Fluid therapy; Perforated peptic ulcer; Peptic ulcer

stem: A 47-year-old man with a history of liver cirrhosis and well known on the general medical ward after recurrent admissions for drainage of ascites. He presents with confusion, fever (38.5°C), ascites and abdominal pain. Which of the following investigations is most important to establish the diagnosis?
option_A: Stool culture and microscopy for ova, cysts and parasites
explanation: Ascitic fluid analysis is crucial in diagnosing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhotic patients.

stem: An 83-year-old man is admitted with acute onset of severe epigastric pain and has ‘board-like’ rigidity of the upper abdomen. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 124bpm, blood pressure 104/75mmHg. A working diagnosis of visceral perforation is made and investigations planned. Which is the single most appropriate fluid prescription to administer?
option_B: IV O-negative blood 2 units, run in
option_E: IV whole cross-matched blood 2 units, over 4h
explanation: A tachycardic patient with peritonitis needs prompt balanced crystalloid resuscitation (500 mL bolus over <15 min, then reassess); blood is for haemorrhage and bicarbonate is not indicated.

stem: 27-year-old woman has had 4 days of gradually increasing, diffuse lower abdominal pain and 6h of acute severe worsening of the pain. Her abdomen is tender with guarding in the lower half. Her temperate is 37.2°C, pulse 104bpm, blood pressure 104/56mmHg, and capillary refill approximately 6sec. Which is the single most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Increasing lower abdominal pain with sudden worsening, guarding, tachycardia and poor capillary refill in a young woman is a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until a pregnancy test excludes it.

stem: Splenic trauma : A 35-year-old man was involved in a motor vehicle collision where he was thrown against the steering column. He sustained a blunt trauma injury to his left upper abdomen. On arrival at the emergency department, he complains of abdominal pain, but is haemodynamically stable. Computed tomography (CT) scanning shows a splenic tear and retained intra-abdominal haematoma. The tear extends through the splenic capsule, but not to the hilum. Which one of the following treatment options is not indicated in this case?
option_E: 24-hour monitoring in the high-dependency/intensive care setting

stem: Management of an abdominal aortic aneurysm A 65-year-old man is admitted following an acute episode of abdominal pain and collapse. The pain is intermittent and radiates to the back and iliac fossae. On examination, the patient appears confused, is sweating and has tachycardia. On inspection, the abdomen appears normal, but on palpation, you discover a pulsatile, expansile swelling in the midline. What is the most important next step?
option_A: Establish large-bore intravenous access, cross-match blood and begin cautious (permissive hypotensive) resuscitation
option_B: Send for a computed tomography scan of the abdomen
option_C: Obtain blood to determine haemoglobin and amylase levels
option_D: Request an abdominal plain film radiograph
answer_text: Establish large-bore intravenous access, cross-match blood and begin cautious (permissive hypotensive) resuscitation
explanation: A shocked patient with a pulsatile mass has a ruptured AAA: secure IV access, cross-match and resuscitate to permissive hypotension en route to theatre; CT only if stable.

stem: A man has fever, malaise and tender hepatomegaly after diarrhoea following travel to Nasiriyah. Ultrasound shows a 7-cm cystic liver lesion; blood cultures are negative. What is the most likely organism?
explanation: Fever, tender hepatomegaly and a liver abscess after dysentery with sterile blood cultures is an amoebic liver abscess.

stem: A man has fever, malaise and tender hepatomegaly after diarrhoea following travel to Nasiriyah. Ultrasound shows a 7-cm cystic liver lesion; blood cultures are negative. How did the organism reach the liver?
option_B: Haematogenous spread via the hepatic artery
option_C: Via the portal vein from the colon
option_D: Ascending infection via the bile duct
answer_text: Via the portal vein from the colon
explanation: Trophozoites invade the colonic mucosa and travel in the portal venous blood to the liver (usually the right lobe).

stem: A man has fever, malaise and tender hepatomegaly after diarrhoea following travel to Nasiriyah. Ultrasound shows a 7-cm cystic liver lesion; blood cultures are negative. He receives a second-generation cephalosporin and metronidazole, and the cyst is aspirated. What does the aspirate show?
explanation: Amoebic abscess fluid is odourless, reddish-brown "anchovy sauce" (liquefied liver); pyogenic abscesses contain yellow pus.

stem: A man has fever, malaise and tender hepatomegaly after diarrhoea following travel to Nasiriyah. Ultrasound shows a 7-cm cystic liver lesion; blood cultures are negative. Which additional treatment is essential?
explanation: After metronidazole, a luminal amoebicide (diloxanide furoate or paromomycin) is needed to clear intestinal cysts and prevent relapse.

stem: A contrast CT of the upper abdomen of a febrile patient is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis on this image?
explanation: A large hypodense collection with an enhancing wall and necrotic debris in the right lobe is a liver abscess.

stem: Which of the following statements is not true?
option_A: The falciform ligament of the liver divides it into functional right and left units.
option_B: The right and left triangular ligaments help to fix the liver and keep it in its place.
option_C: The main blood supply of the liver is derived from the portal vein.
option_D: The right hepatic vein has an extrahepatic course while the middle and left hepatic veins join the inferior vena cava within the liver.
option_E: The left intrahepatic duct has a longer extrahepatic course than the right.
answer_text: The falciform ligament of the liver divides it into functional right and left units.
explanation: The functional division of the liver is determined by Cantlie’s line, not the falciform ligament.

stem: Which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Cantlie’s line passes through the gallbladder fossa and middle hepatic vein.
option_B: The functional right and left units divided by Cantlie’s line are further subdivided into four segments on each side.
option_C: The free edge of the lesser omentum contains the hepatic artery, bile duct and portal vein.
option_D: The portal vein is formed by the union of the superior and inferior mesenteric veins.
option_E: The structures at the porta hepatis are the portal vein, bile ducts, hepatic artery and hepatic veins.
answer_text: Cantlie’s line passes through the gallbladder fossa and middle hepatic vein. | The functional right and left units divided by Cantlie’s line are further subdivided into four segments on each side. | The free edge of the lesser omentum contains the hepatic artery, bile duct and portal vein.
explanation: Cantlie’s line and the segmentation of the liver are as stated; note that the portal vein forms from the superior mesenteric and splenic veins and hepatic veins do not traverse the porta hepatis.

stem: Which of the following liver function tests (LFTs) are abnormal?
answer_text: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 135–240 IU/L | Aspartate transaminase (AST) 55–80 IU/L | Alanine transaminase (ALT) 110–148 IU/L
explanation: Normal adult values: bilirubin <17–21 µmol/L, ALP ~30–130 IU/L, AST/ALT <40 IU/L, GGT <50 IU/L; ranges B, C and D lie wholly above normal.

stem: Regarding liver imaging, which of the following statements are true?
option_B: Nuclear medicine scanning gives an idea of the extent of anatomical derangement.
option_C: The ‘gold standard’ is contrast-enhanced computed tomographic scan (CECT).
option_D: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has advantages over CECT.
option_E: Angiography is best reserved when embolisation is contemplated.
answer_text: Ultrasound (US) is the first-line investigation. | The ‘gold standard’ is contrast-enhanced computed tomographic scan (CECT). | Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has advantages over CECT. | Angiography is best reserved when embolisation is contemplated.
explanation: US is used first, CECT is the gold standard, MRI offers high-resolution detail, and angiography is reserved for embolisation; nuclear scans provide functional rather than anatomical data.

stem: Regarding acute and chronic liver disease, which of the following statements are not true?
option_A: The overall mortality from acute liver failure is about 50%.
option_B: Chronic congestive heart failure is a terminal event in chronic liver disease.
option_C: The most useful clinical sign is flapping tremor.
option_D: Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score depends upon INR, serum bilirubin and serum creatinine.
option_E: Liver transplantation has good short-term results in acute liver failure.
answer_text: Chronic congestive heart failure is a terminal event in chronic liver disease. | Liver transplantation has good short-term results in acute liver failure.
explanation: Chronic CHF is not the terminal event in chronic liver disease and liver transplantation in acute liver failure carries high short-term risk.

stem: Regarding liver trauma, which of the following statements are not true?
option_B: Blunt trauma is often associated with splenic, mesenteric and renal injuries.
option_C: Penetrating trauma is often associated with pericardial or chest injuries.
option_D: CECT scan must be carried out in every case of liver trauma.
option_E: Interventional radiology has a role in the management of liver injury.
answer_text: CECT scan must be carried out in every case of liver trauma.
explanation: False: D — CECT is only for haemodynamically stable patients; unstable patients go straight to laparotomy. The liver is one of the most commonly injured abdominal organs.

stem: Which of these statements are true?
option_A: Penetrating injuries with haemodynamic instability or peritonitis should be explored.
option_B: Blunt injuries are usually treated conservatively.
option_C: Exploration for a liver injury is best done by a long midline incision.
option_D: Severe crush injury is ideally treated by packing.
option_E: Venovenous bypass should be considered in major liver vascular injury.
answer_text: Penetrating injuries with haemodynamic instability or peritonitis should be explored. | Blunt injuries are usually treated conservatively. | Exploration for a liver injury is best done by a long midline incision. | Severe crush injury is ideally treated by packing. | Venovenous bypass should be considered in major liver vascular injury.
explanation: All true: unstable or peritonitic penetrating injuries need laparotomy via a long midline incision; most blunt injuries settle conservatively; packing controls crush injury.

stem: Regarding portal hypertension, all of the following statements are true except:
option_A: Acute haematemesis from portal hypertension occurs most commonly from gastric varices.
option_B: Initial endoscopic treatment of oesophageal varices with banding, as opposed to injection sclerotherapy, has less chance of oesophageal ulceration.
option_C: Long-term beta-blocker therapy coupled with sclerotherapy regime or endoscopic banding is the mainstay of treatment of portal hypertension.
option_D: In failed drug or endoscopic treatment, the ideal choice is the surgical shunt of portocaval anastomosis.
option_E: Ascites in cirrhosis can be treated by a peritoneovenous shunt.
answer_text: Acute haematemesis from portal hypertension occurs most commonly from gastric varices. | In failed drug or endoscopic treatment, the ideal choice is the surgical shunt of portocaval anastomosis.
explanation: Oesophageal varices (not gastric varices) are the most common source of acute haematemesis in portal hypertension, and TIPSS is preferred to surgical shunts.
topics: Upper GI bleeding; Portal hypertension; Oesophageal varices

stem: Which of the following are true of amoebiasis?
option_A: The disease is common in the Indian subcontinent, Africa and parts of Central and South America.
option_B: The majority of sufferers are symptomatic.
option_C: Amoebic liver abscess, the most common extraintestinal manifestation, occurs in more than 50% of cases.
option_D: The mode of infection is via the faeco-oral route due to poor hygiene and sanitation.
option_E: The organism enters the gut via contaminated food and water.
answer_text: The disease is common in the Indian subcontinent, Africa and parts of Central and South America. | The mode of infection is via the faeco-oral route due to poor hygiene and sanitation. | The organism enters the gut via contaminated food and water.
explanation: False: most infected people are asymptomatic (B), and amoebic liver abscess, although the commonest extraintestinal manifestation, occurs in a minority, not >50% (C).
topics: Amoebic liver abscess; Pyogenic liver abscess

stem: Entamoeba histolytica, the causative organism, enters the body as cysts contaminating water or food. Which of the following occurs?
option_A: The cysts hatch in the large bowel and colonise the colon.
option_B: The cysts cause flask-shaped ulcers in the colon.
option_C: The trophozoites may invade the wall of the colon and pass to the liver via the portal circulation, causing focal infarction and liquefactive necrosis in the liver.
option_D: Cysts are passed in the faeces in an infective form.
option_E: The right lobe of the liver is affected in 10% of cases, the left in 80% and the rest are multiple.
answer_text: The cysts cause flask-shaped ulcers in the colon. | The trophozoites may invade the wall of the colon and pass to the liver via the portal circulation, causing focal infarction and liquefactive necrosis in the liver. | Cysts are passed in the faeces in an infective form.
explanation: False: excystation occurs in the terminal ileum, with trophozoites colonising the colon (A), and the right lobe is involved in about 80% of cases, not 10% (E).

stem: A middle-aged man presents with RUQ pain, fever, night sweats, and weight loss, with imaging showing a hypoechoic/hypodense liver lesion. Which statements are true?
option_A: Although the clinical features are suggestive of amoebiasis, a history of travel to an endemic area and bloody diarrhoea may also be present.
option_B: The CT scan is compatible with an amoebic liver abscess.
option_C: The abscess cavity contains blackcurrant jelly-like fluid.
option_D: The collection is normally odourless and sterile but becomes malodorous if secondarily infected.
option_E: Trophozoites may be found in the wall of the abscess cavity in a minority of cases.
answer_text: Although the clinical features are suggestive of amoebiasis, a history of travel to an endemic area and bloody diarrhoea may also be present. | The CT scan is compatible with an amoebic liver abscess. | The collection is normally odourless and sterile but becomes malodorous if secondarily infected. | Trophozoites may be found in the wall of the abscess cavity in a minority of cases.
explanation: C is false: amoebic abscess fluid is classically reddish-brown 'anchovy sauce', not blackcurrant jelly; trophozoites are found in the wall rather than the pus.
topics: Amoebic liver abscess; Pyogenic liver abscess

stem: Which of the following are presenting features of amoebiasis?
option_A: Chronic diarrhoea, often blood-stained, with colicky abdominal pain.
option_B: Pain in the upper right abdomen and right shoulder-tip with hiccoughs and a painful dry cough.
option_C: An apple-core lesion on barium enema due to a chronic granuloma (amoeboma), most commonly in the caecum.
option_D: Features of peritonitis with shock (due to abscess rupture).
explanation: Amoebiasis may present with colitis, liver abscess, amoeboma and, rarely, rupture with peritonitis.

stem: What is the treatment for an amoebic liver abscess?
option_B: Medical treatment with metronidazole or tinidazole.
option_C: Medical treatment with diloxanide furoate alone is sufficient.
option_D: Aspiration may be carried out for abscesses at risk of imminent rupture.
option_E: Surgical treatment is indicated for a ruptured liver abscess, severe haemorrhage/toxic megacolon, and a suspected amoeboma not responding to treatment or where carcinoma cannot be excluded.
answer_text: Medical treatment with metronidazole or tinidazole. | Aspiration may be carried out for abscesses at risk of imminent rupture. | Surgical treatment is indicated for a ruptured liver abscess, severe haemorrhage/toxic megacolon, and a suspected amoeboma not responding to treatment or where carcinoma cannot be excluded.
explanation: Metronidazole or tinidazole is first-line, with aspiration for impending rupture and surgery for complications. Laparotomy is not routine (A); diloxanide alone treats only luminal cysts (C).
topics: Pyogenic liver abscess; Toxic megacolon; Amoebic liver abscess

stem: Which of the following are true regarding hydatid disease caused by Echinococcus granulosus?
option_C: Sheep and cattle are intermediate hosts.
option_D: The disease causes cystic lesions mainly in the liver but may affect any organ.
option_E: The disease causes an infiltrative process in the liver without well-defined margins.
answer_text: Dog is the definitive host. | Sheep and cattle are intermediate hosts. | The disease causes cystic lesions mainly in the liver but may affect any organ.
explanation: False: man is an accidental intermediate host, not definitive (A); E. granulosus forms well-defined cysts, whereas E. multilocularis infiltrates like a tumour (E).

stem: How is hydatid disease transmitted?
option_A: By eating infected meat (thus affecting only non-vegetarians).
option_B: By the faeco-oral route through ingestion of eggs.
option_C: Through skin penetration by larvae in contaminated soil.
option_D: It may be transmitted by vectors.
answer_text: By the faeco-oral route through ingestion of eggs.
explanation: Ingestion of eggs from infected dog faeces is the key mode of transmission.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding cystic hydatid disease are true?
option_A: It contains an outer pericyst formed by living parasites.
option_B: It contains an intermediate ectocyst that is non-infective.
option_C: It contains an inner endocyst with a germinal membrane that contains viable parasites.
option_D: The germinal membrane may give rise to daughter cysts.
option_E: It spreads to the liver by travelling along the intestinal lymphatics.
answer_text: It contains an intermediate ectocyst that is non-infective. | It contains an inner endocyst with a germinal membrane that contains viable parasites. | The germinal membrane may give rise to daughter cysts.
explanation: Hydatid cysts have a host-derived pericyst, a non-infective ectocyst, and a germinal layer that produces daughter cysts; spread is via the portal system.

stem: Which of the following features are common presentations of hydatid disease?
option_A: Chest symptoms of dry cough with fluffy exudates (Loeffler’s syndrome).
option_B: Dull aching pain in the upper right abdomen.
option_C: Abdominal pain, anaphylactic shock, and collapse after trivial trauma (due to cyst rupture).
option_D: Patients often complain of passing live worms in stool.
answer_text: Dull aching pain in the upper right abdomen. | Abdominal pain, anaphylactic shock, and collapse after trivial trauma (due to cyst rupture). | Features of obstructive jaundice.
explanation: False: Loeffler syndrome (A) and passing live worms (D) are features of ascariasis. Hydatid cysts cause dull RUQ pain, anaphylaxis on rupture and jaundice from biliary rupture.

stem: Which ultrasound features characterize a hepatic hydatid cyst?
option_B: A cyst wall with shaggy, irregular outlines.
option_D: A solid lesion with a surrounding rim of oedema.
option_E: A cyst with split walls (the “double-line” or “split-wall” sign).
answer_text: A cyst with multiple septations. | A cyst wall with calcifications. | A cyst with split walls (the “double-line” or “split-wall” sign).
explanation: Septations, calcifications and the split-wall sign are typical ultrasound findings.

stem: A young girl develops skin rash, upper abdominal pain, and eosinophilia with imaging showing a cyst with split wall. Which statements are true?
option_A: The findings are compatible with a ruptured simple liver cyst.
option_B: The features suggest a ruptured hydatid cyst.
option_D: Treatment is exploratory laparotomy under cover of albendazole.
option_E: Anaphylaxis may occur during surgical intervention.
answer_text: The features suggest a ruptured hydatid cyst. | Treatment is exploratory laparotomy under cover of albendazole. | Anaphylaxis may occur during surgical intervention.
explanation: A ruptured hydatid cyst in this setting necessitates urgent surgical management with albendazole cover due to anaphylaxis risk.

stem: A young woman presents with abdominal pain, jaundice, and imaging showing gallbladder calculi, dilated CBD, septated liver cyst, with ERCP delivering membranous structures. Which statements are true?
option_A: The likely diagnosis is cholecystitis with choledocholithiasis and an incidental liver cyst.
option_B: The likely diagnosis is a multiseptated hydatid cyst with biliary communication causing daughter cysts in the CBD and gallbladder calculi.
option_C: Treatment after endoscopic clearance of the CBD requires only a cholecystectomy.
option_D: Treatment should involve cholecystectomy followed by injection of sclerosants into the cyst.
option_E: Injection of scolicidal agents carries a risk of sclerosing cholangitis due to biliary communications.
answer_text: The likely diagnosis is a multiseptated hydatid cyst with biliary communication causing daughter cysts in the CBD and gallbladder calculi. | Injection of scolicidal agents carries a risk of sclerosing cholangitis due to biliary communications.
explanation: This presentation is typical of hydatid disease with biliary involvement; caution is needed with scolicidal agents.
topics: Hydatid disease; Primary sclerosing cholangitis; Ascending cholangitis

stem: Which of the following statements are true of hydatid cysts?
option_A: Anaphylactic shock is more common when treating unilocular cysts than multiloculated cysts.
option_B: Sclerosing cholangitis is more likely following injection of scolicidal agents into multiloculated cysts.
option_C: Small deep cysts with calcified walls may be managed non-surgically with albendazole.
option_D: Surgical curettage of the cyst wall is mandatory.
option_E: Rupture of a cyst may lead to dissemination of the disease.
answer_text: Sclerosing cholangitis is more likely following injection of scolicidal agents into multiloculated cysts. | Small deep cysts with calcified walls may be managed non-surgically with albendazole. | Rupture of a cyst may lead to dissemination of the disease.
explanation: Multiloculated cysts risk cholangitis with scolicidal injection; small calcified cysts may be treated medically and rupture can disseminate the infection.
topics: Primary sclerosing cholangitis; Ascending cholangitis; Hydatid disease

stem: Which of the following is true of thoracic hydatid disease?
option_A: The lung is the most common organ affected.
option_B: The right lower lobe is affected slightly more than any other site.
option_D: Asymptomatic (“silent”) cysts may sometimes present with an allergic reaction.
option_E: Pulmonary hydatid disease characteristically presents with a silent pleural effusion.
answer_text: The right lower lobe is affected slightly more than any other site. | Asymptomatic (“silent”) cysts may sometimes present with an allergic reaction.
explanation: Pulmonary hydatid cysts are often solitary in the right lower lobe and may incite allergic reactions.

stem: A young man develops cough, fever, and chest pain with a chest x-ray showing a rounded cyst and a second lesion with a crescent sign. Which statements are true?
option_A: Air enters as the cyst erodes into an adjacent bronchus, creating a fine radiolucent line.
option_B: The x-ray finding is known as the “meniscus” or “crescent sign.”
option_C: Pulmonary hydatid disease never presents with pleural effusion.
option_D: The “water-lily sign” on CT indicates inactive disease.
option_E: Surgery remains the mainstay of treatment for pulmonary hydatid cysts.
answer_text: Air enters as the cyst erodes into an adjacent bronchus, creating a fine radiolucent line. | The x-ray finding is known as the “meniscus” or “crescent sign.” | Surgery remains the mainstay of treatment for pulmonary hydatid cysts.
explanation: False: a ruptured cyst can cause pleural effusion or empyema (C), and the water-lily sign shows collapsed floating membranes of a ruptured cyst, not inactive disease (D).

stem: A 70-year-old woman with hepatitis C has 1 week of abdominal discomfort and weight loss. Ultrasound shows an isolated liver lesion. Which additional test is most likely diagnostic?
explanation: Elevated in hepatocellular carcinoma, likely in this scenario.

stem: A patient presents with RUQ pain, itching, and jaundice. CT scan of the liver revealed a cystic lesion, with multiple daughter cysts. What is the diagnosis? and what is the next step in the management?
option_C: Hydatid liver cyst; prepare the patient for surgery (cystectomy) with preoperative Albendazole and Praziquantel
answer_text: Hydatid liver cyst; prepare the patient for surgery (cystectomy) with preoperative Albendazole and Praziquantel
explanation: CT findings indicate a hydatid cyst; surgery with preoperative Albendazole and Praziquantel is indicated.

stem: A patient with a hydatid liver cyst is scheduled for surgery. Is there a benefit of giving medication before surgery? Why?
option_A: No, medications before surgery have no impact
option_C: Yes, albendazole (± praziquantel) inactivates the cyst and lowers intracystic pressure, reducing the risk of recurrence
option_D: No, they only increase the risk of infection
option_E: Yes, they are used to anesthetize the patient
answer_text: Yes, albendazole (± praziquantel) inactivates the cyst and lowers intracystic pressure, reducing the risk of recurrence
explanation: Preoperative albendazole (± praziquantel) kills protoscolices and softens the cyst, reducing the risk of secondary hydatidosis and recurrence if spillage occurs.

stem: A jaundiced patient has a hydatid liver cyst with daughter cysts on CT and is planned for surgery. What further imaging would you order before surgery?
explanation: Jaundice suggests cyst–biliary communication; MRCP shows the biliary tree and any communication before surgery. Ultrasound is first-line but adds little after CT.

stem: After surgery for a hydatid liver cyst, what is your plan for minimising the risk of recurrence or reinfection?
option_B: Use prophylactic antibiotics only during surgery
option_C: Continue albendazole (± praziquantel) postoperatively and educate the patient about hand hygiene, clean food and water and avoiding contact with dogs
answer_text: Continue albendazole (± praziquantel) postoperatively and educate the patient about hand hygiene, clean food and water and avoiding contact with dogs
explanation: Postoperative albendazole (usually 1–3 months) kills any spilled protoscolices, and hygiene education (dogs, unwashed vegetables) prevents reinfection.
