stem: Anatomy of the spleen. All of the following statements are true except:
option_A: The spleen lies in front of the left seventh, eighth, and ninth ribs.
option_B: The tail of the pancreas lies in the splenorenal ligament.
option_C: The lymphatics of the spleen ultimately drain into the coeliac nodes.
option_D: The left extremity of the lesser sac lies against the splenic hilum.
option_E: The visceral surface has impressions for the stomach, left kidney and splenic flexure of the colon.
answer_text: The spleen lies in front of the left seventh, eighth, and ninth ribs.
explanation: A is false: the spleen lies deep to the left 9th–11th ribs, its long axis along the 10th rib.

stem: Physiology of the spleen. Which of the following statements is not true?
option_A: The splenic parenchyma consists of white and red pulp.
option_B: Pitting is a specific function of the spleen.
option_C: The spleen plays a role in immune function.
option_D: Haemopoiesis occurs in the foetal spleen.
option_E: The spleen has a major reservoir function of red cell mass.
answer_text: The spleen has a major reservoir function of red cell mass.
explanation: While the spleen contributes to immunity and foetal haemopoiesis, it does not serve as a major reservoir of red blood cells.

stem: Investigations of splenic disease. Which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Plain abdominal x-ray is a common modality of imaging in splenomegaly.
option_B: Splenomegaly with portal hypertension requires upper GI endoscopy (OGD).
option_C: Lymph node biopsy may be required in some cases of splenomegaly.
option_D: CECT is the best imaging modality.
option_E: 99mTc–labelled colloid is useful in certain cases.
answer_text: Splenomegaly with portal hypertension requires upper GI endoscopy (OGD). | Lymph node biopsy may be required in some cases of splenomegaly. | CECT is the best imaging modality. | 99mTc–labelled colloid is useful in certain cases.
explanation: The plain x‐ray is not routinely useful while the other investigations are appropriate.

stem: Splenectomy. Which of the following statements is false?
option_A: Partial splenectomy can result in splenic regeneration.
option_B: Before splenectomy for haemolytic anaemia, abdominal ultrasound is essential.
option_C: A pancreatic or gastric fistula can occur as a post-splenectomy complication.
option_D: In a left hemicolectomy the spleen can be in danger of iatrogenic injury.
option_E: The risk of opportunist post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) is greatest after the first 6 months of splenectomy.
answer_text: The risk of opportunist post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) is greatest after the first 6 months of splenectomy.
explanation: OPSI risk is highest during the first 2–3 years after surgery, making statement E false.

stem: A 14-year-old girl with menorrhagia, frequent nosebleeds, and iron-deficiency anemia is found to have a low platelet count with normal coagulation and abundant megakaryocytes on bone marrow biopsy. What is the most appropriate initial therapy?
option_B: Platelet transfusion when the count drops below 50 000/µL
option_E: Expectant management with intervention only if significant bleeding occurs
explanation: ITP with significant bleeding is treated first with corticosteroids (± IVIg); splenectomy is reserved for refractory or relapsing disease.

stem: A patient with ITP initially responds to steroids, but over 6–12 months the responses become less marked and shorter, with increasing side effects. What is the next step in management?
option_C: Increase in steroid dose and frequency
explanation: Steroid-dependent ITP with waning responses and rising side effects is an indication for splenectomy, which gives durable remission in about two-thirds.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with frequent and multiple areas of cutaneous ecchymosis. Workup demonstrates a platelet count of 15,000/µL, and evaluation of the bone marrow reveals a normal number of megakaryocytes. Ultrasound examination demonstrates a normal-sized spleen. Based on the exclusion of other causes of thrombocytopenia, she is given a diagnosis of immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment upon diagnosis?
option_A: Expectant management with close follow-up of platelet counts
option_B: Immediate platelet transfusion to increase platelet counts to greater than 50,000/µL
option_E: Referral to surgery for laparoscopic splenectomy
explanation: Initial treatment of ITP is with glucocorticoids; splenectomy is reserved for refractory cases.

stem: Which of the following abnormal findings on peripheral blood film is not typical of hyposplenism?
explanation: Bite cells occur in oxidative haemolysis (e.g. G6PD deficiency) as the spleen removes Heinz bodies; Howell–Jolly bodies, target cells and Pappenheimer bodies indicate hyposplenism.

stem: Which is the most common early complication following splenectomy?
explanation: Atelectasis is the most common early postoperative complication after splenectomy.

stem: Splenectomy patients should be immunized against all the following organisms, except
explanation: Vaccination against tetanus is not routinely required for splenectomy patients.

stem: A young woman has recurrent palpitations, headache and sweating. Her BP is 185 mmHg systolic despite a calcium channel blocker, an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Paroxysms of headache, palpitations and sweating with resistant hypertension is phaeochromocytoma.

stem: A young woman has recurrent palpitations, headache and sweating. Her BP is 185 mmHg systolic despite a calcium channel blocker, an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
explanation: Plasma free (or 24-h urinary fractionated) metanephrines are the biochemical test; imaging (CT/MRI) follows.

stem: A young woman has recurrent palpitations, headache and sweating. Her BP is 185 mmHg systolic despite a calcium channel blocker, an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic. Which drug should NOT be used (first) in this condition?
explanation: A beta-blocker alone before alpha-blockade leaves alpha stimulation unopposed and can cause a hypertensive crisis; alpha-block first.

source: Bailey Breast and Neck lumps MCQ
stem: Which of the following statements are true? (Adrenal Incidentalomas)
option_A: A diagnostic work up is unnecessary if it is <6 cm.
option_C: A 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test is helpful in diagnosis.
option_D: An adrenal biopsy is always indicated.
option_E: Adrenal metastasis is more likely in patients with a history of cancer elsewhere.
answer_text: Most incidentalomas are nonfunctioning. | A 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test is helpful in diagnosis. | Adrenal metastasis is more likely in patients with a history of cancer elsewhere.
explanation: Most incidentalomas are nonfunctioning; the dexamethasone test is useful and metastasis is more likely in patients with known cancers.

source: Bailey Breast and Neck lumps MCQ
stem: The following statements are true except: (Adrenal Glands Anatomy and Hormones)
option_A: The weight of a normal adrenal gland is 15 g.
option_C: The right adrenal vein drains into the right renal vein.
option_D: Dehydroepiandrosterone is produced in the zona glomerulosa.
option_E: Aldosterone is produced in the zona reticularis.
answer_text: The weight of a normal adrenal gland is 15 g. | The right adrenal vein drains into the right renal vein. | Dehydroepiandrosterone is produced in the zona glomerulosa. | Aldosterone is produced in the zona reticularis.
explanation: Normal adrenal weight is ~4 g, the right adrenal vein drains into the IVC, DHEA is produced in the zona reticularis and aldosterone in the zona glomerulosa.

stem: A 32-year-old woman reports recurring episodes of panic, sweating, and palpitations. They occur randomly and are increasing in frequency. Examination is unremarkable. Which of the following investigations will be the most helpful in confirming the diagnosis?
explanation: Phaeochromocytoma secretes catecholamines; VMA is a key breakdown product in urine.

stem: A 37-year-old man presents to the GP with a 2-month history of thirst and frequency of urination. He has no significant past medical history and examination is unremarkable. Routine bloods demonstrate the following: random glucose 5.6 mmol/L, sodium 142 mmol/L and potassium 2.9 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Hypokalaemia causes polyuria and thirst; with high-normal sodium in a young adult this suggests primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), usually with hypertension.

stem: A 6-year-old girl is referred by her GP to the paediatric clinic with precocious puberty. On examination, she is found to have clitoromegaly and some pubic hair. She is on the 98th centile for height and weight. Which of the following will be most helpful in determining the underlying diagnosis?
explanation: Elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone suggests congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency).

stem: A 37-year-old woman presents to the emergency department following a faint after standing up from a sitting position. She did not lose consciousness during this episode but reported feeling ‘dizzy and lightheaded’. She has no significant past medical history. On examination you notice multiple areas of skin depigmentation but increased pigmentation in the palmar creases and on the elbows. Which of the following is the best management for her condition?
explanation: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s) requires glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid replacement.

stem: A34-year-old woman presents with a chief complaint of “feeling weak and thirsty as well as urinating a lot.” On presentation, her blood pressure is 165/89, heart rate is 75, and respiratory rate is 14. Her electrolyte panel is as follows: Na 146, K 2.9, Cl 95, HCO3 28. Which of the following is the best initial test given her presentation and laboratory findings?
option_A: Plasma renin activity and plasma aldosterone concentration
answer_text: Plasma renin activity and plasma aldosterone concentration
explanation: Biochemical diagnosis of hyperaldosteronism requires demonstration of elevated plasma aldosterone concentration with suppressed plasma renin activity.

stem: A52-year-old woman presents with hypertension, obesity, and new skin striae. You are concerned about possible Cushing syndrome. Which of the following is the most common cause of Cushing syndrome?
explanation: The most common cause of Cushing syndrome is iatrogenic, due to administration of exogenous glucocorticoids.

stem: A patient with mild skin pigmentation is admitted emergently because of sudden abdominal pain, fever and a rigid abdomen. Her blood pressure is 88/58 mm Hg. Blood tests show WBC 25 000/µL, glucose 55 mg/dL, sodium 119 mEq/L and potassium 6.2 mEq/L. Exploratory laparotomy shows no intra-abdominal pathology. Which of the following is the definitive treatment for her primary condition?
explanation: This patient has adrenal insufficiency and needs treatment with corticosteroids.

stem: A 49-year-old obese man has become irritable, his face has changed to a round configuration, he has developed purplish lines on his flanks, and he is hypertensive. A 24-hour urine collection demonstrates elevated cortisol levels. This is confirmed with bedtime cortisol measurements of 700 ng/mL. Which of the following findings is most consistent with the diagnosis of Cushing disease?
option_B: Glucocorticoid use for the treatment of inflammatory disorders
option_C: A 3-cm adrenal mass on computed tomography (CT) scan
option_D: Suppression with high-dose dexamethasone suppression testing
option_E: A 1-cm bronchogenic mass on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
answer_text: Suppression with high-dose dexamethasone suppression testing
explanation: Cushing disease is cortisol excess caused by an ACTH-hypersecreting pituitary adenoma. In these patients, the ACTH level is normal or elevated and cortisol is suppressed with high-dose dexamethasone.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with hypertension, development of facial hair and a 7-cm suprarenal mass. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The symptoms and large adrenal mass are consistent with adrenocortical carcinoma.

stem: A 36-year-old woman presents with palpitations, anxiety and hypertension. Workup reveals a phaeochromocytoma. Which of the following is the best approach to optimising the patient preoperatively?
option_A: Fluid restriction 24 hours preoperatively to prevent intraoperative congestive heart failure
option_B: Initiation of an α-blocker 24 hours prior to surgery
option_C: Initiation of an α-blocker at 1 to 3 weeks prior to surgery
option_D: Initiation of a β-blocker 1 to 3 weeks prior to surgery
option_E: Escalating antihypertensive drug therapy with β-blockade followed by α-blockade starting at least 1 week prior to surgery
answer_text: Initiation of an α-blocker at 1 to 3 weeks prior to surgery
explanation: Patients with pheochromocytomas should be treated with α-blockade 1-3 weeks before surgery to control blood pressure.

stem: What is the size threshold for resection of an adrenal incidentaloma?
explanation: Adrenal incidentalomas larger than 4 to 6 cm are generally considered for surgical resection due to the increased risk of malignancy.

stem: The following statements are true except:
option_A: Abdominal pain might be a symptom from non-surgical conditions.
option_B: Altered bowel habit usually indicates obstructive and inflammatory pathology.
option_C: A hernia causing abdominal symptoms will always be obvious.
option_D: An inebriated person with abdominal pain should be diagnosed as alcoholic gastritis.
option_E: Abdominal pain related to food habits and associated with other symptoms usually denote pathology in the biliary tract or stomach and duodenum.
answer_text: A hernia causing abdominal symptoms will always be obvious. | An inebriated person with abdominal pain should be diagnosed as alcoholic gastritis.
explanation: C and D are false: a hernia (e.g. femoral, obturator) can easily be missed, and an inebriated patient may still have serious surgical pathology.

stem: Inguinal and femoral hernia : Which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Inguinal hernia is more common in men than in women.
option_B: Femoral hernia is more common than inguinal hernia in women.
option_C: Femoral hernia is felt below and medial to the pubic tubercle.
option_D: The risk of bowel strangulation is greatest in femoral hernia, less in indirect inguinal hernia, and least in direct inguinal hernia.
option_E: A ‘sliding’ inguinal hernia can pass either medial or lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
answer_text: Inguinal hernia is more common in men than in women. | The risk of bowel strangulation is greatest in femoral hernia, less in indirect inguinal hernia, and least in direct inguinal hernia.
explanation: B and C are false: inguinal hernia remains the commonest hernia in women, and a femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
topics: Inguinal hernia; Strangulated hernia; Femoral hernia

stem: Surgery for inguinal hernia : Which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Open repair of inguinal hernia should always involve placement of a mesh.
option_B: The Lichtenstein Open Repair has the lowest recurrence rate of any type of repair.
option_C: Laparoscopic repair has been shown to have less postoperative pain, less chronic pain, accelerated postoperative recovery and fewer wound complications.
option_D: Approximately 5% of cases of inguinal hernia will be bilateral and 10% will be on patients with recurrent inguinal hernia after previous surgery.
option_E: Chronic postoperative pain occurs in more than 20% of cases after surgery.
answer_text: Laparoscopic repair has been shown to have less postoperative pain, less chronic pain, accelerated postoperative recovery and fewer wound complications. | Approximately 5% of cases of inguinal hernia will be bilateral and 10% will be on patients with recurrent inguinal hernia after previous surgery. | Chronic postoperative pain occurs in more than 20% of cases after surgery.
explanation: A and B are false: mesh is standard but not mandatory (e.g. Shouldice in selected cases), and Lichtenstein does not have the lowest recurrence of all repairs.

stem: Mesh for hernia repair: Which of the following are true?
option_A: Mesh should not be used in the presence of infection.
option_B: Mesh is mainly used to induce fibrosis, thus making a strong repair.
option_C: Polypropylene mesh is hydrophobic and monofilament.
option_D: Simple polypropylene is ideal for intraperitoneal use.
option_E: Synthetic, nonabsorbable meshes can contract in size by up to 50% over time.
answer_text: Polypropylene mesh is hydrophobic and monofilament. | Synthetic, nonabsorbable meshes can contract in size by up to 50% over time.
explanation: A, B and D are false: mesh may be used selectively in contaminated fields, it acts as a scaffold for tissue ingrowth, and plain polypropylene causes intraperitoneal adhesions.

stem: Surgery for femoral hernia : Which of the following are true?
option_A: There is no place for laparoscopic surgery in femoral hernia.
option_B: Skin discolouration over the hernia suggests possible strangulation.
option_C: There is a decreased risk of femoral hernia after open inguinal hernia repair.
option_D: A high, abdominal, McEvedy approach is best in patients presenting with a strangulating femoral hernia.
option_E: The femoral nerve is at risk due to its proximity to the neck of a femoral hernia.
answer_text: Skin discolouration over the hernia suggests possible strangulation. | A high, abdominal, McEvedy approach is best in patients presenting with a strangulating femoral hernia.
explanation: A, C and E are false: laparoscopic repair is used, femoral hernia risk rises after open inguinal repair, and the femoral vein (not nerve) is at risk.

stem: Incisional hernia and its repair : Which of the following are not true?
option_A: Incisional hernias never develop more than 2 years after the original surgery.
option_B: Jenkins Rule states that in closing an abdominal incision the length of suture used should be four times the length of the incision. However, this has been disproved.
option_C: Transverse abdominal incisions are less likely to herniate than vertical incisions.
option_D: Non-absorbable meshes placed at initial surgery will reduce the risk of subsequent incisional herniation.
option_E: Laparoscopic mesh repair of incisional hernia has a lower wound infection rate than open mesh repair.
answer_text: Incisional hernias never develop more than 2 years after the original surgery. | Jenkins Rule states that in closing an abdominal incision the length of suture used should be four times the length of the incision. However, this has been disproved.
explanation: A and B are false: incisional hernias can appear many years later, and Jenkins' 4:1 suture-length rule remains valid (now with small bites).

stem: You are a house officer in general surgery clerking a 65-year-old man (with COPD) for elective inguinal hernia repair. He says he had a chest X-ray 6 weeks ago. Which investigation is most highly recommended prior to his surgery?
explanation: NICE guidelines recommend ECG in older patients with cardiorespiratory disease; chest X-ray not repeated if recent.

stem: A 32-year-old man is complaining of increasing pain 2 days post inguinal hernia repair. He is currently on paracetamol 1 g four times a day. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
explanation: According to WHO analgesic ladder, adding an NSAID is next step.

stem: A 67-year-old male has a swelling in the right groin that appears and disappears. It lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle and protrudes on coughing. It reappears despite pressure over the deep inguinal ring. What hernia is this most likely to be?
explanation: Protrudes through posterior wall medial to inferior epigastric vessels; typical direct hernia.

stem: A 25-year-old weightlifter has a lump near his right groin. On exam it reduces upwards and laterally, moves down medially, and is controlled by pressure over deep ring. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Enters internal ring lateral to epigastric vessels, typical indirect path.

stem: A 53-year-old man has a lump near his groin. It reduces on lying down and immediately reaches full size on standing. On coughing it protrudes straight and is not controlled by pressure over the deep ring. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Bulges medially, not controlled by deep ring pressure.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has a lump in her groin. It is below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Femoral hernias present below and lateral to pubic tubercle.

stem: A 25-year-old woman complains of a painful swelling at the navel since birth. On exam there is an obvious swelling at the umbilicus. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A swelling through the umbilical scar present since birth is a persistent congenital umbilical hernia; paraumbilical hernias are acquired, beside the umbilicus.

stem: A 43-year-old man has epigastric pain and a tender, irreducible midline swelling. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Occurs in midline above umbilicus; often tender and irreducible.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has a lump at the lateral edge of the rectus sheath. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Protrusion through Spigelian fascia at the lateral rectus border.

stem: A 65-year-old woman has 2 days of abdominal discomfort and vomiting, plus right-sided hip pain. An abdominal X-ray confirms small bowel obstruction. Emergency laparotomy is performed. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Elderly women; small bowel obstruction passing through obturator canal.

stem: An obese woman with a strangulated paraumbilical hernia causing small bowel obstruction undergoes emergency surgery, and a segment of gangrenous small bowel is resected. What is the best surgical option for the hernia now, and why?
option_C: Herniotomy with suture repair (herniorrhaphy); mesh avoided because of the high infection risk in a contaminated field
answer_text: Herniotomy with suture repair (herniorrhaphy); mesh avoided because of the high infection risk in a contaminated field
explanation: After resecting gangrenous bowel the field is contaminated, so a sutured repair is preferred; a permanent synthetic mesh carries a high infection risk.
topics: Hernia repair; Strangulated hernia; Umbilical hernia
notes: Essay case sequence lost its scenario; logical order is hernia-0002, 0003, 0004, then 0001. Stems rewritten to stand alone.

stem: An obese middle-aged woman presents with a reducible swelling just above the umbilicus that has slowly enlarged over several months. What is the cause of this mass?
option_B: Paraumbilical hernia due to obesity and raised intra-abdominal pressure
answer_text: Paraumbilical hernia due to obesity and raised intra-abdominal pressure
explanation: A reducible swelling beside the umbilicus in an obese adult is a paraumbilical hernia through the linea alba, promoted by raised intra-abdominal pressure.

stem: Which THREE clinical signs best confirm that this supraumbilical swelling is a paraumbilical hernia?
option_B: Palpable lump above the umbilicus, reducibility and an expansile cough impulse
answer_text: Palpable lump above the umbilicus, reducibility and an expansile cough impulse
explanation: A hernia is a lump that reduces and has an expansile cough impulse; redness and tenderness suggest strangulation rather than confirm a hernia.

stem: The same woman later develops bilious vomiting and central colicky abdominal pain with distension; the hernia is now tense, tender and irreducible. Her X-ray is shown. What is the study, what does it show, and what is the most likely diagnosis?
option_A: Upright chest X-ray showing free air under the diaphragm indicating perforation
option_C: Erect Abdominal X-ray showing dilated small bowel loops, indicating small bowel obstruction due to a strangulated umbilical hernia
option_E: Barium study showing a filling defect
answer_text: Erect Abdominal X-ray showing dilated small bowel loops, indicating small bowel obstruction due to a strangulated umbilical hernia
explanation: Dilated central small-bowel loops with air–fluid levels on an erect abdominal film, with a tender irreducible hernia, indicate obstruction from a strangulated paraumbilical hernia.
topics: Small bowel obstruction; Strangulated hernia; Umbilical hernia

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the GP with a lump in the left groin which has been present for over 2 months. On examination, the lump is above the inguinal ligament. It is reducible and has a cough impulse, but does not extend into the scrotum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Protrusion through Hesselbach’s triangle above the inguinal ligament, not reaching scrotum.

stem: Which term best fits the description of the hernia given below? This hernia arises from a triangle bounded by the external oblique muscle, the latissimus dorsi and the iliac crest below.
explanation: Petit’s (lumbar) hernias occur through the inferior lumbar triangle bounded by these muscles.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with an upper midline mass that has been present for over a year. She has a history of a partial gastrectomy for a perforated ulcer. On examination, the mass is 5 cm in size, soft, non-tender and reducible. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Incisional hernias protrude through a previous scar, often soft and reducible with a wide neck.

stem: Which term best fits the description of the hernia given below? A hernia that has two parts, each lying either side of the inferior epigastric artery.
explanation: Pantaloon hernia straddles the inferior epigastric vessels with both direct and indirect components.

stem: A 43-year-old woman presents to the GP with a lump in the right groin, which she says has been there on and off for a few months, but is now persistent. She has no other symptoms of note. On examination, there is a grape-sized lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. It is not tender and there is no cough impulse felt. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Irreducible painless lump below and lateral to pubic tubercle indicates an incarcerated femoral hernia.

stem: A 58-year-old man is admitted to hospital with a strangulated paraumbilical hernia that requires urgent operative intervention. He has a history of severe depression and is currently under Section for treatment of his mental condition. The patient does not consent to treatment even though he understands his condition, the benefits of having an operation and the potential outcomes of not having it. Which is the most appropriate course of action?
option_A: Doctor can consent for the patient
option_B: Doctor can treat the patient under duty of care
option_C: Doctor can treat the patient under the Mental Health Act
option_D: Patient’s refusal to treatment is valid and cannot be overridden
option_E: Patient’s refusal to treatment is invalid and can be overridden
answer_text: Patient’s refusal to treatment is valid and cannot be overridden
explanation: He has capacity despite mental illness, so his informed refusal must be respected.

stem: An 87-year-old woman with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with recurrent episodes of bronchitis comes to see you at the GP practice. She has noticed a lump in the lower abdomen when she stands. It does not cause her any concern but she just wanted to get it checked out. On examination, she is obese and there is a soft, non-tender reducible mass in the lower abdomen. You note lower midline scarring from previous caesarean sections overlying the lump. What would be the best course of management?
explanation: Asymptomatic incisional hernias in high-risk patients can be managed conservatively.

stem: A 56-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with an acutely painful lump in the right groin. She has vomited six times in the last hour and is also complaining of worsening abdominal pain. On examination, there is a grape-sized lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. It is warm, red and exquisitely tender. No cough impulse is felt. What would be the best course of management?
explanation: Acute obstruction/strangulation risk in a femoral hernia mandates immediate surgical repair.

stem: Which term best fits the description of hernia given below? A hernia that contains a ‘W’ loop of intestine within its sac.
explanation: Maydl's hernia has two loops (W) in the sac; the intervening intra-abdominal loop may strangulate unseen, so it must be checked at surgery.

stem: A 39-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a painful lump in the groin. He tells you that this lump has been present on and off for a few months and has previously been asymptomatic. Today, the lump has become painful. On examination, there is an erythematous, tender, irreducible lump above and medial to the pubic tubercle. The patient denies abdominal pain, vomiting or constipation. Which is the best descriptive term for the hernia above?
explanation: Only part of the bowel wall is entrapped, causing pain but no complete obstruction.

stem: An 85-year-old man with a long-standing hiatal hernia presents with acute onset of midepigastric pain, vomiting, and inability to keep food down. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Acute pain and vomiting in an elderly patient with a hiatus hernia suggest an obstructed or volvulised paraoesophageal (rolling) hernia; sliding hernias rarely obstruct.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of a paraesophageal hernia with obstruction?
option_A: Laparotomy or laparoscopy and operative repair
option_B: Continued NG tube decompression and total parenteral nutrition (TPN)
option_C: Thoracotomy or thoracoscopy and operative repair
answer_text: Laparotomy or laparoscopy and operative repair
explanation: An obstructed paraoesophageal hernia risks strangulation and needs prompt (usually laparoscopic) reduction, sac excision and crural repair after decompression.

stem: A 75-year-old woman admitted from a nursing home for abdominal pain and pneumonia develops a tender bulge in the medial left thigh below the inguinal ligament on hospital day 3. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A tender bulge below the inguinal ligament in an elderly woman with coughing (pneumonia) is an incarcerated femoral hernia.

stem: In a 6-month-old previously healthy male infant, an abnormality is noted during routine diaper changes. The finding is a reducible inguinal bulge that comes and goes. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: An intermittent, reducible inguinal bulge in an infant is an indirect inguinal hernia through a patent processus vaginalis.

stem: For the infant described above with an inguinal hernia, what is the most appropriate management at this time?
option_B: Reassurance that the abnormality will resolve without intervention
option_C: Referral to the ED for immediate surgical consultation
explanation: Infant inguinal hernias do not resolve and carry a high incarceration risk, so prompt elective herniotomy is arranged.
topics: Inguinal hernia; Strangulated hernia; Hernia repair

stem: Several weeks later, the same infant presents with 4 hours of irritability, nonbilious vomiting, and refusal to feed, with the same inguinal abnormality noted. What is the most appropriate management at this time?
option_D: Sedation with manual reduction and arrangements for elective surgical repair
option_E: Sedation with manual reduction, admission, rehydration, and surgical repair within 24–48 hours
answer_text: Sedation with manual reduction, admission, rehydration, and surgical repair within 24–48 hours
explanation: An incarcerated infant hernia without peritonitis is reduced under sedation, then repaired within 24–48 h once oedema settles, as re-incarceration is common.

stem: A 33-year-old woman is scheduled for an elective paraumbilical hernia repair. Preoperative evaluation shows the presence of moderate hypothyroidism. Select the most appropriate plan of action:
option_A: Proceed with surgery knowing that minor perioperative complications could develop
option_B: Postpone surgery until a euthyroid state is achieved
option_C: Proceed with surgery while beginning treatment with levothyroxine
option_D: Proceed with surgery while beginning treatment with thioamides
option_E: Proceed with surgery if severe clinical symptoms are not present
answer_text: Postpone surgery until a euthyroid state is achieved
explanation: Moderate hypothyroidism raises anaesthetic risk (hypothermia, hypotension, slow recovery), so elective surgery is postponed until euthyroid.

stem: An otherwise well 78 year-old woman presents with a left groin lump for two months. On examination, there is a unilateral, reducible lump in the left femoral triangle with a cough impulse. Which is the single most appropriate piece of advice which should be given to this patient?
option_A: Discharge with advice to seek her GP advice if symptoms occur
option_B: Recommend an outpatient review in 3 months to assess her hernia status
option_C: Recommend investigation with groin ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis
option_D: Recommend surgical exploration and repair as soon as possible
answer_text: Recommend surgical exploration and repair as soon as possible
explanation: A femoral hernia (femoral triangle lump in an elderly woman) has a high strangulation risk through its narrow neck, so prompt repair is advised.

stem: A 45-year-old multiparous lady noticed a painless lump in her right groin. On examination, the mass was irreducible and located in the upper thigh just below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. Which one among the following conditions is the least likely diagnosis?
explanation: A lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle may be a femoral hernia, saphena varix or node; a Spigelian hernia lies far higher, at the lateral rectus border.

stem: Figure 8.1 shows several key landmarks in the right groin of a man. The bony prominences are labelled. The structure labelled A provides an important landmark in inguinal surgery. Figure 8.1 Key landmarks in the right groin of a man Which single term correctly describes structure A?
explanation: The inferior epigastric artery marks the medial limit of indirect hernias.

stem: A 32-year-old man has a modest sized, freely reducible, indirect inguinal hernia. The hernia can be held in reduction by maintaining pressure over one particular location. Which single term most likely describes this location?
explanation: Pressure at the deep inguinal ring maintains hernia reduction.

stem: A 47-year-old woman has had a swelling in the right side of the abdomen for 2 months. A hernia is suspected and the lump’s physical characteristics are being assessed. Which single clinical feature would confirm the clinical suspicion?
explanation: Only a hernia will truly reduce on palpation.

stem: An otherwise well 78-year-old woman has had a left groin lump for 2 months. A femoral hernia is suspected. There is a unilateral, reducible lump in the left femoral triangle with a cough impulse and thrill. Which is the single most appropriate piece of advice which should be given to the patient?
option_A: Discharge with advice to seek GP advice if symptoms occur
option_B: Recommend an outpatient review in 3 months to assess hernia status
option_C: Recommend investigation with groin ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis
option_D: Recommend surgical exploration and repair within the next 6 weeks
answer_text: Recommend surgical exploration and repair within the next 6 weeks
explanation: Femoral hernias are high-risk and should be surgically repaired promptly to prevent complications.

stem: A 48-year-old woman develops pain in the right lower quadrant while playing tennis. The pain progresses and the patient presents to the emergency room later that day with a low-grade fever, a WBC count of 13,000/mm3, and complaints of anorexia and nausea as well as persistent, sharp pain of the right lower quadrant. On examination, she is tender in the right lower quadrant with guarding and a bulge in that location. An ultrasound is ordered and shows an apparent mass in the abdominal wall. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sudden RIF pain on exertion with a tender abdominal wall mass on ultrasound suggests rectus sheath haematoma from inferior epigastric vessel rupture.

stem: A 22-year-old college student notices a bulge in his right groin. It is accentuated with coughing and straining, but is easily reducible. Which of the following hernias follows the path of the spermatic cord within the cremaster muscle?
explanation: Indirect inguinal hernia follows the path of the spermatic cord through the internal inguinal ring.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is seen in a surgery clinic for a bulge in the right groin. She denies pain and is able to make the bulge disappear by lying down and putting steady pressure on the bulge. She has never experienced nausea or vomiting. On examination she has a reducible hernia below the inguinal ligament. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?
option_A: Observation for now and follow-up in surgery clinic in 6 months
option_B: Observation for now and follow-up in surgery clinic if she develops further symptoms
option_E: Emergent surgical repair of hernia with exploratory laparotomy to evaluate the small bowel
explanation: Elective repair is appropriate for a reducible femoral hernia.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a bulge in his right groin associated with mild discomfort. On examination the bulge is easily reducible and does not descend into the scrotum. Which of the following changes is most concerning for possible strangulation requiring emergent repair of the hernia?
option_A: Increase in size of the hernia
option_B: Descent of hernia into the scrotum
option_C: Development of a second hernia in the left groin
option_E: Worsening pain over the hernia with walking
explanation: Inability to reduce the hernia indicates incarceration and a risk of strangulation.

stem: Which one of the following muscles lies closest to the peritoneal cavity?
explanation: The transversus abdominis is the deepest abdominal muscle and lies adjacent to the peritoneum.

stem: Regarding hernias in females, the most common is
explanation: Inguinal hernia is the most common type in females.

stem: Which of the following structures form a part of both the inguinal and femoral canals?
explanation: The inguinal ligament forms part of both the inguinal and femoral canals.

stem: A 35-year-old professional weightlifter presents with a red and swollen lump in the left groin. An inguinal hernia is suspected and, at the time of operation, the lump is found to contain a small loop of necrotic bowel. This type of hernia is best described as
explanation: Necrotic bowel in the sac means its blood supply has been cut off: a strangulated hernia. Irreducible or obstructed hernias have viable contents.

stem: Management of an inguinal hernia A 78-year-old African Caribbean man presents with severe pain arising from his hernia in the left groin. The patient is also experiencing central colicky abdominal pain. On examination, the abdomen is generally tender and distended and bowel sounds are raised. Examination of the hernial orifices reveals a left-sided, irreducible, tense and extremely tender inguinal hernia. The overlying skin of the hernia is warm and erythematous. What is the most appropriate course of action in managing this patient?
option_A: Alert theatre and send patient for emergency surgery
option_B: Request a computed tomography scan of the abdomen
answer_text: Alert theatre and send patient for emergency surgery
explanation: A tense, tender, red, irreducible hernia with obstruction is strangulated: resuscitate and operate urgently; do not attempt reduction or delay for imaging.

explanation: A small (< 4 cm), non-functioning, homogeneous adrenal incidentaloma is an adenoma; follow-up only.

explanation: A stone impacted in the gallbladder neck compressing the common hepatic duct is Mirizzi syndrome.

explanation: Intrahepatic dilatation with a collapsed gallbladder means a hilar block: cholangiocarcinoma.

option_C: Organisms of >10⁵/mL on a midstream specimen of urine (MSU) is due to contamination.
option_D: Biochemical examination of urine helps in calculus disease.
option_E: Cytological examination of urine is sensitive and specific for poorly differentiated transitional cell cancer.
answer_text: If 30% of kidney function is lost, renal failure becomes evident by blood results. | Organisms of >10⁵/mL on a midstream specimen of urine (MSU) is due to contamination.
explanation: Renal failure typically manifests after >70% loss of function, and a count of >10⁵/mL indicates infection rather than contamination.

stem: Regarding urinary tract infection, the following statements are true except:
option_A: Ascending infection in the urinary tract is the most common route.
option_B: E. coli and other Gram-negative organisms are most commonly responsible.
option_C: Proteus and staphylococci thrive in acidic urine.
option_D: Up to 50% of children with urinary infection have an underlying abnormality.
option_E: All patients present electively with dysuria and frequency of micturition.
answer_text: Proteus and staphylococci thrive in acidic urine. | All patients present electively with dysuria and frequency of micturition.
explanation: C is false: urease-producing Proteus and staphylococci make and thrive in alkaline urine. E is false: UTI often presents acutely, e.g. as pyelonephritis or septicaemia.

stem: Regarding upper urinary tract infection, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Sterile pyuria should alert one to the possibility of renal tuberculosis.
option_B: Chronic pyelonephritis is often associated with vesicoureteric reflux.
option_C: Pyonephrosis is an infected hydronephrosis and is most commonly due to a stone-causing obstruction.
option_D: Renal carbuncle is most commonly seen in the immunocompromised.
option_E: Perinephric abscess might occur from extension of a retrocaecal appendix abscess.
answer_text: Sterile pyuria should alert one to the possibility of renal tuberculosis. | Chronic pyelonephritis is often associated with vesicoureteric reflux. | Pyonephrosis is an infected hydronephrosis and is most commonly due to a stone-causing obstruction. | Renal carbuncle is most commonly seen in the immunocompromised. | Perinephric abscess might occur from extension of a retrocaecal appendix abscess.
explanation: All are true: sterile pyuria suggests renal TB, pyonephrosis usually follows stone obstruction and a retrocaecal appendix abscess can track to the perinephric space.

stem: Regarding urinary fistulae, which of the following statements is not true?
option_B: A combined ureterovaginal fistula might be present in 10% of patients.
option_C: Examination under anaesthesia (EUA), IVU and cystoscopy are necessary to evaluate them.
option_D: When there are multiple tracts, the causes might be radiation, malignancy, or sepsis.
option_E: Conservative management by catheter drainage of the bladder is usually successful in a post-hysterectomy fistula.
answer_text: Conservative management by catheter drainage of the bladder is usually successful in a post-hysterectomy fistula.
explanation: Catheter drainage heals only a minority of small, early post-hysterectomy vesicovaginal fistulae; most need formal vaginal or abdominal repair.

stem: Regarding UTI and cystitis, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: The condition is more common in women.
option_B: In recurrent infections, haematuria and rigors, cystoscopy and imaging are essential.
option_C: Sterile pyuria is a sinister finding.
option_D: In tuberculous cystitis, the route of infection is usually haematogenous or lymphogenous.
option_E: Carcinoma in situ might present as recurrent abacterial cystitis.
answer_text: The condition is more common in women. | In recurrent infections, haematuria and rigors, cystoscopy and imaging are essential. | Sterile pyuria is a sinister finding. | Carcinoma in situ might present as recurrent abacterial cystitis.
explanation: D is false: tuberculous cystitis is almost always secondary to renal TB, spreading down the ureter (descending infection), not by haematogenous or lymphatic routes.

stem: Regarding inflammation of the urethra, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Meatal ulcer occurs in middle-aged men from sexually-transmitted disease.
option_B: Gonorrhoeal urethritis might lead to urethral stricture.
option_C: The causative agent in nonspecific urethritis (NSU) is unknown in 50% of patients.
option_D: In Reiter’s disease conjunctivitis is a feature in 50% of patients.
option_E: Bulbar periurethral abscess might cause urinary extravasation.
answer_text: Gonorrhoeal urethritis might lead to urethral stricture. | The causative agent in nonspecific urethritis (NSU) is unknown in 50% of patients. | In Reiter’s disease conjunctivitis is a feature in 50% of patients. | Bulbar periurethral abscess might cause urinary extravasation.
explanation: A is false: meatal ulcer is typically seen in circumcised infants (ammoniacal dermatitis from wet napkins), not as an STD in middle-aged men.

stem: Regarding epididymo-orchitis, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: The causes are Chlamydia and gonococci as sexually-transmitted infections.
option_B: The initial symptoms are those of urinary tract infection (UTI).
option_C: In mumps, 18% of men might develop this condition.
option_D: It is a common postoperative complication after prostatectomy.
option_E: Treatment is doxycycline for Chlamydia or a broad-spectrum antibiotic.
answer_text: The causes are Chlamydia and gonococci as sexually-transmitted infections. | The initial symptoms are those of urinary tract infection (UTI). | In mumps, 18% of men might develop this condition. | Treatment is doxycycline for Chlamydia or a broad-spectrum antibiotic.
explanation: A, B, C and E are true; epididymo-orchitis is rare after prostatectomy.

stem: A 62-year-old man has sudden onset loin pain, frequency, dysuria, confusion, fever 38.2°C. Next most appropriate initial investigation?
explanation: Suspect complicated UTI or pyelonephritis; check urine first.

stem: A 23-year-old woman with frequency, dysuria, T=38.7°C, blood cultures show gram-negative organisms. First management?
explanation: Gram-negative bacteraemia from a urinary source is urosepsis and needs prompt IV antibiotics (with fluids), not oral therapy.

stem: A 45-year-old man has frequency, dysuria, haematuria, suprapubic tenderness. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Frequency, dysuria and haematuria with suprapubic tenderness but no fever or loin pain indicate lower urinary tract infection (acute cystitis).

stem: A 24-year-old woman has a 2-day history of lower abdominal pain with foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She is tender and guarding in the suprapubic region and right iliac fossa. Urine dipstick shows leukocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: PID can present with lower abdominal pain, guarding, discharge, and urinary findings.

stem: A 4-year-old girl is referred to the urology clinic by the GP as she has been having recurrent urinary tract infections. Examination of the child is unremarkable. Which of the following is most likely to be causing the problem?
explanation: Abnormal retrograde flow of urine from bladder to ureter predisposes to UTIs.

stem: A 24-year-old woman with no past medical history of note comes to see you at the GP practice complaining of a 2-day history of urinary frequency together with a stinging sensation on passing urine. She is systemically well. Which of the following organisms is most likely to have caused her symptoms?
explanation: Coli is the most common cause of uncomplicated UTIs in young women.

stem: A 22-year-old previously healthy male complains of dysuria. Genital examination: there is urethral discharge. Urinalysis shows 30 to 40 white blood cells per high power field. First void urine sample is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. Which of the following antibiotic regimens is most appropriate?
option_A: Azithromycin 1 g orally once and ofloxacin 400 mg orally once.
option_B: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole two tablets orally twice a day for 3 days.
option_C: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice a day for 2 weeks.
answer_text: Azithromycin 1 g orally once and ofloxacin 400 mg orally once.
explanation: Single-dose azithromycin treats Chlamydia (7 days of doxycycline is now first line) and the added single dose of ofloxacin covers co-infecting gonorrhoea.

stem: 42-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes develops groin and loin pain. Her temperature is 38.5°C. Examination reveals right renal angle and suprapubic tenderness. Her urine dip shows blood, nitrites, white cells, protein, and ketones. It has been sent for culture. Which is the single most appropriate next investigation?
explanation: Ketonuria in a febrile type 1 diabetic suggests developing ketoacidosis, so check blood glucose (and ketones) first; imaging follows.

stem: 55-year-old woman develops constant right renal angle tenderness, worse on movement. Her temperature is 37.5°C; urine analysis demonstrates haematuria 1+ and white cells 1+, but no nitrites. Her white cell count is 12.3 × 10^9/L. Which is the single most appropriate initial investigation?
explanation: Loin tenderness with low-grade fever and leucocytosis suggests pyelonephritis or a perinephric collection; renal ultrasound is the first-line test for obstruction or abscess.

stem: A 24-year-old sexually active medical student is diagnosed with a urinary tract infection. Which organism is most commonly associated with community-acquired UTI?
explanation: Escherichia coli is responsible for most community-acquired UTIs.

stem: A 40-year-old female lawyer with recurrent UTIs and chronic pyelonephritis is evaluated. Which sonographic feature is diagnostic?
explanation: An atrophic kidney on ultrasound is diagnostic of chronic pyelonephritis.

stem: Urethral discharge: A 28-year-old student with a 2-day history of dysuria and mucopurulent urethral discharge is confirmed to have Neisseria gonorrhoeae. What type of organism is N. gonorrhoeae?
explanation: Gonorrhoeae is a glucose-fermenting Gram-negative diplococcus.

stem: Regarding pain of urological origin, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Pain of renal origin is a deep-seated sickening ache and ‘bursting’ in nature.
option_B: Pain from a ureteric stone is colicky and radiates to the groin, scrotum, or labium.
option_C: Pain from the urinary bladder is a suprapubic discomfort.
option_D: Perineal pain is a penetrating ache and can be referred to the rectum.
option_E: Large, slow-growing, space-occupying lesions produce a constant ache.
answer_text: Pain of renal origin is a deep-seated sickening ache and ‘bursting’ in nature. | Pain from a ureteric stone is colicky and radiates to the groin, scrotum, or labium. | Pain from the urinary bladder is a suprapubic discomfort. | Perineal pain is a penetrating ache and can be referred to the rectum.
explanation: E is false: large, slow-growing space-occupying lesions (e.g. hydronephrosis, renal tumours) are often painless or cause only vague discomfort.

stem: Regarding imaging in urological conditions, which of the following statements are true?
option_B: Pelvic phleboliths cannot be distinguished from lower ureteric calculi on a plain x-ray.
option_C: Ultrasound scanning (US) provides the same information as an intravenous urogram (IVU).
option_E: The procedure of antegrade pyelography can be used therapeutically.
answer_text: Pelvic phleboliths cannot be distinguished from lower ureteric calculi on a plain x-ray. | IVU can be dangerous. | The procedure of antegrade pyelography can be used therapeutically.
explanation: Phleboliths may mimic calculi on plain films; IVU carries contrast risks, and antegrade pyelography can be used therapeutically.

stem: Regarding urological imaging, the following statements are true except:
option_B: Venography should be used when tumour invasion into the inferior vena cava (IVC) is suspected.
option_C: Non-contrast spiral CT should be routine for diagnosis of urinary calculi.
option_D: CT scan is crucial in the staging of renal carcinoma.
option_E: Radioisotope scanning has a role to ascertain selective renal function.
answer_text: Venography should be used when tumour invasion into the inferior vena cava (IVC) is suspected.
explanation: B is false: tumour extension into the IVC is assessed by CT or MRI; venography is now obsolete.

stem: Regarding renal calculi, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: The common bacteria found as a nidus for urinary stones are staphylococci, streptococci and Proteus.
option_B: Hyperparathyroidism is found in 5% or less of those presenting with radio-opaque calculi.
option_C: If a parathyroid adenoma is found to be the cause of renal calculi, it should be removed before treatment of the calculus.
option_D: Pure uric acid stones are radio-opaque.
option_E: A staghorn calculus is composed of calcium-ammonium-magnesium phosphate.
answer_text: The common bacteria found as a nidus for urinary stones are staphylococci, streptococci and Proteus. | Hyperparathyroidism is found in 5% or less of those presenting with radio-opaque calculi. | If a parathyroid adenoma is found to be the cause of renal calculi, it should be removed before treatment of the calculus. | A staghorn calculus is composed of calcium-ammonium-magnesium phosphate.
explanation: D is false: pure uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain X-ray (visible on CT); staghorn calculi are usually struvite from urease-producing infection.

stem: Regarding renal and ureteric calculi, which of the following statements are false?
option_A: Renal stones are usually visible on a plain x-ray.
option_B: The severity of pain of ureteric colic is related to the size of stone.
option_C: Hydronephrosis or pyonephrosis with a palpable loin swelling is a common clinical presentation.
option_E: There are very few physical signs.
answer_text: The severity of pain of ureteric colic is related to the size of stone. | Hydronephrosis or pyonephrosis with a palpable loin swelling is a common clinical presentation.
explanation: Pain intensity does not correlate with stone size and palpable swellings are rare.

stem: Which of the following imaging techniques are used for urinary calculus disease?
option_A: Plain kidney, ureter and bladder (KUB) x-ray
answer_text: Plain kidney, ureter and bladder (KUB) x-ray | Spiral CT scan | IVU | Ultrasound (US) | Retrograde pyelography
explanation: All are used: non-contrast CT KUB is now the investigation of choice; KUB, US and IVU still have roles, and retrograde pyelography is used in selected cases.

stem: Regarding management of urinary calculi, the following statements are true except:
option_A: Ureteric calculi smaller than 1 cm will pass spontaneously.
option_B: Infection in the presence of upper urinary tract obstruction due to a stone requires surgical intervention.
option_C: Most urinary calculi can be treated by minimal-access surgical techniques.
option_D: In bilateral renal stones, the kidney with poorer function is treated first.
option_E: Open operations for renal stones are performed through an extraperitoneal loin approach.
answer_text: Ureteric calculi smaller than 1 cm will pass spontaneously. | In bilateral renal stones, the kidney with poorer function is treated first.
explanation: A is false: stones under 5 mm usually pass but many 5–10 mm stones do not. D is false: with bilateral stones the better-functioning kidney is usually treated first.

stem: Which of the following statements are true in ureteric stones?
option_B: If a stone has not passed after 6 weeks, intervention is required.
option_C: Stones are commonly arrested at the two sites of ureteric narrowing.
option_D: Most stones are treated by ureteroscopic electrohydraulic fragmentation.
option_E: Severe renal pain subsiding after a day or two suggests that the stone has passed.
answer_text: The majority pass spontaneously. | If a stone has not passed after 6 weeks, intervention is required.
explanation: C is false: stones lodge at several narrowings (PUJ, pelvic brim, VUJ). D is false: most pass, the rest mainly by laser ureteroscopy/ESWL. E is false: pain may settle despite obstruction.

stem: Regarding bladder stones, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Men are more often affected than women.
option_B: An oxalate calculus develops in sterile urine.
option_D: Treatment is crushing with an optical lithotrite in all cases.
option_E: In men with stones and outflow obstruction from enlarged prostate, both can be dealt with at the same time.
answer_text: Men are more often affected than women. | An oxalate calculus develops in sterile urine. | A cystine calculus is radio-opaque. | In men with stones and outflow obstruction from enlarged prostate, both can be dealt with at the same time.
explanation: D is false: most bladder stones are fragmented endoscopically, but large or hard stones may need percutaneous or open cystolithotomy.

stem: A 68-year-old man has urinary urgency/frequency worse on exercise over weeks. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Irritative voiding, especially with movement, can indicate bladder calculi.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with severe colicky pain in his right loin radiating to his groin. On examination you note tenderness in the right loin. A urine dipstick is positive for blood. What is the next most appropriate initial investigation?
explanation: Loin-to-groin colic with haematuria suggests a ureteric stone; non-contrast CT KUB is the first-line imaging test (sensitivity about 97%).

stem: A 75-year-old male with gout and recent chemotherapy has right flank pain radiating to groin, onset was rapid. Microscopic haematuria. USS KUB negative but CT confirms the diagnosis. What to prevent this in future?
explanation: Uric acid stones (gout, tumour lysis after chemotherapy) are prevented by urinary alkalinisation with potassium citrate, plus hydration and allopurinol.

stem: A previously fit 45-year-old with severe left loin-to-groin colicky pain. Plain abdominal X-ray shows a left ureteric calculus, urine dipstick trace of blood only. Stone composition?
explanation: Most common type, typically radio-opaque on X-ray.

stem: A 31-year-old man has acute colicky right flank-to-groin pain, frequency, dysuria, haematuria. Most common metabolic abnormality with this condition?
explanation: Most calcium stones are linked to elevated urinary calcium.

stem: A 26-year-old man with severe colicky right loin-to-groin pain, urine dipstick positive for blood. IVU shows a 3 mm ureteric stone. After analgesia, what next?
explanation: <5 mm stone often passes spontaneously.

stem: A 26-year-old man with severe right loin-to-groin colic, dipstick positive for blood/nitrites, IVU shows a 4 mm ureteric stone. What first?
explanation: Priority is pain control; then consider tamsulosin if indicated.

stem: A 73-year-old man presents with sudden-onset right-sided back pain radiating to the abdomen. He is stable, afebrile, tender in the right abdomen. Trace blood on dipstick. Which investigation next?
explanation: To exclude AAA or renal stone; CT is definitive to distinguish these pathologies.

stem: A 27-year-old man has severe left-sided loin pain for 2 hours, constant but fluctuates, with vomiting. Mild left loin tenderness. Dipstick shows 2+ blood. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Flank pain radiating anteriorly plus haematuria is characteristic of ureteric stone.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 3-hour history of left loin pain radiating to the left groin. He is known to have benign prostatic hypertrophy and recurrent urinary tract infections. The intravenous urogram (IVU) shows a standing column on the left. Which of the following types of stone is most likely to have caused his symptoms?
explanation: Struvite stones are associated with chronic UTIs by urease-producing organisms.

stem: A 40-year-old previously healthy man presents with sudden onset of severe right flank pain radiating to the groin, associated with nausea, sweating, and urinary urgency. Examination is normal except for distress. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Classic colicky flank-to-groin pain suggests a ureteric stone.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of a suspected ureteral stone?
option_B: IV fluid hydration, IV analgesics, and nonenhanced computed tomography (CT) scan
option_C: IV fluid hydration, IV analgesics, and arrangements for lithotripsy
option_E: urine culture, followed by antibiotic therapy
answer_text: IV fluid hydration, IV analgesics, and nonenhanced computed tomography (CT) scan
explanation: Noncontrast CT is the best imaging to confirm and locate the stone; treat pain and hydrate.

stem: A 35-year-old healthy patient presented with left loin pain and microscopic hematuria. K.U.B. revealed radio-opacity at the left flank. Native CT scan revealed a stone with a maximum diameter 12 mm in the left renal pelvis. Which among the following is the most appropriate treatment option?
option_C: Alkalization of urine by using potassium citrate.
option_D: Trial of tamsulosin 0.4 mg nocte for 2 weeks.
explanation: For a renal pelvic stone under 2 cm, ESWL (or flexible ureteroscopy) is first line; PCNL is for stones over 2 cm, and tamsulosin helps only distal ureteric stones.

stem: A 42-year-old male presents to the emergency unit with severe left loin pain and high-grade fever for the past three days. His native CT shows severe left hydroureteronephrosis ending at an impacted 8-mm lower ureteric stone. The next most appropriate line of treatment for this scenario is:
option_B: Antibiotics and analgesia until the fever subsides.
option_D: Analgesia, antibiotics, and stenting of left ureter.
answer_text: Analgesia, antibiotics, and stenting of left ureter.
explanation: An infected obstructed kidney is a urological emergency: antibiotics plus urgent decompression (ureteric stent or nephrostomy); definitive stone treatment is delayed.

stem: 45-year-old man has severe colicky right-sided pain radiating from loin to groin, with nausea and vomiting. He is restless and tender in the right renal angle. Urinalysis shows blood +. Which is the single most appropriate investigation?
explanation: Renal tract CT scan is the gold standard for imaging urinary stones.

stem: 47-year-old man develops sudden onset of colicky pain in his right loin, radiating into his testicle. The pain is severe and is associated with vomiting. A junior colleague asks for teaching about calculi. Which single statement with respect to urinary calculi is correct?
option_A: Calcium phosphate stones are associated with renal tubular alkalosis
option_B: Cystine stones are associated with urinary tract infection
option_C: Staghorn calculi are associated with high urinary uric acid
option_D: Struvite stones are the most common in UK patients
option_E: There is seasonal variation in presentation of urinary tract lithiasis
answer_text: There is seasonal variation in presentation of urinary tract lithiasis
explanation: Urinary stone presentation varies seasonally, often peaking in summer due to dehydration.

stem: A 36-year-old man presents to the emergency room with renal colic. His vital signs are normal and a urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria. A radiograph reveals a 1.5-cm stone. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?
option_E: Open surgery to remove the stone
explanation: Extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy is appropriate for a 1.5-cm renal stone.

stem: A 40-year-old office executive presents with excruciating left loin pain and a 4 mm radio‐opaque stone in the left ureter. What type of stone is more likely?
explanation: Calcium oxalate (alone or mixed with calcium phosphate) forms most urinary stones (about 75–80%), and these are radio-opaque.

stem: A 30-year-old PhD student has acute colicky left loin pain suggestive of a urinary calculus. Which initial investigation should he have?
explanation: Of these options, a plain KUB film is the initial test (about 90% of stones are radio-opaque); non-contrast CT KUB is now the definitive investigation.

stem: A 35-year-old housewife with dysuria, frequency and a large left pelvicalyceal calculus is evaluated; which microorganism is NOT associated with such stones?
explanation: Mycobacteria are not typically implicated in infection-related renal stones.

stem: A 75-year-old man with a 24-hour history of left loin pain and a history of gout is suspected to have a urinary calculus. Which substance is most likely the major component?
explanation: Gout (hyperuricosuria and persistently acidic urine) predisposes to uric acid stones, which are radiolucent on plain film but seen on CT.

stem: A 49-year-old postmenopausal woman is admitted following severe attacks of abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. The pain is colicky in nature, starting from the left flank and radiating to the left groin. You are unable to obtain a history as she is writhing in pain. On examination, she is sweating profusely. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Colicky pain radiating from the loin to groin with diaphoresis suggests renal colic.

stem: A 49-year-old woman has severe colicky left flank pain radiating to the left groin, with nausea and vomiting; renal colic is suspected. Which investigation will be of most diagnostic value?
option_A: Computed tomography scan of the abdomen
answer_text: Computed tomography scan of the abdomen
explanation: Non-contrast (low-dose) CT KUB is the gold standard for diagnosing urinary stones, showing size and site and excluding other causes such as an aortic aneurysm.

stem: Which of the following statements about Wilms’ tumour is false?
option_A: It is a tumour of embryonic nephrogenic tissue occurring below the age of 5 years.
option_B: Haematuria and fever are the most common presentations.
option_C: Haematogenous spread is mainly to the lungs.
option_D: Imaging modalities are US, CT and MRI.
option_E: Treatment is by chemotherapy, surgery and radiotherapy.
answer_text: Haematuria and fever are the most common presentations.
explanation: Wilms’ tumour most commonly presents as an abdominal mass.

stem: Which of the following statements about hypernephroma (renal cell carcinoma) are true?
option_A: In 25% of patients there are no local symptoms.
option_B: A left-sided varicocele might be a presenting feature in a male.
option_C: Haematuria and clot colic are the most common presentations.
option_D: US and contrast-enhanced CT are the imaging methods of choice.
option_E: Following nephrectomy, chemotherapy and radiotherapy should be given.
answer_text: In 25% of patients there are no local symptoms. | A left-sided varicocele might be a presenting feature in a male. | Haematuria and clot colic are the most common presentations. | US and contrast-enhanced CT are the imaging methods of choice.
explanation: E is false: renal cell carcinoma is resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, so these are not given after nephrectomy; a left varicocele may signal renal vein involvement.

stem: A 49-year-old woman has loin pain and haematuria. On exam, a mass in the right loin. Investigation?
explanation: A loin mass with haematuria suggests a renal tumour; contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen characterises the mass and stages it.

stem: A middle-aged man diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma of the left kidney, no distant metastasis. Next step?
explanation: Potentially curative resection for localized RCC.

stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the GP practice by his mother. He has been complaining intermittently about abdominal pain. His mother feels that his abdomen is distended. On examination, there is a large mass on the left side of the abdomen which does not cross the midline. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Wilms tumour arises from embryonic renal tissue and typically doesn’t cross midline.

stem: A 45-year-old male is planning a kidney donation for his wife who has an end stage renal disease. Which of the following reasons listed below would most likely prevent the husband from donating his kidney?
option_A: The donor has a body mass index (BMI) of 28 kg/m².
option_B: The donor has hypertension controlled by one medication.
option_C: The donor’s blood group is O negative.
option_D: The donor has a family history of benign prostatic hyperplasia.
option_E: The donor has a GFR of 40 ml/min per 1.73 m².
answer_text: The donor has a GFR of 40 ml/min per 1.73 m².
explanation: Living donors need adequate renal reserve; a GFR of 40 mL/min/1.73 m² excludes donation, whereas BMI 28, single-drug-controlled hypertension and group O are acceptable.

stem: A 68-year-old female with unexplained persistent asymptomatic microscopic hematuria underwent CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast; there was a 3x2 cm solid irregular enhancing mass arising from the parenchyma of the right kidney. The patient is asymptomatic and vitally stable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A solid enhancing parenchymal renal mass in an adult is renal cell carcinoma until proven otherwise; TCC arises from the collecting system and AML contains fat.

stem: An ultrasound scan in a 50-year-old blind man with painless haematuria suggests the presence of adenocarcinoma of the kidney. A subsequent CT scan of his chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirms the diagnosis and shows renal vein invasion by the tumour (see Figure 9.1). The patient is anaemic but serum creatinine is 92µmol/L, potassium is 4.8mmol/L, calcium is 2.4mmol/L, and alkaline phosphatase is 33U/L. Which is the single most appropriate next step?
explanation: Renal cancer in a blind man suggests von Hippel–Lindau disease (retinal angiomas), so genetic counselling and family screening are indicated.

stem: A 45-year-old otherwise healthy woman presents with a 7-cm renal cell carcinoma without radiologic evidence of abdominal lymph node involvement and with no distant metastases. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
explanation: Surgery with radical nephrectomy is the main treatment for localized renal cell carcinoma.

stem: What is the most common type of renal cell carcinoma?
explanation: Clear cell carcinoma is the most common histological subtype of renal cell carcinoma.

stem: What syndrome associated with renal cell carcinoma is caused by a mutation in a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3?
explanation: Von Hippel–Lindau disease is caused by mutation of the VHL tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 3p and predisposes to clear cell renal cell carcinoma.

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding renal cell carcinoma is true?
option_A: It is an incidental finding in fewer than 10% of patients
option_B: Women are more commonly affected than men
option_D: Renal cell carcinoma accounts for around 3% of adult cancers
option_E: Metastases are poorly visualized by standard imaging techniques
answer_text: Renal cell carcinoma accounts for around 3% of adult cancers
explanation: Renal cell carcinoma represents about 3% of adult cancers.

stem: A young girl with fever, left loin swelling and microscopic haematuria is ultimately diagnosed with Wilms tumour. Which statement about Wilms tumour is true?
option_A: The tumour may be associated with anophthalmia
option_B: 5-year survival in stage IV disease is approximately 65%
option_C: Children most commonly present at the age of 8–10 years
option_D: Some cases are associated with a gene mutation on chromosome 13
option_E: It commonly metastasizes to the brain
answer_text: 5-year survival in stage IV disease is approximately 65%
explanation: By elimination: Wilms tumour is linked to aniridia and WT1 on chromosome 11, peaks at 3–4 years and spreads to the lungs; stage IV survival is roughly 65–80%.

stem: Regarding urethral stricture, the following statements are true except:
option_A: Urinary flow trace will show a prolonged flow with a plateau-shaped curve.
option_B: In acute retention suprapubic catheterisation is required.
option_C: Causes are inflammatory, traumatic and iatrogenic.
option_D: Traumatic strictures are best treated by urethroplasty.
option_E: The ideal treatment in the majority is urethral dilatation.
answer_text: The ideal treatment in the majority is urethral dilatation.
explanation: Urethral dilatation is not the ideal treatment in most cases; the other statements accurately describe urethral stricture.

stem: Regarding female urethra, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: The bladder neck is the most important entity for urinary continence.
option_B: Urethral prolapse occurs as a result of childbirth.
option_C: Fowler’s syndrome is best treated by urethral dilatation.
option_E: Urethral diverticulum is more common in women than men.
answer_text: Urethral prolapse occurs as a result of childbirth. | Urethral diverticulum is more common in women than men.
explanation: A false: in women the urethral (mid-urethral) sphincter matters most; C false: Fowler syndrome is treated by sacral neuromodulation; D false: a caruncle is benign.

stem: Regarding surgical conditions of the foreskin, the following statements are true except:
option_A: The most common indication for circumcision is cultural reasons.
option_B: In children circumcision is the treatment for non-retractile foreskin due to adhesions.
option_C: Circumcision is indicated in true phimosis with balanoposthitis.
option_E: Monopolar diathermy should never be used during a circumcision.
answer_text: In children circumcision is the treatment for non-retractile foreskin due to adhesions.
explanation: Non-retractile foreskin due to adhesions is usually physiological; the other statements are correct.

stem: A 33-year-old man has increasing difficulty passing urine with poor flow. He had gonorrhoea thrice. Which investigation best establishes the cause?
explanation: A history of gonococcal infection suggests urethral stricture investigated by urethrography.

stem: A 27-year-old man who has just returned from a holiday in Asia presents to the GP surgery having noticed a painless hard ulcer over the penile glans. He is otherwise well. On examination, the patient has generalized painless lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: A painless ulcer (chancre) and painless lymphadenopathy is classic for primary syphilis.

stem: A 55-year-old male patient with multiple comorbidities presents with an erectile dysfunction. Which of the following of his medications listed below is least likely to cause an erectile dysfunction?
explanation: Beta-blockers, thiazides, SSRIs such as fluoxetine and 5α-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride can all cause erectile dysfunction; metformin does not.

stem: A 35-year-old man on an alpha blocker for hypertension is undergoing an infertility evaluation for secondary infertility. Has a normal physical examination, including genitals and DRE. Two semen analyses both demonstrate semen volume of less than 1 ml; with normal sperm count, motility, and morphology. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to be recommended next in this case?
explanation: Low-volume ejaculate with normal sperm in a man on an α-blocker suggests retrograde ejaculation, confirmed by finding sperm in post-ejaculatory urine.

stem: A 75-year-old lady with a long history of uncontrolled DM presented with chronic retention of urine and frequent unaware leakage of urine with wetting of her clothes. Ultrasound revealed a post void residue (PVR) of 200 ml on two separate occasions. This condition is most appropriately described as:
explanation: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy causes a hypotonic bladder with chronic retention and dribbling overflow incontinence, as shown by the large post-void residue.

stem: 50-year-old stonemason develops erectile dysfunction. Which of the single points arising from his history is least likely to be related to his erectile problem?
option_A: He has a Dupuytren’s contracture of his right palmar fascia
option_B: He has become progressively deaf during the last 3 years
option_C: He has had an inguinal hernia repair complicated by ilioinguinal nerve damage
option_D: He reports that his GP is struggling to control his hypertension
option_E: He suffered a slipped intervertebral disc at work last year
answer_text: He has had an inguinal hernia repair complicated by ilioinguinal nerve damage
explanation: Damage to the ilioinguinal nerve is not typically associated with erectile dysfunction.

stem: 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has an inability to maintain an erection during intercourse. He reports morning erections. His only medication is for glycaemic control. He has a normal neurological examination. Which is the single most appropriate initial investigation?
option_C: Check hormone profile (testosterone, FSH/luteinizing hormone, prolactin, thyroid function)
explanation: Morning erections suggest a psychogenic cause; a validated questionnaire is appropriate for initial assessment.

stem: A 18-year-old high school football player is kicked in the left flank. Three hours later he develops hematuria. His vital signs are HR 80, BP 123/67, and RR 14. A CT scan demonstrates a nonexpanding perirenal hematoma confined to the renal retroperitoneum. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
explanation: A non-expanding perirenal haematoma in a stable patient is a low-grade (AAST grade II) renal injury, managed non-operatively with bed rest and monitoring.

stem: A 32-year-old man is in a high-speed motorcycle collision and presents with an obvious pelvic fracture. On examination, he has a scrotal hematoma and blood at his urethral meatus. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in his management?
explanation: Blood at the meatus with pelvic fracture and scrotal haematoma suggests urethral injury: retrograde urethrogram before any catheter; suprapubic catheter if disrupted.

stem: A 26-year-old man complains of pelvic pain after a motorcycle collision. Physical and radiologic examinations confirm a pelvic fracture. Urologic workup reveals a normal urethrogram and an extraperitoneal bladder injury. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the treatment of his bladder injury?
explanation: Uncomplicated extraperitoneal bladder rupture heals with urethral catheter drainage for about 10–14 days; intraperitoneal rupture needs surgical repair.

stem: All of the following statements regarding carcinoma of the penis are true, except
option_A: It is a squamous cell carcinoma
option_B: Incidence is lower in men infected with the human papilloma virus
option_C: Incidence is lower in men circumcised at birth
option_D: Staging of disease is by the tumour node metastasis (TNM) system
option_E: 5-year survival in patients with localized disease is around 80%
