stem: A 75-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and heart failure (EF 40%) was caught in a house fire when his clothes ignited. He has extensive white, leathery burns of the arms and legs with red blistered margins; pulse 110/min, BP 90/60 mmHg. What is the best initial management?
option_D: Airway assessment and IV fluid resuscitation
answer_text: Airway assessment and IV fluid resuscitation
explanation: Burns follow ATLS: secure the airway (inhalation risk) and start IV resuscitation; dressings and surgery come later.

stem: A 75-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and heart failure (EF 40%) was caught in a house fire when his clothes ignited. He has extensive white, leathery burns of the arms and legs with red blistered margins; pulse 110/min, BP 90/60 mmHg. What is the depth of these burns?
explanation: White, leathery, painless skin is full-thickness burn; the red blistered margins are partial thickness.

stem: A 75-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and heart failure (EF 40%) was caught in a house fire when his clothes ignited. He has extensive white, leathery burns of the arms and legs with red blistered margins; pulse 110/min, BP 90/60 mmHg. What is the most common complication in the first 24 hours?
explanation: Capillary leak causes hypovolaemic burn shock in the first 24–48 h; sepsis and contractures come later.

stem: A 75-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and heart failure (EF 40%) was caught in a house fire when his clothes ignited. He has extensive white, leathery burns of the arms and legs with red blistered margins; pulse 110/min, BP 90/60 mmHg. Given his diabetes and heart failure, what is the key consideration in fluid resuscitation?
option_A: Use the standard formula without change
option_C: Start Parkland cautiously and titrate to urine output
answer_text: Start Parkland cautiously and titrate to urine output
explanation: Parkland is only a starting point; titrate to urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h to avoid both under-resuscitation and fluid overload in heart failure.

stem: A 45-year-old man is brought after a car crash. The right chest moves paradoxically with bruising, reduced expansion and diminished breath sounds. He is conscious but distressed; BP 95/60 mmHg, SpO2 86%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Paradoxical movement of a chest segment after blunt trauma is flail chest (two or more ribs broken in two or more places).

stem: A 45-year-old man is brought after a car crash. The right chest moves paradoxically with bruising, reduced expansion and diminished breath sounds. He is conscious but distressed; BP 95/60 mmHg, SpO2 86%. Which mechanism mainly compromises his lungs?
explanation: Hypoxia in flail chest is caused mainly by the underlying pulmonary contusion, aggravated by pain-limited ventilation.

stem: A 45-year-old man is brought after a car crash. The right chest moves paradoxically with bruising, reduced expansion and diminished breath sounds. He is conscious but distressed; BP 95/60 mmHg, SpO2 86%. Chest X-ray and CT show a massive haemothorax. What is the next immediate step?
explanation: Massive haemothorax is treated with a large-bore chest drain and resuscitation; thoracotomy if > 1500 mL initially or > 200 mL/h.

stem: A 45-year-old man is brought after a car crash. The right chest moves paradoxically with bruising, reduced expansion and diminished breath sounds. He is conscious but distressed; BP 95/60 mmHg, SpO2 86%. He improves but remains hypoxic with paradoxical movement. What is the next definitive step?
explanation: Persistent hypoxia despite analgesia and oxygen needs intubation and ventilation (internal splinting); rib fixation is increasingly used to wean.

stem: An elderly patient has headache 3 weeks after a minor head injury; CT shows a crescent-shaped collection. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: A crescentic (hypodense) collection weeks after minor trauma in an elderly patient is a chronic subdural haematoma: burr-hole drainage.

stem: A man cuts his forearm on glass; the wound is not deep and its edges are everted. Which closure and immediate drug are most appropriate?
option_A: Simple interrupted non-absorbable monofilament (e.g. 4/0 nylon) sutures and tetanus prophylaxis
option_B: Absorbable braided sutures and IV antibiotics
option_C: Leave open and give oral steroids
answer_text: Simple interrupted non-absorbable monofilament (e.g. 4/0 nylon) sutures and tetanus prophylaxis
explanation: Superficial lacerations are closed with interrupted non-absorbable monofilament sutures; check tetanus status and give prophylaxis.

stem: A man cuts his forearm on glass; the wound is not deep and its edges are everted. If the wound is deep, how should it be closed?
option_A: Layered closure: absorbable subcutaneous sutures, then skin sutures
option_C: Leave open to heal by secondary intention
answer_text: Layered closure: absorbable subcutaneous sutures, then skin sutures
explanation: Deep wounds need layered closure with absorbable (e.g. polyglactin) deep sutures to close dead space and reduce tension, haematoma and infection.

stem: Regarding trauma, which of the following statements is true?
option_A: It is the fifth most common cause of death overall.
option_B: It is the second most common cause of death and disability below 40 years of age.
option_C: One-year mortality following a proximal femoral fracture in patients over 65 years is 30%.
option_D: Trauma is predominantly secondary to high-energy injuries.
option_E: Less than 25% of children who die of abuse have had previous contact with health or social services.
answer_text: One-year mortality following a proximal femoral fracture in patients over 65 years is 30%.
explanation: About 30% of over-65s die within a year of a proximal femoral fracture; trauma is the leading (not second) cause of death under 40 and most injuries are low-energy.

stem: Regarding trauma assessment, which of the following statements is false?
option_A: The patient, mechanism of injury, and injury are the keystones of management.
option_B: It is as essential to identify obvious injuries as it is to identify the occult (hidden) injuries.
option_C: High-velocity bullet injuries are associated with cavity formation.
option_D: Blunt injuries can be direct (impact) or indirect (force transmission).
option_E: Knife injury over a limb is easy to evaluate.
answer_text: Knife injury over a limb is easy to evaluate.
explanation: Knife injuries may be deceptively complex despite an unassuming appearance.

stem: In relation to blunt injuries, which of the following statements is false?
option_A: The mechanisms are direct or indirect.
option_B: In indirect injury, associated injuries may be present and should be sought.
option_C: In chest injuries, damage to abdominal organs is rare.
option_D: Overt injury should lead the clinician to look for covert (hidden) injuries.
option_E: Significant internal injury may be present with little external evidence.
answer_text: In chest injuries, damage to abdominal organs is rare.
explanation: Blunt injury to the lower chest commonly damages the liver and spleen lying under the lower ribs, so abdominal injury must always be sought.

stem: In relation to covert injuries, which of the following statements is true?
option_A: A deductive approach is not necessary.
option_B: A look-everywhere approach is not helpful.
option_C: A focused approach that limits the scope of your assessment is not useful.
option_D: Head to pelvis CT is part of a look-everywhere approach.
option_E: Screen patients where clinical signs are obvious.
answer_text: Head to pelvis CT is part of a look-everywhere approach.
explanation: A comprehensive CT from head to pelvis aids in detecting hidden injuries.

stem: In relation to covert injuries, which of the following statements is false?
option_A: Electrocution = burn (obvious) and posterior dislocation of the shoulder (covert).
option_B: Dashboard = patella fracture (obvious) and posterior dislocation of the hip (covert).
option_C: Inhalational injury = facial burns (obvious) and laryngeal oedema (covert).
option_D: Left-side impact RTA = left pneumothorax with chest wall contusions (obvious) and liver laceration (covert).
option_E: Flexion-distraction = head injury (obvious) and cervical spine fracture (covert).
answer_text: Left-side impact RTA = left pneumothorax with chest wall contusions (obvious) and liver laceration (covert).
explanation: Left-side impact typically causes splenic rather than liver injury.

stem: In relation to NAI in children, which of the following statements is false?
option_A: History is inconsistent with the injury sustained.
option_C: There are likely to be injuries of differing ages or duration.
option_D: There may be aggressive behaviour from the carers.
option_E: A femoral shaft fracture in a 6-month-old is not suspicious of NAI.
answer_text: A femoral shaft fracture in a 6-month-old is not suspicious of NAI.
explanation: Femoral shaft fractures in non‐ambulatory infants are highly suspicious for non-accidental injury.

stem: Which of the following statements is false with regard to a polytrauma patient?
option_A: A drop in body temperature occurs.
option_B: There is a generalised immune response.
option_C: The patient has compensatory mechanisms to blood loss.
option_E: Diversion from protocol should be avoided.
answer_text: Diversion from protocol should be avoided.
explanation: Early polytrauma care is protocol-driven, but the experienced clinician may need to deviate from the protocol when the clinical situation demands it.

stem: Regarding mechanisms of trauma, which of the following statements is false?
option_A: The most common cause of blunt trauma is a motor vehicle accident (MVA).
option_B: A 10% increase in impact speed equates to a ~40% increase in pedestrian fatality.
option_C: Seat belts reduce the risk of death or serious injury for front-seat occupants by ~20%.
option_D: For head-on collisions, airbags reduce the risk of fatality by ~30%.
option_E: Motorcyclists have a higher rate of mortality than car occupants involved in a MVA.
answer_text: Seat belts reduce the risk of death or serious injury for front-seat occupants by ~20%.
explanation: Seat belts reduce death or serious injury in front-seat occupants by about 45–50%, not 20%; airbags reduce fatality in head-on collisions by about 30%.

stem: Regarding airway assessment, which of the following statements is false?
option_A: If the patient is talking, he or she does not have an imminently compromised airway.
option_B: Suction of the airway may be required.
option_C: Nasopharyngeal and Guedal airways are useful adjuncts.
option_D: GCS of 7 is not an indication for a definitive airway.
option_E: Cervical spine control is required throughout airway assessment.
answer_text: GCS of 7 is not an indication for a definitive airway.
explanation: A GCS of 8 or less mandates a definitive airway, so a GCS of 7 is an indication; a patient who is talking has a patent airway for now.

stem: Regarding assessing disability, which of the following can be responsible for a reduced consciousness level?
explanation: Head injury, hypovolaemia, hypoglycaemia, and alcohol can all lower consciousness.

stem: Which of the following is not a routine adjunct to the primary survey?
option_C: Bloods including FBC, U&Es, clotting screen and glucose
option_D: Radiographs of the C-spine, chest and pelvis
explanation: CT (± angiography) follows in the stable patient after the primary survey; pulse oximetry, catheter, bloods and chest/pelvic films are primary-survey adjuncts.

stem: Regarding the secondary survey, which of the following is not part of the AMPLE assessment?
explanation: Pain assessment is important clinically but not part of the AMPLE mnemonic.

stem: Regarding paediatric trauma, which of the following combination of observations is optimal for a preschool child (<5 years)?
option_A: Pulse 160 bpm, SBP 90, RR 40, UO 1.5 mL/kg/hour
option_B: Pulse 160 bpm, SBP 90, RR 40, UO 1 mL/kg/hour
option_C: Pulse 140 bpm, SBP 80, RR 30, UO 1 mL/kg/hour
option_D: Pulse 140 bpm, SBP 90, RR 40, UO 1.5 mL/kg/hour
option_E: Pulse 140 bpm, SBP 90, RR 30, UO 1.5 mL/kg/hour
answer_text: Pulse 140 bpm, SBP 90, RR 30, UO 1.5 mL/kg/hour
explanation: Bailey & Love quotes normal values for a preschool child of pulse 140/min, systolic BP 90 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min and urine output 1.5 mL/kg/h.

stem: Regarding the hazards of imaging and radiation, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Low-osmolality contrast media (LOCM) are safer than their higher-osmolality counterparts.
option_B: Routine steroid prophylaxis is recommended before use of contrast in the high-risk patient.
option_C: In the diabetic, metformin should be stopped before using contrast.
option_D: The majority of ionising radiation comes from medical exposure from investigations.
option_E: Radionuclide imaging allows function to be studied.
answer_text: Low-osmolality contrast media (LOCM) are safer than their higher-osmolality counterparts. | Radionuclide imaging allows function to be studied.
explanation: B false: routine steroid prophylaxis is not recommended; C false: metformin need not be stopped if eGFR >30; D false: most exposure is natural background radiation.

stem: Regarding diagnostic imaging, which of the following statements is false?
option_A: Conventional x-rays will delineate different soft tissue reliably.
option_C: Dedicated transducers can help in endocavitary ultrasound (US).
option_D: Change in the frequency of an US wave can be caused by red blood cells.
option_E: The higher the frequency of the US wave, the greater the resolution of the image.
answer_text: Conventional x-rays will delineate different soft tissue reliably.
explanation: Plain radiographs do not reliably differentiate soft tissues.

stem: Regarding imaging modalities, which of the following statements are true?
option_B: Computed tomography (CT) scan has a higher resolution than plain radiographs.
option_C: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans give excellent contrast resolution.
option_E: Radionuclide imaging allows function to be studied.
answer_text: Computed tomography (CT) scan has a higher resolution than plain radiographs. | Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans give excellent contrast resolution. | Radionuclide imaging allows function to be studied.
explanation: A and D are false: US is operator-dependent and blocked by bone and gas, and MRI is slow, costly and contraindicated with some implants; radionuclide imaging shows function.

stem: The following statements are true except:
option_A: The clinician referring the patient must balance risk against benefit.
option_B: The clinician must give as much information as possible.
option_C: Use portable machines and fluoroscopy wherever possible.
option_D: Take all precautions when using an image intensifier.
option_E: The lungs, heart and pancreas are especially vulnerable to irradiation.
answer_text: Use portable machines and fluoroscopy wherever possible. | The lungs, heart and pancreas are especially vulnerable to irradiation.
explanation: Portable films and fluoroscopy give higher doses and should be minimised; the most radiosensitive tissues are the gonads, lens, thyroid, breast and marrow.

stem: Regarding orthopaedic imaging, which of the following statements is false?
option_A: Synovitis can be detected by plain x-ray.
option_B: MR arthrography is the ideal imaging for articular cartilage damage.
option_C: MRI is the ideal method for local staging of a malignant bone tumour.
option_D: X-ray is the first investigation in destructive bone lesions.
option_E: US is used to examine mass lesions of soft tissues.
answer_text: Synovitis can be detected by plain x-ray.
explanation: Plain radiographs cannot reliably detect synovitis; advanced imaging is needed.

stem: Regarding imaging in trauma, which of the following statements is false?
option_A: In a multiply injured patient, CT of head and spine should be the first line of imaging.
option_B: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) helps in detecting intraperitoneal fluid and cardiac tamponade.
option_C: CT should not be used when a patient is unstable.
option_D: US is useful for diagnosing occult pneumothorax.
option_E: CT is the main imaging method for intracranial, intra-abdominal and vertebral injuries.
answer_text: In a multiply injured patient, CT of head and spine should be the first line of imaging.
explanation: Initial management relies on plain films and FAST; CT is reserved for stable patients.

stem: Which of the following statements are true about skin incisions?
option_A: Skin incisions are best made along tension lines.
option_B: Incisions should avoid bony prominences and skin creases.
option_C: The 22-blade scalpel is ideal for all incisions.
option_D: Incisions should be made bearing in mind cosmesis.
option_E: Transverse abdominal incisions have fewer respiratory complications.
answer_text: Skin incisions are best made along tension lines. | Incisions should be made bearing in mind cosmesis. | Transverse abdominal incisions have fewer respiratory complications.
explanation: B is false: incisions should avoid bony prominences but are best placed in skin creases; C is false: no single blade suits all incisions (the 10 and 15 are standard).

stem: Regarding wound closure, all of the following statements are true except:
option_A: Mass closure technique is the usual method used for abdominal wall.
option_B: Sutures lose 50% of their tensile strength at the knot.
option_C: Non-absorbable suture material should be used in the biliary and urinary tract.
option_D: Synthetic suture materials elicit minimal tissue reaction.
option_E: Round-bodied needles are used in intestinal surgery.
answer_text: Non-absorbable suture material should be used in the biliary and urinary tract.
explanation: Non-absorbable sutures in the biliary or urinary tract act as a nidus for stone formation, so absorbable sutures are used; the other statements are true.

stem: Regarding the principles of anastomosis, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: The current favoured technique of bowel anastomosis is the one-layer extramucosal interrupted method.
option_B: The bowel must be prepared prior to any anastomosis.
option_C: It is essential that in end-to-end anastomosis the bowel ends should match the diameter.
option_D: In vascular anastomosis, polypropylene is the suture material to be used.
option_E: A transverse arteriotomy should always be used to prevent stenosis after closure.
answer_text: The current favoured technique of bowel anastomosis is the one-layer extramucosal interrupted method. | In vascular anastomosis, polypropylene is the suture material to be used.
explanation: B false: routine bowel preparation is not required; C false: size mismatch is overcome by a Cheatle slit or side-to-side join; E false: a longitudinal arteriotomy with patch is often used.

stem: Regarding surgical drains, which of the following statements are false?
option_A: A drain is best inserted through the end of a wound so as not to have another scar.
option_B: ‘When in doubt drain’ should be the motto.
option_C: Drains are mandatory after a thoracotomy.
option_D: Drains are usually used following exploration of the common bile duct.
option_E: During removal of a chest drain, the patient should be asked to do a Valsalva manoeuvre.
answer_text: A drain is best inserted through the end of a wound so as not to have another scar. | ‘When in doubt drain’ should be the motto.
explanation: Drains should exit via a separate incision and their use is now selective; post-thoracotomy drainage and Valsalva on removal are standard.

stem: Regarding the principles of diathermy, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: The two types of diathermy in use are monopolar and bipolar.
option_B: Monopolar diathermy is ideal for microsurgery and delicate procedures.
option_C: Bipolar diathermy is ideal for patients who have pacemakers.
option_D: Accidental burns are more common when monopolar diathermy is used.
option_E: Capacitance coupling can occur when a metal port is used in laparoscopic surgery.
answer_text: The two types of diathermy in use are monopolar and bipolar. | Bipolar diathermy is ideal for patients who have pacemakers. | Accidental burns are more common when monopolar diathermy is used. | Capacitance coupling can occur when a metal port is used in laparoscopic surgery.
explanation: B is false: bipolar (not monopolar) suits microsurgery and delicate work; bipolar is safer with pacemakers, monopolar causes more burns and capacitance coupling can occur.

stem: Which of the following statements about filariasis are true?
option_A: It is mainly caused by the parasites Brugia malayi and Brugia timori; in 10% of cases, Wuchereria bancrofti is the cause.
option_B: Infective larvae inoculated by a mosquito bite migrate to the lymphatics, where they mature into adult worms.
option_C: The adult worms cause lymphatic blockage leading to massive limb oedema; secondary bacterial infections may worsen lymphatic fibrosis and lead to elephantiasis.
option_D: Chyluria and chylous ascites seen in cancers blocking lymphatics are never seen in filariasis.
option_E: A mild form affecting the respiratory tract, presenting with dry cough, is called tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.
answer_text: Infective larvae inoculated by a mosquito bite migrate to the lymphatics, where they mature into adult worms. | The adult worms cause lymphatic blockage leading to massive limb oedema; secondary bacterial infections may worsen lymphatic fibrosis and lead to elephantiasis. | A mild form affecting the respiratory tract, presenting with dry cough, is called tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.
explanation: A false: Wuchereria bancrofti causes ~90% of cases and Brugia ~10%; D false: filariasis is a classic cause of chyluria and chylous ascites.
notes: Filariasis (0031, 0032) is not trauma; no infection chapter exists, so left here; editor may prefer to move both.

stem: Which of the following statements about filariasis are true?
option_A: Blood tests often reveal an elevated lymphocyte count.
option_B: Immature worms can be seen in nocturnal peripheral blood smears.
option_C: Medical treatment with diethylcarbamazine is effective even in cases of advanced elephantiasis.
option_D: Hydroceles are treated in the usual way, although excess skin may need surgical trimming.
option_E: Elephantiasis can be treated easily with operations to reduce limb size.
answer_text: Immature worms can be seen in nocturnal peripheral blood smears. | Hydroceles are treated in the usual way, although excess skin may need surgical trimming.
explanation: A false: blood shows eosinophilia; C false: diethylcarbamazine kills microfilariae but cannot reverse established elephantiasis; E false: limb-reduction surgery is difficult.

stem: A 19-year-old man is brought into the emergency department following a gunshot wound to the abdomen. Despite resuscitation he remains haemodynamically unstable. The decision is made to take him to theatre for exploration. Which of the following surgical incisions would be most appropriate?
explanation: A midline laparotomy is rapid, provides excellent access, and is easily extended for trauma exploration.

stem: A 33-year-old man is brought into the emergency department following an assault with a baseball bat. He has bruising over the abdomen and right loin and complains of abdominal pain. On examination, his chest is clear with good air entry but his abdomen is rigid. On arrival, his heart rate is 140/min and blood pressure 90/60 mmHg. He is given O-negative blood in the resuscitation room but his observations remain unchanged. What would be the next step in his management?
explanation: Haemodynamic instability with suspected intra-abdominal bleed necessitates urgent surgical exploration.

stem: A 45-year-old man in an automobile crash is hypotensive (BP 80/40), tachycardic, with a distended abdomen, and shows no response to 2 L of saline. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
option_D: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST)
explanation: A hypotensive non-responder with a distended abdomen after blunt trauma has intra-abdominal haemorrhage and needs immediate laparotomy; CT is only for stable patients.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department after sustaining a single gunshot wound to the right chest. He is awake and alert and complaining of significant abdominal pain and chest pain. He has a pulse of 110, blood pressure (BP) of 90/60, respirations of 24. On examination, his breath sounds are decreased on the right. His chest is dull to percussion on the right. His abdomen is slightly distended and diffusely tender. His pulse oximeter shows 88% on 6 L oxygen by face mask. A right chest drain is inserted and he responds to resuscitation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: A gunshot wound to the lower chest with abdominal distension and tenderness implies transdiaphragmatic injury and mandates laparotomy once the haemothorax is drained.

stem: A 17-year-old teenager who suffers a direct blow to the upper abdomen and develops progressive bilious emesis 48 hours later is most likely to have?
explanation: Delayed bilious vomiting after trauma is characteristic of a duodenal hematoma.

stem: Which is the treatment of choice for a post-traumatic duodenal haematoma causing obstruction?
explanation: Most duodenal haematomas resolve within 2–3 weeks with NG decompression and parenteral nutrition; surgery only if obstruction persists or perforation is suspected.

stem: A 26-year-old man with a stab wound to the fifth left intercostal space has tachycardia, hypotension, midline trachea, distant heart sounds, and equal breath sounds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A precordial stab wound with hypotension, distant heart sounds, midline trachea and equal breath sounds is tamponade; tension pneumothorax or haemothorax alters breath sounds.

stem: A 26-year-old man with a stab wound to the left fifth intercostal space is tachycardic and hypotensive with distant heart sounds, a midline trachea and equal breath sounds. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
option_A: insertion of a left chest tube
option_D: rapid infusion of an IV fluid bolus
explanation: Pericardiocentesis relieves tamponade as a temporising measure; definitive repair is by sternotomy or thoracotomy in theatre. ED thoracotomy is for traumatic arrest.

stem: A 30-year-old driver sustained an abdominal trauma after a road traffic accident. He was transferred to the emergency department in a haemodynamically unstable state. He was resuscitated with an intravenous fluid and a blood transfusion, after which vital signs became normal. An abdominal CT scan revealed a capsular laceration of 6 cm in depth in the liver. Which of the following grades of liver injury does this patient suffer from?
explanation: AAST grade III liver injury is a parenchymal laceration >3 cm deep (or subcapsular haematoma >50% of surface); grade II is 1–3 cm deep.
topics: Liver injury; Abdominal trauma; Blood transfusion

stem: A 35-year-old man is involved in a motor vehicle collision in which he was thrown against the steering column, sustaining blunt trauma to his left upper abdomen. On arrival at the emergency department he complains of abdominal pain but is haemodynamically stable. CT shows a splenic tear with a small intra-abdominal haematoma; the tear extends through the splenic capsule but not to the hilum. Which one of the following treatment options is least likely to be indicated at this time?
option_B: Serial haemoglobin measurement and abdominal examination.
explanation: A haemodynamically stable patient with a non-hilar splenic laceration is managed non-operatively (HDU monitoring, cross-match, serial examination/imaging); laparotomy is for instability or peritonitis.

stem: A teenage boy falls from his bicycle and is run over by a truck. On arrival in the emergency room (ER), he is awake and alert and appears frightened but in no distress. The chest radiograph suggests an air-fluid level in the left lower lung field and the nasogastric tube seems to coil upward into the left chest. Which of the following is the next best step in his management?
option_A: Placement of a left chest tube
explanation: An NG tube coiling into the left chest after blunt trauma means acute diaphragmatic rupture; repair via laparotomy, which also allows assessment of associated abdominal injuries.

stem: A 10-year-old boy was the backseat belted passenger in a high-speed motor vehicle collision. On presentation to the ER, he is awake and alert. His heart rate is 110 beats/minute. He is complaining of abdominal pain and has an ecchymosis on his anterior abdominal wall where the seatbelt was located. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrates free fluid in the absence of solid organ injury. Which of the following is the next best step in his management?
explanation: A seatbelt sign with free fluid but no solid-organ injury on CT suggests hollow viscus or mesenteric injury; diagnostic laparoscopy (or laparotomy) is indicated.

stem: A 36-year-old man who was hit by a car presents to the ER complaining of abdominal pain. His vital signs are HR 92, BP 127/65, and RR 16. On examination, he has tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant. An ultrasound examination is performed and reveals fluid between the liver and the kidney in Morison’s pouch. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in his management?
explanation: A haemodynamically stable patient with a positive FAST should have CT of the abdomen and pelvis to define the injury; laparotomy is for instability or peritonitis.

stem: A 25-year-old woman arrives in the ER following an automobile accident. Her heart rate is 125 beats/minute, blood pressure is 140/90, respirations are 40 breaths/minute, pulse oximetry is 94% on 4 L/min via nasal cannula, and temperature is 99°F. Breath sounds are markedly diminished on the right side. Which of the following is the best first step in the management of this patient?
option_B: Draw arterial blood for blood-gas determination
explanation: Severe respiratory distress with markedly reduced breath sounds on one side after trauma needs immediate pleural decompression (then chest drain) before any imaging.

stem: A 17-year-old adolescent boy is stabbed in the left seventh intercostal space, midaxillary line. He presents to the ER with a heart rate of 86 beats/ minute, blood pressure of 125/74 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation of 98%. Breath sounds are equal bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in his workup?
explanation: A stable patient with a stab wound to the left lower chest (thoracoabdominal zone) needs diagnostic laparoscopy to exclude a diaphragmatic injury, which CT may miss.

stem: An 18-year-old man sustains a right-sided neck laceration after an assault. Which of the following is a relative, rather than an absolute, indication for neck exploration?
explanation: Expanding haematoma, dysphagia, dysphonia and haemoptysis signal major vascular or aerodigestive injury and mandate exploration; pneumothorax needs a chest drain and is only relative.

stem: Following blunt abdominal trauma, a 12-year-old girl develops upper abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. An upper gastrointestinal series reveals a total obstruction of the duodenum with a coiled spring appearance in the second and third portions. In the absence of other suspected injuries, which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?
explanation: Coiled-spring duodenal obstruction after blunt trauma is an intramural duodenal haematoma: manage non-operatively with NG decompression and parenteral nutrition.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He has weakness of his left arm and leg. His head CT is negative for intracranial hemorrhage and a cervical spine CT is negative for fracture. Face CT shows a mandibular fracture. What is the most appropriate next test in his evaluation?
explanation: Lateralising neurology with a normal head CT and a high-risk mechanism (mandibular fracture) suggests blunt cerebrovascular injury; CT angiography of the neck is the screening test.

stem: An 18-year-old man was assaulted and sustained significant head and facial trauma. Which of the following is the most common initial manifestation of increased intracranial pressure?
explanation: A falling level of consciousness (GCS) is the earliest sign of rising ICP; pupillary dilatation, hemiparesis and the Cushing response are late signs.

stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the ER for a severe head injury after a fall. He was intubated in the field for his decreased level of consciousness. He is tachycardic and hypotensive. On examination, he is noted to have an obvious skull fracture and his right pupil is dilated. Which of the following is the most appropriate method for initially reducing his intracranial pressure?
option_A: Elevation of the head of the bed
explanation: In a hypotensive patient mannitol and head-up tilt worsen hypotension, so brief hyperventilation (PaCO₂ ~4–4.5 kPa) is the initial temporising measure.

stem: A 31-year-old man is brought to the ER following an automobile accident in which his chest struck the steering wheel. His vital signs are heart rate of 78 beats/minute, blood pressure of 129/65, respirations of 14 breaths/minute, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Examination reveals no evidence of respiratory distress, but the patient exhibits multiple right-sided palpable rib fractures. A right-sided chest wall segment appears to move inward rather than outward during inspiration and outward rather than inward during expiration. Chest x-ray shows no evidence of pneumothorax or hemothorax. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management of this patient?
explanation: Flail chest without respiratory compromise is managed with good analgesia (e.g. epidural or regional block) and physiotherapy; ventilation only if respiratory failure develops.

stem: A 23-year-old, previously healthy man presents to the ER after sustaining a single gunshot wound to the right chest. The entrance wound is 3 cm inferior to the nipple and the exit wound is just below the scapula. A chest tube is placed that drains 400 mL of blood and continues to drain 50 to 75 mL/h during the initial resuscitation. His blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg after 1 U packed red blood cells and 1 U fresh frozen plasma. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. Chest x-ray reveals a reexpanded lung and no free air under the diaphragm. Which of the following is the best next step in his management?
explanation: A gunshot wound below the nipple line may cross the diaphragm and needs laparotomy; thoracotomy is reserved for massive or persistent chest drain output.

stem: A patient is brought to the ER after a motor vehicle accident. He is unconscious and has a deep scalp laceration and one dilated pupil. His heart rate is 120 beats/minute, blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg, and respiratory rate is 35 breaths/minute. Despite initiation of massive transfusion protocol after 1 L normal saline via two large-bore IVs, the patient’s vital signs do not change significantly. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the workup of his hypotension?
option_D: CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
option_E: Focused assessment with sonography in trauma (FAST)
answer_text: Focused assessment with sonography in trauma (FAST)
explanation: Hypotension after trauma is haemorrhage until proven otherwise, not head injury; FAST rapidly identifies abdominal bleeding in the unstable patient.
topics: Abdominal trauma; Head injury; Blood transfusion

stem: A 25-year-old man is involved in a gang shoot-out and sustains multiple abdominal gunshot wounds. At laparotomy, he has a liver laceration requiring packing and multiple small-bowel and colon injuries that are resected. The patient has a persistent coagulopathy despite ongoing transfusions. The anesthesiologist notes that the patient’s temperature is 33.5°C (92.3°F). Intra-operative ABG: pH 7.19, P_CO2 42, P_O2 80, and lactate of 9 mmol/L. In addition to rewarming, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
explanation: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy form the lethal triad; correct with rewarming and balanced blood product transfusion (damage-control resuscitation), not bicarbonate.
topics: Blood transfusion; Acid–base disorders; Liver injury

stem: A 27-year-old man presents to the ER after a high-speed motor vehicle collision with chest pain and marked respiratory distress. On physical examination, he is hypotensive with distended neck veins and absence of breath sounds in the left chest. Which of the following is the proper initial treatment?
explanation: Hypotension, distended neck veins and absent unilateral breath sounds are tension pneumothorax: immediate needle decompression (4th/5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line), then chest drain.

stem: A 22-year-old woman who is 21-weeks pregnant presents after a high-speed motor vehicle collision complaining of abdominal pain and right leg pain. She has an obvious deformity of her right femur. Her heart rate is 125 beats/minute and blood pressure is 118/52 mm Hg. FAST exam shows fluid in the pelvis. Which of the following is the best next step in her management?
option_C: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
option_D: MRI of the abdomen and pelvis
answer_text: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
explanation: A normotensive pregnant patient with a positive FAST needs CT abdomen/pelvis; maternal stabilisation and diagnosis take priority over fetal radiation risk.

stem: A 56-year-old woman sustains blunt abdominal trauma from an assault. Her blood pressure is 107/56 mm Hg and her pulse is 92. She complains of abdominal pain. She undergoes CT scanning of the abdomen and pelvis, which demonstrates a splenic injury without evidence of extravasation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
explanation: A haemodynamically stable patient with splenic injury and no contrast extravasation is managed non-operatively with observation; angioembolisation if there is a blush.

stem: A 22-year-old man undergoes an exploratory laparotomy after a gunshot wound to the abdomen. The patient has multiple injuries, including a significant liver laceration, multiple small-bowel and colon injuries, and an injury to the infrahepatic vena cava. The patient receives 35 U of packed RBCs, 15 L of crystalloid, 12 U of fresh frozen plasma (FFP), and 12 packs of platelets. The patient’s abdomen is packed closed and he is taken to the intensive care unit for further resuscitation. Which of the following warrants a decompressive laparotomy?
explanation: Abdominal compartment syndrome raises peak airway pressure and lowers cardiac and urine output; with bladder pressure >20–25 mmHg it warrants decompressive laparotomy.
topics: Compartment syndrome; Liver injury; Fluid therapy

stem: A 10-year-old girl is the unrestrained backseat passenger in a high-speed motor vehicle collision. She is intubated in the field for unresponsiveness and on presentation to the ER, her heart rate is 160 beats/minute, and her blood pressure is 60/35 mm Hg. She weighs 30 kg. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for her initial fluid resuscitation?
explanation: ATLS: the initial bolus for a hypotensive child is 20 mL/kg warmed isotonic crystalloid (600 mL for 30 kg); give 10 mL/kg packed red cells if there is no response.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents to the ER after falling 10 ft from a ladder. Examination reveals stable vital signs, no evidence of respiratory distress, and multiple right-sided rib fractures. Chest x-ray shows a hemothorax on the right side and a right tube thoracostomy is performed in the ER. Approximately 700 mL of blood is immediately drained with placement of the thoracostomy tube. Over the next 4 hours he continues to drain 300 mL/h after the original evacuation. His coagulation profile is normal. Which of the following is the definitive treatment for this patient?
explanation: Initial drainage ≥1500 mL or ongoing loss of >200 mL/h for 2–4 hours (here 300 mL/h) indicates thoracotomy to control the bleeding.

stem: Which of the following clinical triads is indicative of cardiac tamponade and includes muffled heart tones, jugular venous distention, and hypotension?
explanation: Beck’s triad is a classic presentation of cardiac tamponade, consisting of muffled heart tones, jugular venous distention, and hypotension.

stem: According to Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) guidelines, in the context of a traumatic hemothorax, thoracotomy is indicated if the initial output from chest tube insertion reaches or exceeds what volume?
explanation: Per ATLS, an immediate thoracotomy is warranted if the initial chest tube output is ≥1500 mL, indicating massive hemothorax.

stem: What are the anatomical landmarks used to define the three zones of the neck used in trauma assessment?
option_A: Zone I is below the clavicles, zone II is between the clavicles and cricoid, and zone III is above the cricoid
option_B: Zone I is from the base of the skull to the cricoid cartilage, zone II is below the cricoid to the clavicle, zone III is the thoracic inlet
option_C: Zone I is inferior to the cricoid cartilage, zone II is between the cricoid cartilage and the angle of the mandible, and zone III is between the angle of the mandible and the skull
option_D: Zone I includes the thoracic outlet, zone II is the mid-neck, zone III is the cranial vault
option_E: Zone I is from the thoracic inlet to the mandible, zone II is from mandible to skull base, zone III is the brainstem region
answer_text: Zone I is inferior to the cricoid cartilage, zone II is between the cricoid cartilage and the angle of the mandible, and zone III is between the angle of the mandible and the skull
explanation: Zone I: clavicles/sternal notch to cricoid; zone II: cricoid to angle of the mandible; zone III: angle of the mandible to the skull base.

stem: In the context of retroperitoneal hemorrhage, what are the anatomical zones used to categorize the bleeding areas?
option_A: Zone I includes pelvis, Zone II includes kidneys laterally, Zone III includes upper abdominal structures
option_B: Zone I includes kidneys laterally, Zone II includes pelvis, Zone III includes diaphragmatic structures
option_C: Zone I includes diaphragm to aortic bifurcation, Zone II includes kidneys laterally to paracolic gutters, Zone III includes the pelvis
option_D: Zone I includes the pelvis and iliac arteries, Zone II includes the upper mesentery, Zone III includes lower retroperitoneum
option_E: Zone I includes liver and pancreas, Zone II includes kidneys and adrenals, Zone III includes ureters
answer_text: Zone I includes diaphragm to aortic bifurcation, Zone II includes kidneys laterally to paracolic gutters, Zone III includes the pelvis
explanation: The zones of retroperitoneal hemorrhage are: Zone I from diaphragm to aortic bifurcation, Zone II includes kidneys laterally, Zone III includes the pelvis.

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis in a trauma patient presenting with a liver injury, jaundice, and gastrointestinal bleeding?
explanation: Hemobilia refers to bleeding into the biliary tree, often seen in trauma involving the liver. It classically presents with the triad of right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and gastrointestinal bleeding.

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding diagnostic peritoneal lavage is not true?
option_A: A positive test would follow injury to spleen, liver, pancreas or intestine
option_B: It is more sensitive than computed tomography and focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) scanning
option_C: It is the technique of choice when attempting to confirm the hollow viscus injury
option_D: Urinary catheterization and nasogastric tube insertion is required prior to diagnostic peritoneal lavage
option_E: Diagnostic peritoneal lavage is contraindicated in the presence of an indication for explorative laparotomy
answer_text: A positive test would follow injury to spleen, liver, pancreas or intestine
explanation: DPL misses retroperitoneal injuries (pancreas, duodenum, kidney), so a pancreatic injury may give a negative lavage; it is very sensitive for intraperitoneal blood.

stem: Which of the following is not an independent indication for laparotomy following trauma?
option_E: Blunt abdominal trauma with free intraperitoneal air on erect chest radiograph
explanation: Not every stab wound penetrates the peritoneum, so exploratory laparotomy is not automatically indicated.

stem: The following factors detract from the diagnostic sensitivity of focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) scanning, except:
option_B: A patient with high body mass index
explanation: A large volume of free fluid actually enhances the sensitivity of FAST scanning.

stem: As well as measuring oxygen saturation, a pulse oximeter also gives useful information regarding what other factor in the initial assessment of the traumatised patient?
explanation: The plethysmographic trace and a reliable signal depend on pulsatile flow, so a poor trace indicates poor peripheral perfusion; oximetry gives no CO2 or acid–base information.

stem: A 42-year-old construction worker is admitted following a crush injury. The patient is in great distress, complaining of chest pain and working hard to breathe, with paradoxical movement of the chest wall. Arterial blood gases show pO2 7.5 kPa and pCO2 8.2 kPa. A chest radiograph shows multiple rib fractures. The life-saving intervention is
option_E: Adequate analgesia to allow effective respiration
explanation: Flail chest with type 2 respiratory failure (hypoxia and hypercapnia) needs intubation and positive-pressure ventilation; oxygen and analgesia alone are insufficient.

stem: A male patient is admitted following a fall from height. On arrival his Glasgow Coma Scale score is 5/15 and he is therefore intubated. During primary resuscitation a chest film is taken which shows a widened mediastinum and right-sided deviation of the trachea. The diagnosis is
explanation: A widened mediastinum with tracheal deviation is highly suggestive of an aortic injury.

stem: A 20-year-old woman was resuscitated in the emergency department and required the insertion of a chest drain. The drain was removed 2 days later before she was discharged. She re-presents 10 days later complaining of chest pain associated with high fever and sweats. An empyema is suspected and a chest radiograph confirms a collection. The most appropriate next course of action is
option_D: Computed tomography scan of the thorax
explanation: Ultrasound characterises the collection (fluid, loculation, septation) and guides aspiration and chest-drain placement; blind drain insertion is avoided.

stem: A sedated, intubated patient in the ICU needs a nasogastric tube. What is the most dangerous complication of insertion?
explanation: In a sedated, intubated patient the tube can pass into the airway unnoticed (no cough reflex); feeding into the lung is the danger.

stem: A sedated, intubated patient in the ICU needs a nasogastric tube. After NG insertion and feeding he becomes hypotensive and desaturates with secretions around the mouth and tube. What happened?
option_A: Aspiration of feed into the lungs
answer_text: Aspiration of feed into the lungs
explanation: This is aspiration: stop feeds and suction. Prevent it by checking aspirate pH ≤ 5.5 or X-ray before feeding and nursing 30–45° head-up.

stem: A 72-year-old sedated, ventilated ICU patient needs an NG tube. What are the possible complications and how are they minimised?
explanation: Misplacement into the airway is the major danger; confirm placement (pH ≤ 5.5 or X-ray) before use.

stem: A 72-year-old sedated, ventilated ICU patient needs an NG tube. After feeding he desaturates with secretions. What happened and what is the immediate management?
option_A: Aspiration of feed into the lungs
answer_text: Aspiration of feed into the lungs
explanation: Aspiration: stop feeds, suction and oxygen; confirm tube position before feeding.

stem: Which one of the following statements about homeostasis is false?
option_A: It is defined as a stable state of the normal body.
option_B: The central nervous system, heart, lungs, kidneys and spleen are the essential organs that maintain normal homeostasis.
option_C: Elective surgery should cause little disturbance to homeostasis.
option_D: Emergency surgery should cause little disturbance to homeostasis.
option_E: Return to normal homeostasis after an insult (operation, injury, infection) would depend upon the presence of comorbid conditions.
answer_text: Emergency surgery should cause little disturbance to homeostasis.
explanation: Emergency surgery markedly disrupts homeostasis due to unprepared physiology and severe pathology, unlike elective procedures.

stem: Neuroendocrine pathways of the stress response consist of the following except:
explanation: The thyroid is not directly involved; spinal cord, thalamus, hypothalamus and pituitary mediate the response.
topics: Neuroendocrine tumour; Metabolic response to injury

stem: Changes in body metabolism that occur in response to trauma are the following except:
explanation: Trauma induces lipolysis, gluconeogenesis, protein breakdown and hypermetabolism—not hypoglycaemia.

stem: Which of the following statements about mediators are true?
option_A: They consist of neural, endocrine and inflammatory.
option_B: Every endocrine gland plays a part.
option_C: They play an important role in the flow phase.
option_D: These mediators are released over several days.
option_E: They play an important role in the recovery process.
answer_text: They consist of neural, endocrine and inflammatory. | Every endocrine gland plays a part. | They play an important role in the flow phase. | They play an important role in the recovery process.
explanation: Mediators are rapidly released and jointly modulate the stress response; they are not released over several days.

stem: Which of the following statements are true of optimal perioperative care?
option_A: Surgery should be carried out by the use of adequate large incisions to give good exposure.
option_D: Avoid ongoing insults and secondary trauma.
option_E: Maintain good fluid load with several litres of normal saline.
answer_text: Adequate pain relief is essential. | Early mobilisation. | Avoid ongoing insults and secondary trauma.
explanation: Effective pain control, early mobilisation and prevention of secondary trauma are key; large incisions and excess fluids are not recommended.

stem: The following statements are true regarding Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) programmes except:
option_A: It optimises rehabilitation following major surgery.
option_C: Patient engagement is an integral part.
option_D: It is only used in colorectal surgery.
option_E: Blocking afferent painful stimuli is important in reducing stress response.
answer_text: It is only used in colorectal surgery.
explanation: ERAS programmes are now applied across many specialties, not solely in colorectal surgery.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes controlled on oral hypoglycaemic agents is to undergo a major abdominal operation. What is the best way to control her blood glucose perioperatively?
option_A: Increase the dose of her oral hypoglycaemic agents
option_B: Continue oral agents on the morning of surgery and check glucose after the operation
option_D: Switch to intermittent subcutaneous sliding-scale insulin
option_E: Stop oral agents and give an IV infusion of soluble insulin with glucose and potassium (KCl)
answer_text: Stop oral agents and give an IV infusion of soluble insulin with glucose and potassium (KCl)
explanation: For major surgery oral agents are stopped and a variable-rate IV soluble insulin infusion with glucose and potassium (GKI) is given, adjusted to hourly capillary glucose.

stem: Select the most likely diagnosis for this patient with polyuria: A 25-year-old man with severe head injury and basal skull fracture. Urine osmolality 150 mOsm/L, serum osmolality 350 mOsm/L, no change after fluid restriction, but urine osmolality rises to 300 mOsm/L after IV vasopressin.
explanation: Head trauma damaging posterior pituitary; responds to vasopressin.

stem: A 70-year-old man in the ICU with multiple renal insults and amphotericin therapy develops polyuria; no change with vasopressin. Serum osmolality is high, urine remains dilute. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Acquired from nephrotoxic injury; unresponsive to ADH.

stem: A 25-year-old woman with severe head injury, pulmonary contusion, and pelvic fracture is unresponsive in the ICU. Which of the following is the best initial approach to her nutritional needs?
option_A: insertion of a subclavian venous catheter and initiation of central IV hyperalimentation
option_B: wait for extubation and improvement of neurologic status, allowing institution of oral intake
option_C: early institution of NG or nasojejunal tube feeding with an elemental formulation
option_D: wait for resolution of the associated ileus, followed by delayed hypercaloric regimen
answer_text: early institution of NG or nasojejunal tube feeding with an elemental formulation
explanation: Early enteral feeding aids GI mucosal integrity and is preferable to parenteral nutrition.

stem: A 65-year-old diabetic man presents with a penetrating buttock wound from a wooden stump. The wound shows violaceous discoloration, bullae, crepitus, and grayish drainage. What is the optimal treatment?
option_A: high-dose IV penicillin G and broad-spectrum antibiotics
option_B: high-dose IV penicillin G, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and local wound care with unroofing of bullae and culture
option_C: high-dose IV penicillin G, broad-spectrum antibiotics, with surgical debridement only if no improvement
option_E: high-dose IV penicillin G, broad-spectrum antibiotics, radical surgical debridement, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy
answer_text: high-dose IV penicillin G, broad-spectrum antibiotics, radical surgical debridement, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy
explanation: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection requires aggressive surgical debridement plus antibiotics and adjunctive hyperbaric oxygen.

stem: A 45-year-old woman involved in a motor vehicle crash with prolonged parenteral nutrition develops diarrhea, mental depression, alopecia, and perioral/periorbital dermatitis. Which trace element supplementation is most likely to reverse these complications?
explanation: Zinc deficiency from prolonged PN causes these symptoms.

stem: A 65-year-old hypertensive man scheduled for TURP shows a serum potassium of 2.7 mmol/L. Which ECG change is NOT characteristic of hypokalaemia?
explanation: Left bundle branch block is not a typical ECG finding in hypokalaemia.

stem: A 28-year-old man is brought after a road traffic accident with a deep right-thigh laceration and pulsatile bleeding. He is pale and anxious; BP 85/60 mmHg, HR 130/min. What type of bleeding is this?
option_A: Arterial: bright red and spurting in time with the pulse
answer_text: Arterial: bright red and spurting in time with the pulse
explanation: Arterial bleeding is bright red and pulsatile; venous bleeding is dark and flows steadily. Control with direct pressure or a tourniquet.

stem: A 28-year-old man is brought after a road traffic accident with a deep right-thigh laceration and pulsatile bleeding. He is pale and anxious; BP 85/60 mmHg, HR 130/min. What is the maximum safe tourniquet time?
option_E: No limit if the limb is cooled
explanation: Limit tourniquet time to about 2 h (record it); complications are nerve palsy, ischaemia, compartment syndrome and reperfusion injury.

stem: Which of the following statements are true in the pathophysiology of shock?
option_A: In shock, cells switch from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism.
option_B: The product of anaerobic respiration is carbon dioxide, resulting in respiratory acidosis.
option_C: Hypoxia and acidosis generate oxygen free radicals and cytokine release.
option_D: Renal ischaemia leads to decreased glomerular filtration (GFR), thus activating the renin-aldosterone-angiotensin system (RAAS).
option_E: Once shock has been treated and circulation restored, the physiological disturbances return to normal.
answer_text: In shock, cells switch from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism. | Hypoxia and acidosis generate oxygen free radicals and cytokine release. | Renal ischaemia leads to decreased glomerular filtration (GFR), thus activating the renin-aldosterone-angiotensin system (RAAS).
explanation: B is false: anaerobic metabolism produces lactate (metabolic acidosis); E is false: reperfusion injury and organ dysfunction may persist after circulation is restored.

stem: Regarding the severity of shock, which of the following statements are false?
option_A: In compensated shock, blood flow is maintained to the brain, lungs and kidneys.
option_B: Loss of 15% of circulating blood volume will overload the body’s compensatory mechanisms.
option_C: Capillary refill time is an accurate clinical parameter in all types of shock.
option_D: Hypotension is an early sign of shock.
option_E: Prolonged systemic ischaemia and reperfusion injury contribute to multi-organ failure.
answer_text: Loss of 15% of circulating blood volume will overload the body’s compensatory mechanisms. | Capillary refill time is an accurate clinical parameter in all types of shock. | Hypotension is an early sign of shock.
explanation: Up to 15% blood loss is compensated and neither capillary refill nor early hypotension are reliable indicators.

stem: Regarding resuscitation, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: In a patient who is shocked from a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm or a bleeding peptic ulcer, time should not be wasted in instituting high-volume fluid resuscitation.
option_B: In a patient with intestinal obstruction with hypovolaemic shock, time should be spent in optimising with adequate fluid resuscitation.
option_C: In hypovolaemia, inotropes must be started as soon as possible as first-line therapy.
option_D: The ideal fluid is colloid in hypovolaemia.
option_E: The shock status is best determined by an initial fluid challenge.
answer_text: In a patient who is shocked from a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm or a bleeding peptic ulcer, time should not be wasted in instituting high-volume fluid resuscitation. | In a patient with intestinal obstruction with hypovolaemic shock, time should be spent in optimising with adequate fluid resuscitation. | The shock status is best determined by an initial fluid challenge.
explanation: Bleeding (AAA, ulcer) needs haemorrhage control, not prolonged fluid loading; obstruction needs full resuscitation first. Inotropes are not first-line and crystalloid is preferred.
topics: Abdominal aortic aneurysm; Peptic ulcer; Fluid therapy

stem: Regarding monitoring in shock, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: CVP monitoring is a dynamic reflection on fluid challenge.
option_B: Measurement of cardiac output (CO) helps in distinguishing the type of shock.
option_C: Mixed venous oxygen saturation is an indicator of systemic perfusion.
option_D: Pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP) measurement should be instituted in all shocked patients in the ICU.
option_E: It is mandatory to perform Allen’s test prior to insertion of an arterial line.
answer_text: CVP monitoring is a dynamic reflection on fluid challenge. | Measurement of cardiac output (CO) helps in distinguishing the type of shock. | Mixed venous oxygen saturation is an indicator of systemic perfusion.
explanation: D false: PAWP catheters are not routine in shocked ICU patients; E false: Allen's test has poor predictive value and is not mandatory before radial arterial cannulation.

stem: Regarding haemorrhage, all of the following statements are true except:
option_A: Haemorrhage with hypovolaemic shock results in a state of coagulopathy.
option_B: Haemoglobin level is an accurate indicator of the degree of haemorrhage.
option_C: The acid-base disturbance is metabolic acidosis.
option_D: Permissive hypotension is a strategy to be followed until haemorrhage is controlled.
option_E: Haemorrhagic shock can be classified into three groups – mild, moderate and severe.
answer_text: Haemoglobin level is an accurate indicator of the degree of haemorrhage. | Haemorrhagic shock can be classified into three groups – mild, moderate and severe.
explanation: Acute blood loss does not immediately change haemoglobin and shock is classically divided into four classes.

stem: Regarding blood transfusion, which of the following statements are true?
option_A: Blood group ‘O’ is regarded as universal donor.
option_B: Blood group ‘AB’ is regarded as universal recipient.
option_C: The vast majority of the population is Rhesus negative.
option_D: In coagulopathy packed red blood cells should be transfused.
option_E: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) has a shelf life of 2 years.
answer_text: Blood group ‘O’ is regarded as universal donor. | Blood group ‘AB’ is regarded as universal recipient. | Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) has a shelf life of 2 years.
explanation: C false: about 85% of people are RhD positive; D false: coagulopathy needs FFP, platelets and cryoprecipitate, not red cells. FFP keeps about 2 years frozen.

stem: Regarding conscious sedation, which of the following statements is false?
option_A: Sedation has no significant dangers and can be used without restrictions.
option_B: All sedated patients require secure intravenous access.
option_C: Co-administration of opiates and benzodiazepines has a synergistic effect and opiates administered wherever possible before benzodiazepines.
option_D: Use of supplemental oxygen is essential in sedated patients.
option_E: All sedated patients require pulse oximetry to monitor oxygen saturations.
answer_text: Sedation has no significant dangers and can be used without restrictions.
explanation: Sedation is not without risk – it may cause hypoventilation and airway obstruction, so proper monitoring (IV access, oxygen, pulse oximetry) is essential.

stem: A 54-year-old woman is 2 days post an open appendicectomy for perforated appendicitis. She is tender in the lower abdomen, has a temperature of 38.9°C, blood pressure of 100/54 mmHg, pulse rate 95 beats/min, white cell count 21 x 10⁹/L, and CRP 154 mg/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Postoperative fever, high WCC/CRP, hypotension; consistent with sepsis.

stem: A 56-year-old woman is brought into the resuscitation room. Three days ago she suffered an insect bite to the abdomen which has now spread, causing redness across the whole of her abdomen. On examination, she is confused, with a temperature of 38.3°C, heart rate 106/min and blood pressure 100/56 mmHg. Which of the following is specific to the treatment of this type of shock?
explanation: Septic shock requires prompt antibiotic therapy in addition to supportive measures.

stem: A 45-year-old man has walked into the emergency department following his involvement in a road traffic collision. On arrival at the hospital he is anxious, but otherwise fine. Later, he suddenly becomes faint. He is taken into the resuscitation room where he is found to have a heart rate of 46/min and a blood pressure of 80/48 mmHg. Primary examination is unremarkable and the patient has warm peripheries. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: Sudden loss of sympathetic tone leads to hypotension with bradycardia and warm peripheries.

stem: A 56-year-old man is one day post appendicectomy and becomes acutely short of breath. He has just been given his first dose of cyclizine. On arrival, he is breathless with heart rate 122/min, blood pressure 86/48 mmHg, saturations 85% in air. Which of the following would you administer first?
explanation: Acute anaphylaxis is managed first with intramuscular adrenaline to relieve shock and bronchospasm.

stem: A 22-year-old man is brought in following a road traffic collision. He is suspected to have intra-abdominal injuries and there is bruising over his trunk. On arrival, he has a pulse rate of 140/min and his systolic blood pressure is 80 mmHg. Which of the following fluids would raise the patient’s blood pressure most rapidly?
explanation: Red cells stay intravascular and restore oxygen-carrying capacity, whereas only about a quarter of infused saline remains intravascular; dextrose spreads through all body water.

stem: A 30-year-old man with a pelvic fracture is hypotensive and tachycardic. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.24, PaCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3− 14 mmol/L and base deficit −10. What is the most appropriate management of his acid–base derangement?
option_A: Administration of sodium bicarbonate to correct the base deficit
option_B: Restoration of blood volume with aggressive IV fluid and blood resuscitation
option_E: No treatment; this patient has no acid–base abnormality
answer_text: Restoration of blood volume with aggressive IV fluid and blood resuscitation
explanation: Lactic (metabolic) acidosis from hypoperfusion is corrected by restoring circulating volume and perfusion; bicarbonate does not treat the cause and may worsen intracellular acidosis.

stem: A 70-year-old man admitted after AAA repair has low pulmonary wedge pressure, tachycardia, and low urine output. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation: A low wedge pressure with tachycardia and oliguria after AAA repair means hypovolaemia, so a crystalloid bolus is given; diuretics or vasodilators would worsen it.
topics: Fluid therapy; Abdominal aortic aneurysm; Hypovolaemic shock

stem: A 70-year-old man is given IV fluids for hypovolaemia after AAA repair. Several hours later his BP is 150/85 mmHg with distended neck veins and an elevated pulmonary wedge pressure, and urine output remains low. What is the next step?
explanation: Hypertension with high filling pressures and poor output after fluid loading responds to afterload reduction with nitroprusside, improving cardiac output and renal perfusion.

stem: A 39-year-old multiparous woman has a retained placenta 60 minutes after vaginal birth of a 3650‐g healthy boy. There was no episiotomy or lacerations. She now has profuse vaginal bleeding with BP 80/50 mmHg and pulse 120/min; her uterine fundus is firm. Which treatment is most appropriate?
explanation: She is in haemorrhagic shock, so blood volume is restored first, then the placenta is removed manually; with a firm fundus, uterotonics or packing for atony will not help.

stem: A 65-year-old diabetic male, postoperative day 3 after duodenal ulcer surgery, has a large amount of salmon colored fluid draining from his midline wound. What is the next appropriate step?
option_E: immediate exploration of wound in the operating room (OR)
answer_text: immediate exploration of wound in the operating room (OR)
explanation: Salmon-coloured (serosanguinous) wound discharge on day 3 heralds fascial dehiscence, so the wound is explored and the abdomen closed in theatre.

stem: A 65-year-old diabetic man develops spiking fever on the 6th day after laparotomy for duodenal ulcer, with incisional discomfort and a small amount of wound drainage. Appropriate evaluation and management should include which of the following?
option_A: blood, urine, and sputum cultures; chest x-ray and abdominal CT scan
option_B: discharging the patient on oral antibiotics
option_C: culture of the wound drainage, and initiation of IV antibiotics
option_D: opening the incision, culture of the wound drainage, and initiating local wound care
option_E: opening the incision, culture of the wound drainage, and initiating IV antibiotics
answer_text: opening the incision, culture of the wound drainage, and initiating local wound care
explanation: A superficial wound infection is treated by opening the incision, sending pus for culture and local wound care; antibiotics only if there is cellulitis or systemic sepsis.

stem: A 33-year-old woman is seen in the ER with severe rectal bleeding. She has a history of ulcerative colitis. Her blood pressure is 95/56 mm Hg and her pulse is 110. Her base deficit is –8 mEq/L. What percent of her blood volume has been lost?
explanation: Hypotension with tachycardia and a base deficit of −6 to −10 indicates ATLS class III haemorrhage, a 30–40% loss of blood volume.
topics: Hypovolaemic shock; Lower GI bleeding; Ulcerative colitis

stem: Following a 2-hour firefighting episode, a 36-year-old fireman begins complaining of a throbbing headache, nausea, dizziness, and visual disturbances. He is taken to the ER, where his carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) level is found to be 31%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in his treatment?
explanation: Give 100% oxygen via a tight-fitting mask at once (COHb half-life ~80 min vs ~5 h on air); hyperbaric oxygen is reserved for coma, seizures or severe cases.

stem: A 75-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus undergoes a right hemicolectomy for colon cancer. On the second postoperative day, he becomes hypotensive with depressed mental status and is immediately transferred to the intensive care unit. After intubation, an echocardiogram is performed which demonstrates a hypokinetic left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 15%. His central venous pressure is 18 mm Hg, and his hemoglobin is 10 g/dL. Which of the following is the most likely etiology for the patient’s acute decompensation?
option_E: Pulmonary embolism of the main pulmonary arterial trunk
explanation: Hypotension with a very low ejection fraction (15%) and high CVP in a patient with coronary disease is cardiogenic shock (pump failure, probably perioperative MI).

stem: A patient is admitted following a motorcycle accident. He has fractured his left femur, tibia, fibula and pelvis. His blood pressure is 70/35 mmHg, pulse 140 beats/min, respiratory rate 35 breaths/min and Glasgow Coma Scale score 9/15. You wish to resuscitate the patient. Which one of the following procedures may be contraindicated in such a patient?
explanation: A pelvic fracture may tear the urethra, so a urethral catheter is avoided until urethral injury is excluded (blood at meatus, retrograde urethrogram).

stem: A patient is admitted following an assault. On assessment, he has a stab wound to his chest. Clinically, he has a massive haemothorax and his Glasgow Coma Scale score is 4/15. Without further management, this patient will succumb to which cause of death first?
explanation: A very low GCS indicates an inability to protect the airway, making airway compromise the most immediate threat.

stem: Which of the following techniques does not provide a definitive airway?
explanation: A definitive airway is a cuffed tube in the trachea (oro/nasotracheal, surgical); a laryngeal mask sits above the larynx and does not protect against aspiration.

stem: A patient is admitted following a road traffic accident. He has sustained significant blunt injury to his head, chest and abdomen and has a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8/15. His saturations are poor at 89% on 15 L of oxygen via a non-rebreathing mask. You note bruising around both eyes and blood-stained fluid issuing from his left ear, which forms concentric rings when dripped on a white sheet. You wish to support his airway to improve oxygenation. The first choice of airway adjunct would be:
option_E: Positive pressure ventilation (continuous positive airway pressure)
explanation: Raccoon eyes and CSF otorrhoea suggest a basal skull fracture, so a nasopharyngeal airway is avoided; an oropharyngeal airway is used pending a definitive airway.

stem: A 35-year-old man is admitted after severing his arm on industrial machinery. His airway is patent and there is no identifiable hindrance to breathing. His pulse is 110 beats/min, blood pressure is 130/105 mmHg, and respiratory rate is 25 breaths/min. Which stage of shock is this patient in?
option_E: Impossible to say from given information
explanation: The vital signs indicate moderate blood loss corresponding to Class II shock.

stem: A 35-year-old butcher is admitted after inadvertently stabbing himself with a knife. His airway is patent and there is no identifiable hindrance to breathing. His pulse is 110 beats/min, BP 130/105 mmHg and respiratory rate 25 breaths/min. Assuming a body mass of 70 kg, what is the best estimate of the volume of blood lost?
option_E: Impossible to say from given information
explanation: Tachycardia, narrowed pulse pressure and RR 25 with normal systolic BP is class II shock (15–30% loss, 750–1500 mL in a 70 kg adult), i.e. about 1000 mL.

stem: A patient is admitted in haemorrhagic shock following a road traffic accident. A final year medical student has inserted a pink (20 G) cannula in the antecubital fossa. What rate of flow into the patient will this allow?
explanation: A pink (20 G) cannula typically allows a flow rate of about 55 mL/min.

stem: A homeless man is admitted unresponsive after being found by police on a park bench. He has no external signs of injury. An oesophageal temperature probe records his core body temperature to be 34 °C. Which of the following management options is not routinely indicated in this case?
explanation: At 34 °C (mild hypothermia) passive and active external rewarming with warmed IV fluids suffice; invasive core rewarming such as peritoneal lavage is for severe hypothermia.

stem: Which of the following defines morbid obesity?
option_B: BMI greater than 35 Kg/m² with comorbidity
answer_text: BMI greater than 35 Kg/m² with comorbidity | BMI greater than 40 Kg/m²
explanation: Morbid obesity is defined as a BMI ≥40 kg/m² or ≥35 kg/m² when significant comorbidities are present.

stem: Which of the following constitute the selection criteria for performing bariatric surgery as per international norms?
option_C: No alcoholism or major untreated psychiatric illness
option_D: Avoid if likely to get pregnant within 1 year
option_E: Acceptable operative risk on preoperative assessment
answer_text: Minimum of 5 years obesity | Failure of conservative treatment | No alcoholism or major untreated psychiatric illness | Acceptable operative risk on preoperative assessment
explanation: D is a counselling point (avoid pregnancy for 12–18 months after surgery), not a selection criterion; the others are standard international selection criteria.

stem: Preoperative nutritional screening of morbidly obese patients includes which of the following?
option_A: Vitamins A, D and E, parathyroid hormone
option_D: Ferritin, vitamin B12, folate and coagulation screen
option_E: Zinc, selenium, copper and C-reactive protein
answer_text: Vitamins A, D and E, parathyroid hormone | Magnesium, calcium and phosphate | Ferritin, vitamin B12, folate and coagulation screen | Zinc, selenium, copper and C-reactive protein
explanation: B is false: corticosteroid hormones are not part of nutritional screening; fat-soluble vitamins, PTH, minerals, iron studies, B12/folate and trace elements are checked.

stem: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass is which type of bariatric procedure?
explanation: The procedure creates a small gastric pouch and bypasses part of the small intestine, providing both restrictive and malabsorptive effects.

stem: Which of the following are specific complications of bariatric procedures?
option_A: Internal herniation in gastric bypass and bilio-pancreatic diversion (BPD)
option_B: Staple line or anastomotic leak in gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy and BPD
option_C: Pouch dilatation in gastric band, gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy
option_D: Erosion in BPD and sleeve gastrectomy
answer_text: Internal herniation in gastric bypass and bilio-pancreatic diversion (BPD) | Staple line or anastomotic leak in gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy and BPD | Pouch dilatation in gastric band, gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy | Band slippage in gastric banding
explanation: D is false: erosion complicates gastric banding, not BPD or sleeve gastrectomy; internal hernia, leaks, pouch/sleeve dilatation and band slippage are recognised.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with a BMI of 45 kg/m² has an HbA1c of 7% (53 mmol/mol) and a fasting blood glucose of 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L). What metabolic disorder does she have?
option_C: Insulin resistance with impaired glucose control (type 2 diabetes)
answer_text: Insulin resistance with impaired glucose control (type 2 diabetes)
explanation: HbA1c ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol) and fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) confirm type 2 diabetes, driven by obesity-related insulin resistance.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with a BMI of 45 kg/m² has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7%) despite lifestyle measures. What is the most appropriate surgical management of her metabolic disorder?
explanation: BMI ≥40 (or ≥35 with comorbidity such as diabetes) qualifies for bariatric/metabolic surgery, which often induces remission of type 2 diabetes.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a BMI of 37 kg/m² has a fasting blood glucose of 6.5 mmol/L (117 mg/dL) and an HbA1c of 6.2% (44 mmol/mol) on two occasions, despite 6 months of diet and exercise. Does he need any treatment for his blood sugar?
option_A: No, because his fasting blood sugar is normal
option_B: Yes, he should start insulin immediately
option_C: No, because lifestyle modification is sufficient
option_D: Yes, after lifestyle modifications, the patient should start Metformin
answer_text: Yes, after lifestyle modifications, the patient should start Metformin
explanation: He has prediabetes (non-diabetic hyperglycaemia); if intensive lifestyle change fails, metformin reduces progression to diabetes, especially when BMI ≥35.

stem: A 45-year-old obese man has fasting triglycerides of 600 mg/dL (6.8 mmol/L), LDL cholesterol 95 mg/dL (2.5 mmol/L) and HDL 38 mg/dL, despite 3 months of diet and exercise. Does he need any treatment for his lipid profile?
option_B: Yes, he should be started on statins
option_D: Yes, he should be started on niacin
option_E: Yes, due to hypertriglyceridemia, fibrates should be started if lifestyle modifications are not effective
answer_text: Yes, due to hypertriglyceridemia, fibrates should be started if lifestyle modifications are not effective
explanation: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (>500 mg/dL) with normal LDL risks pancreatitis and is treated with a fibrate when lifestyle measures fail; statins mainly lower LDL.
